t.component around mission beach@-17.9,146:
The cassowary crossing signs around Mission Beach are not a joke, and the bird they warn you about is not a small one. This stretch of coast between Tully and Innisfail is one of the last strongholds of the southern cassowary, a dinosaur-looking creature with a blue head and a horned casque, and the rainforest that runs right down to the sand here is part of the Wet Tropics of Queensland World Heritage area. Few places on earth put ancient forest and a palm-fringed beach this close together.

Mission Beach is really a string of small settlements, Wongaling Beach, South Mission, Bingil Bay and Mission Beach itself, strung along about fourteen kilometres of shore, with Dunk Island lying just offshore. The name goes back to an Aboriginal mission established in the area in the early twentieth century and destroyed by a cyclone in 1918. Cyclones are part of the local story; Larry in 2006 and Yasi in 2011 both hit hard, and you can still read their marks in the forest canopy.

The roads in from the Bruce Highway, through El Arish or from Tully, are lovely tropical rides: narrow, winding through cane fields and dense rainforest, often wet, sometimes slick with fallen leaves and fruit. Speed limits are low for good reason, so take the bends gently and look well ahead for those birds. Traffic is mostly local, with backpacker vans and the odd tour bus in the dry season.

Wongaling Beach has a fuel station and supermarket, and there are cafés and places to eat spread along the coast. Tully, about eleven kilometres inland, is the working town of the district, surrounded by sugar cane and bananas, and it likes to remind visitors that it is among the wettest towns in Australia, with a giant golden gumboot to prove it.

Come in the dry season, roughly May to October, when the humidity eases and the sky clears. In the wet, expect warm downpours that arrive suddenly and leave everything steaming. Swimming in the sea is a seasonal question too: from late spring box jellyfish make stinger suits or netted areas wise. Watch the light go gold over Dunk Island with a cold drink in your hand, and you will understand why people come here and forget to leave.
t.component around hugh nelson range@-17.4:
The Atherton Tableland is the bit of tropical Queensland that feels like it has wandered in from somewhere cooler. At seven or eight hundred metres above the sea, the plateau behind Cairns has red volcanic soil, dairy pastures, crater lakes and patches of rainforest that cling to the ridges. The forested country around these coordinates sits in the southern part of the Tablelands between Atherton, Malanda and Ravenshoe, part of the Wet Tropics World Heritage area, where higher ground and steady rain keep the forest dense and green.

The riding up here is some of the best in north Queensland. The Kennedy Highway runs south from Atherton toward Ravenshoe through rolling farmland and timbered hills, while the back roads toward Malanda and Millaa Millaa wind between pastures and rainforest with lovely flowing corners. Surfaces vary from smooth to patched, and in the wet season you will meet mud washed across the road from farm tracks. Mist often hangs in the valleys early in the morning and burns off by mid-morning, leaving a clear, cool day that is a gift after the steamy coast.

Atherton, about eighteen kilometres away, is the main town with fuel, supermarkets and a decent spread of cafés. Malanda is smaller and known for its dairy industry and its waterfall pool, which is a popular cool-off spot. Ravenshoe, to the south, likes to claim the highest pub in Queensland and is a fine place for a cold drink and a look at the old timber country around it.

This is tree-kangaroo country. Lumholtz's tree kangaroos live in the rainforest remnants of the Tablelands, and if you are very lucky and very patient you may see one hunched in a tree near a roadside reserve. The volcanic history is everywhere: crater lakes like Eacham and Barrine sit in old eruption craters to the north-east, and the soil that feeds all those cows came out of the ground as ash.

Go between May and September for the clearest weather, and pack a warm layer, since mornings up here can be genuinely chilly. In the wet, rain arrives in long soaking sessions. Either way, it is a place that reminds you how varied Australia can be in a single morning's ride.
t.component around moresby range@-17.6,146:
Innisfail had to rebuild itself after a cyclone flattened much of the town in 1918, and it chose to do so in the latest style. As a result, this sugar town on the Johnstone River has one of the finest collections of Art Deco buildings in Australia, with colourful façades, geometric patterns and elegant shopfronts lining the main streets. Just to the east, the Moresby Range runs down to the coast in a band of steep, rainforest-covered hills, part of the Wet Tropics of Queensland World Heritage area, one of the oldest continuously surviving tropical rainforests on earth.

The range shelters small bays and beaches, including Etty Bay, a quiet cove where cassowaries are known to wander out of the forest onto the sand, and Flying Fish Point, at the mouth of the river, with its fishing boats and views over the sea. The rainforest is dense, humid and full of life, with tree ferns, palms, vines and the calls of birds you will rarely see.

Inland, Paronella Park at Mena Creek is a striking oddity: a Spanish-style castle and gardens built by a Catalan immigrant, José Paronella, in the 1930s, now partly overgrown by the rainforest, with a waterfall, tunnels and moss-covered stairways. It is one of the most unusual attractions in north Queensland.

The riding around Innisfail is a mix of the busy Bruce Highway, which runs north and south through cane fields, and quieter roads into the hills and along the coast, where the corners come thick and the surfaces can be damp, leafy and slippery. Traffic includes cane trains crossing the road during the crushing season, roughly June to November, so watch for the warning lights. Rain is frequent, especially in the wet season from December to April, when downpours can flood roads quickly.

Innisfail has fuel, supermarkets, cafés and pubs, and the town has a strong Italian heritage from the migrants who came to work in the cane fields, so a good coffee and a plate of pasta are easy to find. Come in the dry season, from May to October, when the weather is warm and clear. Ride out along the river to Flying Fish Point in the late afternoon, and watch the light fade over the sea and the green hills of the range.
t.the maximov s datcha@59.9,29.7:
The south shore of the Gulf of Finland west of St Petersburg is a strip of dachas, palaces and old military ground, and the place marked here as Maximov's Datcha sits within it, a couple of kilometres from the town of Lomonosov. I cannot vouch for what remains of the house itself, so think of it as a marker in a landscape thick with history rather than a single sight.

Lomonosov was known until 1948 as Oranienbaum, and its palace ensemble is one of the great estates of the St Petersburg area, part of the city's World Heritage listing. It was begun by Prince Alexander Menshikov, Peter the Great's favourite, and later expanded by Catherine the Great, whose Chinese Palace is one of the most exquisite rococo buildings in the country. Unusually, Oranienbaum was never occupied by German forces during the Second World War. A coastal bridgehead around the town held out throughout the siege of Leningrad, supported by the guns of Kronstadt across the water, and the rides that pass through here link that bridgehead with the old sea forts and coastal batteries scattered along the gulf.

Kronstadt itself, the island naval fortress founded by Peter, is now reachable by road over the flood barrier, a long dam with a tunnel under the shipping channel that runs from the north shore to the south near Lomonosov. Riding across it on a clear day, with the gulf on both sides and the domes of the Naval Cathedral ahead, is one of the more memorable things you can do on two wheels around St Petersburg. Wind on the dam can be strong and gusty.

The roads along the coast are a mix of busy highways, especially in summer when the whole city heads to the dachas, and quieter lanes through birch and pine woods. Surfaces vary from smooth to badly potholed, and the riding season is short: snow and ice from November to March, and long, light evenings in June when the white nights make it possible to ride late.

Lomonosov and Petrodvorets, home of the famous Peterhof fountains, both have fuel and plenty of places to eat. Anyone planning to ride here should check current entry rules, insurance and travel advice carefully, because the practicalities for foreign riders have changed a great deal in recent years.
t.gisakura natural forest@-2.5,29.1:
In the far southwest of Rwanda, a small patch of forest surrounded by tea plantations is home to one of the most charming wildlife encounters in Africa. Gisakura forest lies on the western edge of Nyungwe National Park, near the tea estate that shares its name, and a large troop of Ruwenzori colobus monkeys lives there, black and white with long tails and flowing capes of fur. Watching them leap through the canopy, sometimes in groups of dozens, is a joy. The forest is a remnant of the great montane rainforest that once covered these mountains, isolated now by the tea fields.

Nyungwe itself is one of the largest and oldest montane forests in Africa, covering a vast area of ridges and valleys along the border with Burundi. It is home to a remarkable variety of primates, including chimpanzees, which can be tracked with guides, as well as several species of monkey. The birdlife is spectacular, with many species found only in the Albertine Rift. A canopy walkway near the Uwinka visitor centre lets you walk high above the forest floor, suspended between trees on a swaying bridge, with views over the ridges and valleys.

The tea estates around Gisakura are beautiful, with bright green rows of bushes covering the hillsides, workers in colourful clothes picking leaves, and the smell of tea drying in the factory. You can visit some of them to learn about the process and taste the result.

The main road through Nyungwe, linking Huye in the east with Rusizi on Lake Kivu in the west, is one of the most spectacular in East Africa: a smooth ribbon of asphalt winding for kilometres through the forest, with endless bends, steep climbs and descents, and views over the forested ridges. Traffic is light, but watch for buses, trucks and the occasional troop of monkeys on the road. Stopping is restricted in the park except at designated places, so plan accordingly.

Fuel is available in Rusizi and Huye, but not inside the park, so fill up before entering. Rusizi, also called Cyangugu, sits on the southern tip of Lake Kivu, a lovely spot to end a day. The weather in the forest is cool and wet, with rain at any time of year; bring waterproofs and a warm layer. Rwanda drives on the right, and roads are generally well maintained.
t.component around kurrimine beach@-17.7,1:
Kurrimine Beach is a sleepy stretch of sand and coconut palms on the coast of Far North Queensland, between Innisfail and Mission Beach, and it sits at the meeting point of two World Heritage sites. Behind it, the rainforest-covered hills belong to the Wet Tropics of Queensland, listed by UNESCO in 1988 for their ancient forests, which are among the oldest continuously surviving rainforests on earth. In front of it, the Great Barrier Reef stretches out to sea. At very low tides, King Reef, just offshore, is exposed and you can walk out across the reef flats, one of the few places where the reef comes so close to the mainland.

The forests here are home to some extraordinary animals. The southern cassowary, a huge flightless bird with a blue neck and a horny casque on its head, lives in the rainforest and is sometimes seen crossing roads or wandering near houses. It is an endangered species, and signs along the roads ask drivers to slow down. Cassowaries can be dangerous if approached, so keep your distance. Tree kangaroos, possums, frogs and countless birds also live in the forest.

The coast is beautiful but comes with warnings. Saltwater crocodiles live in the rivers, estuaries and sometimes on the beaches, and swimming outside designated areas is risky. From roughly November to May, box jellyfish and other stingers are present in the water, and stinger nets or protective suits are recommended. Signs at the beaches explain the risks.

The riding in the area is pleasant and scenic. The Bruce Highway, the main road along the Queensland coast, runs a few kilometres inland, busy with trucks, caravans and cane trains crossing on narrow-gauge tracks. The side roads to the coast wind through sugar cane fields and banana plantations, with views of the mountains. Further inland, the roads climb onto the Atherton Tableland, with excellent bends, waterfalls and crater lakes.

The nearest towns with full services are Innisfail and Mission Beach, both with fuel, supermarkets and cafés. The weather is tropical: hot and humid year-round, with a wet season from December to April that brings heavy rain, flooding and the risk of cyclones. The dry season, from May to October, is the best time for riding. Watch for wildlife on the roads at dawn and dusk.
t.the palace and park ensemble of the vill:
Ropsha is one of those places where the scenery is gentle and the history is anything but. The village sits on the low Izhora Upland southwest of St Petersburg, between Krasnoe Selo and the coast road at Lomonosov, and the palace that gives the estate its name looks down over a chain of spring-fed ponds and a slow, wooded park. It was here, in July 1762, that the freshly deposed Emperor Peter III was held after his wife Catherine seized the throne, and here that he died a few days later under circumstances nobody at court cared to explain. Catherine became "the Great"; Ropsha became a footnote with a chill on it.

The house itself has had a hard couple of centuries. It passed through several noble owners, was used and abused in the Soviet years, and took heavy damage during the Second World War, when the front line ran close by. What you find today is a handsome but battered classical palace, partly fenced and long awaiting restoration, set in a park whose terraces, cascades and old trout ponds still hint at how grand it once was. The springs here are clear and cold, and the ponds were famous in imperial times for supplying fish to the court table.

For riding, the roads around Ropsha are the pleasant surprise of the Petersburg hinterland. The upland lifts the land just enough to break the flatness of the Gulf shore, and the lanes toward Kipen, Russko-Vysotskoye and Gostilitsy roll through birch and spruce woods, small fields and scattered dachas. Surfaces vary a lot: some stretches are newly laid, others are patched asphalt with frost heave and potholes that appear without warning after a wet spring. Keep your speed honest through the villages, where dogs, chickens and kids on bicycles all share the road with you. Summer evenings are the reward this far north; in June the light lingers almost to midnight and the woods smell of resin and wet moss.

Practicalities are simple. Ropsha has small shops, but for proper fuel and a choice of places to eat, the larger settlements along the main roads, such as Gorbunki toward Peterhof or the town of Krasnoe Selo, are the better bet. Bring water and a snack, park somewhere you can watch the bike, and give yourself half an hour to walk down past the ponds. It is a quiet, slightly melancholy spot, and that is exactly why it sticks in the memory.

Gostilitsy is a village on the Izhora Upland, west of Ropsha and south of Peterhof, and it is one of those places near St Petersburg where the imperial past hides behind fences and overgrown trees. The estate here is associated with Alexei Razumovsky, the Ukrainian Cossack singer who rose to become the favourite and, by many accounts, the secret husband of Empress Elizabeth in the eighteenth century. The palace and park ensemble that grew up around the manor included a house, a church, ponds and landscaped grounds fed by springs, and it is listed among the monuments of the historic centre of St Petersburg and related groups, a UNESCO site that includes many of the palaces and estates around the city.

The estate passed through several hands after Razumovsky, and like many of the country houses around St Petersburg, it suffered in the twentieth century, especially during the Second World War, when German forces occupied the area during the siege of Leningrad. The front line ran nearby, and the region saw fierce fighting. What survives today is a mix of restored and neglected elements, with the church being a focal point of the village. The springs and ponds of the upland give the area a fresh, green feel.

The riding around Gostilitsy is a pleasant escape from the traffic of St Petersburg. The roads cross the Izhora Upland through forests of birch and pine, fields and small villages, with gentle hills and curves. The road from Gostilitsy toward Ropsha and Kipen is quiet, while the route north to Peterhof descends toward the coast of the Gulf of Finland, with views of the sea. Surfaces vary greatly, from good asphalt to potholed stretches, and spring thaw can leave roads damaged. Watch out for wildlife, pedestrians and drivers who may not expect a motorcycle.

Gostilitsy has basic shops, and fuel is available in larger places such as Kipen, Ropsha or Peterhof, which is around twenty kilometres away and has a full range of services. Peterhof is also home to the grand palace and fountains of Peter the Great, one of the most famous sights in Russia. Stop at the church, walk around the old park and ponds, and enjoy the quiet of a village where history sits lightly among the trees. Then ride to Peterhof for the fountains, if you have time.
t.component around curtain fig@-17.3,145.6:
A single tree, but what a tree. The Curtain Fig near Yungaburra, on the Atherton Tablelands of tropical north Queensland, is a strangler fig that started life as a seed dropped by a bird high in the canopy of another tree. Its roots grew down to the ground, wrapping and eventually killing the host, which then fell against a neighbour, leaving the fig at an angle. The roots kept dropping down from the tilted trunk, creating a hanging curtain of aerial roots that reaches the forest floor. A boardwalk lets you walk around it, and it is one of the most photographed trees in Australia.

The tree is part of the Wet Tropics of Queensland World Heritage Site, inscribed in 1988, which protects one of the oldest continuously surviving rainforests on Earth. Patches of rainforest survive on the tablelands among farmland, and they are home to tree kangaroos, possums, cassowaries and a huge variety of birds. The forest around the Curtain Fig is a remnant of the original mabi forest, a rare type of rainforest that grows on rich volcanic soils.

Getting here from Cairns means climbing one of the great motorcycle roads of Queensland: the Gillies Range Road from Gordonvale up to the tablelands, which packs a couple of hundred bends into a short, steep climb through rainforest. It is tight, technical and popular, with plenty of police attention, and the surface can be slippery when wet, which in the tropics is often. The Kuranda Range to the north and the Palmerston Highway to the south are alternative routes onto the tablelands.

Yungaburra, just under two kilometres away, is a charming small town with heritage buildings, cafés and a creek where you can sometimes see platypus in the early morning or late afternoon. Atherton, ten kilometres away, has fuel, supermarkets and workshops. The tablelands are cooler than the coast, thanks to the altitude, and the weather is generally pleasant, though the wet season from December to March brings heavy rain.

Drive on the left, remember that wildlife is most active at dawn and dusk, and give cassowaries a wide berth: they are large, powerful birds and can be dangerous if provoked.
Lake Barrine fills a volcanic crater on the Atherton Tablelands, a deep round lake fringed by dense rainforest, formed by a violent volcanic explosion many thousands of years ago when rising magma met groundwater. Its sister lake, Lake Eacham, lies a few kilometres away, and both are part of the Wet Tropics World Heritage Site. The water is clear and deep, and the rainforest around it is home to some remarkable creatures: Lumholtz's tree kangaroos, musky rat-kangaroos, Boyd's forest dragons and many birds.

A walking track circles the lake through the forest, passing giant trees, strangler figs and a pair of huge kauri pines near the teahouse. The teahouse on the shore has been a stop for travellers for generations, and a boat cruise on the lake offers a chance to see turtles, eels and birds. Early morning, with mist on the water and the calls of birds in the forest, is magical.

Lake Barrine sits right on the Gillies Highway, the road that climbs from Gordonvale on the coastal plain up to the tablelands. Coming up from the coast, the road is a seemingly endless series of hairpins and switchbacks through the rainforest, and Lake Barrine is often the first stop after the climb, a place to catch your breath and have a cup of tea. Going down, the road is equally demanding, with steep descents and tight bends, and it requires full concentration, especially in the wet.

The tablelands are a patchwork of farmland, rainforest remnants and small towns, with volcanic cones and crater lakes scattered across the landscape. The soil is rich and red, and dairy farms, avocado orchards and sugar cane fields surround the towns. The climate is mild, and the roads across the tablelands are relaxed and scenic, with plenty of opportunities to explore.

Fuel is available in Yungaburra, six kilometres away, and in Atherton and Malanda. Lake Eacham is a popular swimming spot, with clear water and a small beach, and swimming there on a hot day is a delight. Cassowaries are sometimes seen in the area; if you meet one, keep your distance and do not feed it.
t.the english park@59.9,29.9:
Everybody who comes to Peterhof heads for the fountains, the Grand Cascade and the gilded Samson tearing open the lion's jaws, and almost nobody walks the few hundred metres west into the English Park. That is their loss. Catherine the Great, who found Peter the Great's straight avenues and clipped hedges old-fashioned, had this park laid out from 1779 by the English gardener James Meader, in the natural landscape style then sweeping Europe: a chain of ponds, meadows, clumps of oak and lime, and paths that wander rather than march. It belongs to the World Heritage Site covering the historic centre of Saint Petersburg and its ring of palaces and estates.

The centrepiece was the English Palace, a severe classical building by Giacomo Quarenghi, Catherine's favourite architect. It did not survive the Second World War. Peterhof lay on the front line during the siege of Leningrad, was occupied by German troops and left in ruins, and while the main palace and fountains were rebuilt with enormous effort, the English Palace was not. What remains is the park itself, softer and wilder than its famous neighbour, with old trees, reeds and ducks, and the Gulf of Finland glinting beyond.

The setting rewards an evening visit in June, when the white nights keep the sky pale until past midnight and the light lies flat and silvery over the water. Mosquitoes are part of that bargain near the ponds.

Getting here means the coastal road west from Saint Petersburg, a slow, built-up run past suburbs, palaces and endless traffic lights, continuing to Oranienbaum and the fortifications facing Kronstadt. Surfaces are patchy and local driving is assertive. The bigger question is whether you can come at all: since 2022, sanctions, insurance gaps, payment problems and visa rules have made Russia very hard for most European riders, and official advice in many countries is against travel. Look that up before anything else.

Peterhof is a town of seventy thousand people, so fuel and food are easy. Russian cafés here serve blini, pelmeni and soups at prices that make a long lunch tempting, and a slice of honey cake with tea on a bench by the ponds is a very Russian way to spend an hour.
t.component around malbon thompson and gra:
South of Cairns, the coastal plain narrows between the sea and a wall of mountains that includes Bartle Frere, at 1,622 metres the highest peak in Queensland, and its neighbour Bellenden Ker. The ranges here are covered in dense rainforest, among the oldest on earth, and they form part of the Wet Tropics of Queensland, listed by UNESCO in 1988. The coordinates fall in the component around the Malbon Thompson and Graham ranges, a block of forested hills between the coast and the Bruce Highway, near the towns of Gordonvale and Babinda.

The rainforest here is extraordinarily rich, with ancient plant lineages, giant trees, palms, vines and ferns, and animals found nowhere else, including tree kangaroos, the musky rat-kangaroo and many species of frogs and birds. The southern cassowary, a large, flightless bird with a bright blue head and a horn-like casque, lives in these forests; it is endangered and can be dangerous if approached, so slow down when you see warning signs on the road. Rainfall here is among the highest in Australia, and Babinda is often cited as one of the wettest towns in the country.

The riding is varied. The Bruce Highway along the coast is busy and fairly straight, running through sugar cane fields with the mountains rising to the west. But just west of Gordonvale, the Gillies Range Road climbs steeply up to the Atherton Tableland, with a famous sequence of hundreds of bends in a short distance, a challenging and exhilarating ride through rainforest, with views back over the coast. On the Tableland, roads wind through dairy country, past crater lakes and waterfalls. Watch out for slippery surfaces after rain, which is frequent, and for cane trains crossing the roads during the harvest season.

Gordonvale has a curious claim to fame: it was here, in 1935, that cane toads were first released in Australia to control pests in the sugar cane, a decision with disastrous consequences, as the toads spread across the continent. A statue of a cane toad in the town commemorates the event. Nearby, the Babinda Boulders, a series of pools and granite boulders in a rainforest creek, are a popular swimming spot, though people have drowned there, so heed the warnings.

Gordonvale, about twenty kilometres away, has fuel, shops and cafés; Cairns has everything. The best time to ride is the dry season, from May to October, when the weather is warm and sunny; the wet season brings heavy rain, flooding and the risk of cyclones.
t.the datcha of the hospital@59.9,29.7:
Somewhere between Bolshaya Izhora and Lomonosov, along the southern shore of the Gulf of Finland, stood a summer house known as the Datcha of the Hospital. The name suggests one of the many country retreats built along this coast in the nineteenth century, when the road west from St Petersburg was lined with the estates of the aristocracy, merchants and institutions. Few of these houses survive intact, and the exact remains of this one are hard to pin down; it is better to take it as a pause on one of the most historic stretches of shore in Russia.

The coast here was the imperial riviera. Peter the Great gave land along the Peterhof road to his courtiers, and they competed to build palaces and gardens facing the sea. Oranienbaum, now called Lomonosov, was the estate of Prince Menshikov, Peter's closest companion, who built a grand palace there; later Catherine the Great added the Chinese Palace, an exquisite rococo pavilion in a wooded park. The town was renamed in 1948 after the scientist Mikhail Lomonosov, who ran a glass and mosaic factory nearby. Unlike Peterhof, Oranienbaum was never occupied by German forces during the Second World War, as it lay inside the bridgehead that held out through the siege of Leningrad, and its palaces survived in much better condition.

The landscape is a narrow coastal plain at the foot of a low ridge, the old shoreline of a post-glacial sea. Streams cut down from the ridge to the gulf, and parks and forests of oak, lime and pine cover the slopes. In spring the woods fill with birdsong; in autumn the colours are rich and the light is low and golden.

Riding along the coastal road is gentle and pleasant, with villages, forest, glimpses of the sea and, in places, the ruins of old estates. Traffic can be heavy near Peterhof, especially on summer weekends, when tour buses crowd the roads. Further west, beyond Lomonosov, things calm down. The road surface is generally decent, with patches and potholes in places.

Lomonosov and Peterhof have fuel, cafés and shops. If you are planning a trip to Russia, check entry requirements, insurance and travel advice carefully, and be aware that foreign payment cards are unlikely to work.
t.knossos@35.3,25.2:
Five kilometres south of Heraklion, on a low hill above the Kairatos stream, lie the ruins that gave Europe its oldest legend of a labyrinth. Knossos was the greatest centre of Minoan Crete, a sprawling palace complex of courtyards, storerooms, staircases and shrines that flourished in the second millennium BC. Its confusing plan, with hundreds of interlocking rooms on several levels, may well have inspired the Greek myth of King Minos, the craftsman Daedalus and the Minotaur imprisoned in the maze, waiting for Theseus.

The site was excavated from 1900 by the British archaeologist Arthur Evans, who spent a fortune on it and then did something modern archaeologists still argue about: he partly rebuilt it. The bright red columns tapering downward, the painted walls, the restored upper storeys are Evans's interpretation in reinforced concrete. Some visitors find them kitsch, others find they make the place readable. Either way, the frescoes you see on site are replicas; the originals, including the famous bull-leaping scene and the elegant figures known as the Ladies in Blue, are in the Archaeological Museum in Heraklion, which is essential to understand what you are looking at.

Go early. By late morning in summer the site is packed with tour groups, and the Cretan sun bounces off the stone with real violence. The first hour after opening, or the last before closing, is far more pleasant, and the pine trees around the entrance offer some shade.

The riding on Crete is wonderful, and the roads south of Knossos are a good introduction. A short ride leads to Archanes, a well-kept village among vineyards at the foot of Mount Giouchtas, the mountain whose profile is said to resemble the face of sleeping Zeus. From there, roads wind through the wine country of Peza, with tight bends, olive groves and village tavernas. The surface can be polished and slippery in places, especially after the first autumn rain, and goats are a frequent hazard. Further south, the road climbs over the island's spine towards the Messara plain and the Minoan palace of Phaistos.

Heraklion has fuel, garages and every kind of service; it can be chaotic to ride through, with heavy traffic and aggressive scooters. In the villages, stop for a Greek coffee, a plate of dakos, the Cretan barley rusk topped with tomato and cheese, and a glass of cold water before the next climb.
t.cyamudongo natural forest@-2.6,29.0:
In the far southwest corner of Rwanda, the land drops toward Lake Kivu and the Ruzizi river, and the green hills here are mostly tea, banana and small farms. Cyamudongo is the exception: a patch of natural forest, a few hundred hectares at most, standing as an island of tall trees in the middle of cultivation. It is separated from the great Nyungwe forest by a belt of farmland, yet it still shelters a small population of chimpanzees, along with other primates and a remarkable range of birds and butterflies.

The forest is a reminder of how much of Africa's highland rainforest has been cut back, and how much can be saved in small pieces. Researchers and conservation groups have worked with the local people here on planting corridors and protecting what remains, and the benefit is visible in the dense green of the canopy against bare, ploughed slopes. The nearest town, Cyangugu, now usually called Rusizi, lies on the shore of the Ruzizi river, with Bukavu in the Democratic Republic of the Congo visible across the border. That proximity matters: carry your passport, avoid wandering toward the border posts, and check current conditions before you go.

Riding in Rwanda is a pleasure by African standards. Main roads are well paved, speed limits are enforced, and helmets are the rule rather than the exception, since motorbike taxis carry passengers everywhere. The roads to Cyamudongo wind along steep hillsides with hairpins, small bridges and long views over terraced fields, and the last stretch is likely to be a rough, red-earth track that turns slippery in the rains. The best months are June to September, in the dry season, though mornings can be misty and cool at altitude.

Cyangugu has fuel, shops and restaurants, and I would fill up there rather than count on anything in the villages. Food on the road is simple, with grilled brochettes, beans, plantain and sweet milky tea, and the local coffee deserves a cup if you find a place that serves it. Entering the forest itself usually requires a guide and a permit, so arrange that in advance. Go early, when the birds are loudest and the air is cool and sweet with the smell of wet leaves.
t.the park of the farm of prince of oldenb:
Peterhof is the palace complex that Peter the Great built on the south shore of the Gulf of Finland, and the parks around it were developed over two centuries, taking in farms, menageries and small country estates. The Farm of Prince Oldenburg belongs to that later layer, a corner of the estate laid out in the nineteenth century as a working landscape, and I cannot say precisely what remains of it. What you will find nearby is parkland of old trees, ponds and paths, and the sense of the wide, flat coast opening northward.

The main attraction in Peterhof is the Grand Cascade and the fountains of the Lower Park, a sequence of golden statues, water jets and terraces falling toward the sea, fed by gravity without pumps, and the Samson fountain at its heart. They run from spring to autumn, and in the right light the effect is startling. The palace and parks are part of the UNESCO listing of the historic centre of Saint Petersburg and related groups of monuments. The Germans destroyed much of the complex in the Second World War, and the rebuilding is one of the great restoration projects of the twentieth century.

Riding here is straightforward. The coast road from Saint Petersburg to Peterhof is wide and fast but very busy, with heavy traffic at weekends and in the tourist season, and speed cameras are numerous. Inside Peterhof the roads are quieter, with tree-lined streets and parks. Summer evenings are very long and light, which is beautiful, though mosquitoes are a nuisance in the damp woods. Winter brings snow and ice, and riding is not practical then. The best time is June to September.

Peterhof has fuel stations, shops, restaurants and hotels in good number, as does the neighbouring Petrodvorets, so there is no need to plan ahead. Try a bowl of borscht or a plate of pelmeni, small dumplings served with sour cream, and a pastry from one of the bakeries. If you visit the fountains, arrive early, since queues build quickly, and bring a rain jacket, because the Baltic weather changes rapidly.
t.historical centre of the town of lomonos:
Lomonosov was called Oranienbaum until 1948, and its history is a story of ambition. Prince Alexander Menshikov, Peter the Great's close friend and favourite, began a grand palace here in the early eighteenth century, on the shore of the Gulf of Finland, and the name, meaning orange tree, came from its greenhouses. Later, the estate passed to the imperial family, and in the 1760s Catherine the Great had the Chinese Palace built in the park, a small, richly decorated pavilion with painted ceilings and exotic interiors. The ensemble is part of the UNESCO listing of Saint Petersburg and related monuments.

What sets Oranienbaum apart from Peterhof, a few kilometres to the east, is that it escaped destruction in the Second World War. The Germans never took it, because the Red Army held a small pocket of land here, known as the Oranienbaum bridgehead, for nearly three years, and the palaces survived in good condition. The town's historic centre is therefore a place where the old streets, merchant houses and churches are largely original, and the park retains a wilder, more overgrown air than the manicured gardens of its neighbours.

Riding to Lomonosov from Saint Petersburg, you follow the coast road through Peterhof, with a stream of traffic, or take the quieter back roads through woods and fields. The roads in the town are narrow and sometimes cobbled, with trams and heavy lorries in the port area. The park is pleasant to walk through, with birch, lime and pond. Early mornings and late evenings are the quietest times, and summer is mild with long days, while winter brings snow and ice.

Lomonosov has fuel stations, shops and restaurants, and the nearby towns have the same. Taste pirozhki, small stuffed buns, and a glass of tea from a samovar if a café offers it. Allow at least a couple of hours for the palaces and park, and check opening times, because some buildings close on certain weekdays and the parks charge small fees.
t.heraion of samos@37.7,26.9:
Samos was rich in the sixth century BC, and the Heraion is the proof. This was the sanctuary of Hera, queen of the gods, on the south coast of the island, near the sea and the plain where the airport now sits. The first temple here was among the largest of the Greek world, the work of the architects Rhoikos and Theodoros, and it was reputed to be the biggest temple ever built in Greece. It was never quite finished, and it was damaged by earthquake, but a single column still stands to its full height, which is why the site is known to visitors as the place of the lone column.

The money came from the tyrant Polycrates, who ruled Samos in the sixth century BC and made it a naval power. He also built the famous tunnel of Eupalinos, a water channel driven through a mountain from both ends at once, and a great harbour mole at Pythagoreion, the main town. Pythagoras was born on Samos, as were the astronomer Aristarchus, who argued the earth moves round the sun, and the philosopher Epicurus. UNESCO listed Pythagoreion and the Heraion together in 1992.

The site is flat and open, with wild olives, reeds and sea air, and the ruins are low walls and foundations, with a sacred way that led from the town. The ground is quiet, with insects humming, and in spring red poppies grow among the stones.

For riders, Samos is a joy. The coast road around the island is smooth, with bends through pine forest, vineyards and small harbours, and the roads inland climb over the mountains toward Mount Kerkis, nearly fifteen hundred metres. Vathy, the capital, and Karlovasi, on the north-west coast, are the bigger towns with petrol stations, and Pythagoreio has a pump or two, but mountain villages often do not, so plan fuel. Samian muscat wine, sweet and golden, is the island's pride, and the dry wines are good too. Spring and autumn are lovely, summers hot with strong winds, and ferries from the mainland run daily. Do take the time to sit in a harbour taverna with a plate of grilled fish.
t.the ratkov rozhnov a estate dubki@59.9,2:
Lomonosov used to be called Oranienbaum, and the name still describes it well: an orange tree, a German version of a Russian palace town. Prince Menshikov, Peter the Great's closest associate, began building it in the early eighteenth century, and later it passed to the imperial family. The town lies on the south shore of the Gulf of Finland, a few kilometres west of Peterhof, and the palaces and parks of Oranienbaum are part of the UNESCO listing for the historic centre of Saint Petersburg. The Ratkov-Rozhnov estate called Dubki belongs to the same belt of country dachas and manors, and it takes its name from the little oaks that once grew there. I do not know what survives of the buildings, so I will not describe rooms.

What I can tell you is the feel of the coast. The land is flat and wooded, with pine, birch and oak on sandy soil, and lanes that wander between small estates, allotment gardens and the occasional ruined manor house. In the war, the Oranienbaum area held out as a bridgehead surrounded by German troops, and the traces of that time are everywhere in memorials and trenches. The Chinese Palace of Catherine the Great, a delicate little building in the park, is the best thing to see.

The riding is mostly practical. Roads between Lomonosov, Petrodvorets and Bolshaya Izhora are busy at commuting hours and patchy in the countryside. Once off the main road you find shaded lanes where you can roll at a quiet pace. Spring brings mud and potholes, summer brings dust and sunshine, and autumn is the most pleasant. In midsummer the long evening light makes the sea glow.

With forty thousand people in Lomonosov and sixty thousand in Petrodvorets, fuel and food are never far. The smaller places have little. Whatever else you do, take time for the Chinese Palace and a walk by the shore at the end of the day, when the light turns low and gold over the water.
t.component around cowley@-17.7,146.1:
The Wet Tropics of Queensland are a long, narrow strip of rainforest between Townsville and Cooktown, and they hold the oldest continuously surviving tropical rainforest on earth, some of it unchanged for well over a hundred million years. The World Heritage listing, from 1988, covers not one block but a patchwork of national parks and other protected land, which is why the label calls this a component around Cowley. Here, the mountains run down almost to the sea, and on the flat, fertile coastal plain around Innisfail, sugar cane and banana plantations stand beside beaches, mangroves and remnants of forest.

Nature here is strange and abundant. The southern cassowary, a huge flightless bird with a blue neck and a bony casque on its head, lives in the lowland forest and is one of the most dangerous birds in the world if provoked, so you should never approach one. It is also one of the most important seed dispersers in the forest. Tree kangaroos, musky rat kangaroos, pythons and thousands of insect species share the canopy, and the estuaries hold saltwater crocodiles, so check signs before swimming. From November to May, box jellyfish make the sea unsafe, and the sea is best left to the tourists with stinger suits.

The riding is on the Bruce Highway and the quieter coastal roads, which run through cane fields, over rivers and along the foot of the mountains. It is long, flat and open, with flowing bends in places, and sometimes it narrows into green tunnels where the rainforest closes over the road. The area has been hit by cyclones, including Larry in 2006 and Yasi in 2011, and the forest shows the scars of both. The best season is the dry winter, from May to October, when the days are warm and clear. In the wet season, heavy rain and flooding can cut the roads.

Innisfail, fifteen kilometres away, is a town with fuel, a bakery and pubs, and a relaxed tropical atmosphere. Further away, the banana and sugar towns have little. Carry water, sunscreen and insect repellent, and slow down at dusk when wildlife is on the move. Fruit stalls along the road sell mangoes, bananas and exotic fruit in season.
t.pythagoreion and heraion of samos@37.7,2:
Two things that the ancient Greeks did better than anyone are on show on this corner of Samos, and one of them is a tunnel. In the sixth century BC, the tyrant Polycrates ruled the island, and he commissioned an engineer from Megara, Eupalinos, to bring water to his capital through a mountain. The tunnel is about a kilometre long, and Eupalinos had his workers dig from both ends at once, meeting in the middle with an error of only a few metres, which is a stunning achievement for the time. Visitors can walk through a part of it today, in a hard hat, and the sloping channel for water still runs beside the walkway.

The second wonder is the Heraion, the sanctuary of Hera, a few kilometres along the coast. The goddess was said to have been born on Samos, beside a river in a marshy hollow, and the shrine here was one of the largest temples in the Greek world. Today only a single column stands, rising from a field of foundations and scattered stones, but the scale of the base shows how grand it was. A sacred way once ran to the temple from the town, lined with statues, and the harbour of Pythagoreion, named after the philosopher Pythagoras, who was born on Samos in the sixth century BC, still has the remains of its ancient mole. The two sites together were inscribed on the World Heritage list in 1992.

Samos is a green, mountainous island, and its roads are a pleasure. The route from Pythagoreion to Vathy and on to the north coast climbs through pine woods and vineyards, with views of the Turkish coast just a few kilometres across the strait. The island is famous for its sweet muscat wine, made from the grapes that ripen on the terraced slopes, and for thyme honey. The surface is generally good but with occasional loose gravel, and goats appear on the road without warning. May and late September are the best times, and in the high summer the heat and the meltemi, the dry northerly wind, can be strong.

Pythagoreion is a small place of about thirteen hundred people with a pretty harbour and several tavernas. The ferries bring bikes from the mainland, and Samos town has petrol stations, a larger shopping area and more services. Eat grilled fish at the harbour and drink a cold glass of the local wine.
t.the palace and park ensemble sobstvennay:
Peterhof is the one everyone has seen in photographs, with the golden statue of Samson tearing open a lion's jaws and the long canal running down to the Gulf of Finland. The Sobstvennaya Dacha, the Tsar's Own Dacha, is a quieter corner of the same ensemble, tucked into the parkland on the southern shore of the gulf. The ground here is the Izhorsky bench, a limestone shelf running east to west with a sudden step down toward the water.

That step is the key to understanding the whole landscape. Peter the Great chose to build his seaside residence at the top of it from 1710 onwards, so that spring water could be led downhill and made to fountain without any pumps. Later tsars added their own pavilions, cottages and chapels in the surrounding parks, each generation wanting a private retreat away from the formal palace. The whole estate was shattered in the Second World War, the great palace burned and the fountains dismantled or stolen, and the restoration afterwards is one of the great labours of Soviet and Russian conservation. Some of the smaller buildings are still catching up, which gives the lesser corners a quiet, slightly unfinished charm.

On a bike you arrive through Petrodvorets, a town of nearly sixty-two thousand people, where a petrol station and a meal are never far. The road from the city along the coast is fast and wide and rather dull, with heavy traffic at rush hour. Come out of season, or early, and the quieter side streets through the old residential districts, with their wooden houses and gardens, are far more pleasant. The shoreline woods are good for a short walk if the wind is not coming in cold off the gulf.

Be ready for crowds in summer. The fountains run from late spring to early autumn, and the parks fill with tour groups from midday. Early morning is the time to go, when the gravel is empty and the gilded statues catch the low sun. Winter has its own appeal, with the frozen canal and bare lime trees, but the roads then are icy and not for riders.
t.jacobstadt jekabpils@56.5,25.9:
Jēkabpils lies on the Daugava, Latvia's great river, in the region called Sēlija, and its older German name, Jacobstadt, tells you who founded it. Duke Jacob Kettler of Courland, who ruled this land in the seventeenth century, planted a town here in 1670 and gave it his name, in the same decade he was trying to found colonies in Tobago and Gambia. The duchy was a small, wealthy state that punched above its weight. Across the river sits Krustpils, an older settlement with a castle, and the two towns grew together over the centuries and were merged in 1962.

The Daugava is the key to the place. It is wide, slow and brown here, with sandbanks and reeds, and for centuries it carried timber and grain down to Riga. A long bridge crosses it, and from the middle you see church spires on both banks. The town's most unexpected claim is scientific. In the nineteenth century, the astronomer Friedrich Struve measured a chain of triangles from Norway to the Black Sea to find the shape of the earth, and Jēkabpils was one of the points on this Struve Geodetic Arc, which is a World Heritage site.

The roads around are flat and open, crossing farmland, birch woods and old estates. The A6 highway links Riga and Daugavpils, and carries a lot of heavy traffic, so for pleasure it is better to take the smaller roads along the river and toward the Sēlija hills. Surfaces vary, and frost damage is common in spring. Winter is long and snowy, and the best time to ride is from May to September, when the evenings are very long.

Jēkabpils is a town of twenty-seven thousand and has fuel stations, supermarkets and cafes. Latvian food is simple and filling, with rye bread, smoked fish, grey peas with bacon, and in summer cold beetroot soup. Walk the river embankment in the evening, when the light turns gold and the swallows skim the water.
t.the alexandriysky park@59.9,29.9:
The garden at Alexandria is a nineteenth-century romantic dream laid out at Peterhof for Tsar Nicholas I and his wife, Alexandra, a place of Gothic towers, winding paths and a small cottage palace by the sea. It lies a little to the west of the great fountains of the lower park, on the shore of the Gulf of Finland, and its mood is quite different: quiet, wooded and slightly melancholy. The Gothic Chapel, designed in the style of an English country church, stands among the trees, and the Cottage Palace beside it was a family retreat where the emperor could escape the formality of court life.

Peterhof is a town of over seventy thousand people, and everything a rider needs is there: fuel, cafes, parking and a supermarket or two. The road from Saint Petersburg runs along the coast through a string of old palace towns, past the Sergievka estate and the Strelna palace, and in summer it is busy, with tour coaches and queues at the junctions. The corners are gentle and the surface is mostly in good order, but traffic makes the going slow. Leave early in the morning if you want to ride at speed, or come in the evening when the crowds have gone.

The fountains of the Great Cascade, a short way east, run from May to early autumn, and their water comes from springs on the high ground to the south by gravity alone, with no pumps. The system was designed in the time of Peter the Great and still works as it did. The cooling air by the water is welcome on a hot day.

Alexandria itself is a park for strolling. Pine and oak shade the paths, and the gulf glints through the trees. The ground can be damp, and mosquitoes are a nuisance in June. The best months are May and September, when the park is green or golden and the crowds are thinner.

Bring a lock for the bike helmet and gloves, since many places in the park require you to carry your gear, and leave plenty of time, because the park is larger than it first appears.
t.the palace and park ensemble sergievka@5:
Peterhof is the tsars' answer to Versailles, strung along the southern shore of the Gulf of Finland about thirty kilometres west of St Petersburg, and Sergievka belongs to its quieter western fringe. Think of it less as one famous building than as a country estate in the old Peterhof manner, with a house, an overgrown park, ponds and lawns, laid out when noble families built summer retreats close to the court. I would not claim to know every owner, but it sits within the same belt of grand dachas and gardens that grew up around Peter the Great's seaside palace after 1710, when the fountains and the Grand Cascade began to take shape.

The ride out follows the shore road from St Petersburg, the old Peterhof highway, which runs more or less straight past Strelna and into the town, and it is a dull road made worse by traffic, lorries and a surface that holds puddles. Sunday evenings out of the city can be slow. Summer is the season for it: the white nights make a ride at ten in the evening entirely practical, the sky holding a soft pink glow over the bay long after midnight. In winter the gulf freezes and the park is bare, snow-streaked and very quiet.

Peterhof town has some seventy thousand people, which means petrol stations, cafes, a market and no shortage of places to sit, and the neighbouring old quarter, Petrodvorets, has the faded grandeur you expect from a place that was nearly razed in 1941 to 1944. The Germans held it for nearly three years, the fountains were looted and the Great Palace burnt out, and the post-war restoration took decades. The sight of those gilded statues glinting again is a small triumph of obstinacy.

Parking is the one practical hurdle. The main palace grounds charge entrance and have their own queues, while Sergievka and the neighbouring parks are more relaxed, and a bike can usually slip in where a car cannot. Take water, because the walk through the grounds is longer than it looks on a map, and bring a rain jacket, since the Baltic weather can turn within the hour.
t.murambi@-2.5,29.6:
Murambi sits on a green hill in southern Rwanda, and the buildings on it were meant to be a technical school. In April 1994, tens of thousands of Tutsi from the surrounding area gathered here, told that they would be protected, and instead the school became a place of mass killing. The number who died in a few days is estimated at around fifty thousand, though the exact toll is not known. After the genocide, bodies were exhumed and preserved with lime, and some are displayed in the school's classrooms, as a stark testimony that no visitor forgets. It is one of the most harrowing places in Africa, and it is now a national memorial and, since 2023, a World Heritage site along with Nyamata, Bisesero and the memorial in Kigali.

I will not dress it up. A visit here is an act of remembrance, and the guides, often survivors, ask for quiet and respect. Many visitors say they needed a long time afterwards just to sit. The hill itself has a gentle beauty, with eucalyptus, tea and banana terraces, and a view over the valley, a contrast that makes the place all the more disturbing.

The nearest towns are Nyamagabe, formerly Gikongoro, close by, and Huye, formerly Butare, home to the national university and the national museum, about thirty kilometres away. Fuel and food are in both. The ride from Kigali to the south, through Muhanga and Huye, takes about three hours on a well-kept, winding road across hills, with views of terraced fields, tea estates and valleys filled with morning mist. Beyond Murambi, the road continues toward Nyungwe Forest, one of the oldest rainforests in Africa, with chimpanzees and colobus monkeys, and a spectacular high road through tea and forest.

Rwanda has a strict helmet law, and police checks are common but courteous. Roads can be wet in the long rains from March to May, and mist and fog are common on the hills in the early morning. The dry seasons are best. Altitude means that mornings can be chilly, so carry a layer.

Do not plan too much for the day of your visit. Leave time to be quiet, and to ride slowly afterwards.
t.ancient city of ephesus@37.9,27.3:
Ephesus is the sort of place where the scale arrives slowly, one marble block at a time. It lies in the plain beside Selçuk, less than three kilometres from the town centre and about twelve from the resort of Kuşadası, and once stood on the sea. The Cayster river kept dropping silt until the harbour became fields, and the city that had been one of the great ports of the Roman province of Asia was left stranded a few kilometres inland.

What stays standing is astonishing. The facade of the Library of Celsus, the long colonnaded Marble Street, the Great Theatre cut into the hillside and big enough for tens of thousands of spectators, the terraced houses where wealthy families painted walls and laid mosaics. Ephesus was also a place of pilgrimage twice over. Artemis was worshipped here in a temple counted among the seven wonders of the ancient world, and today a single re-erected column in a field near Selçuk is all that marks it. Later Saint Paul preached and caused a riot among the silversmiths, and tradition says John spent his last years on the hill above, where a basilica was built over the grave.

For riders, the approach is easy and unremarkable: a flat run from Izmir by the main roads or a short hop up the coast from Kuşadası, with traffic that gets thicker as you near the gates. The ruins themselves are walked, and the stones are slick and hot, so wear shoes you can handle in. Go at opening time in summer, when the heat comes down hard by late morning and the cruise-ship crowds fill the Marble Street shoulder to shoulder. Autumn and early spring are kinder, with softer light and room to breathe.

Selçuk is the practical base. It has fuel, restaurants serving grilled meat and fresh gözleme, and an old aqueduct that storks nest on in season. Fill the tank there rather than hunting along the farm roads, and finish with a drive up to the museum and the Basilica of Saint John for the view across the plain to where the sea used to be.
t.bright@-36.7,147.0:
Bright is a town where autumn is a seasonal event. In the Ovens Valley, in northeast Victoria, rows of maples, poplars and oaks that settlers planted turn blazing orange and yellow in late April and May, and the whole valley fills with visitors with cameras. Out of season Bright is a peaceful country town of around two and a half thousand people, with cafes, a brewery, and the Ovens River running through the middle of a park.

The town grew out of the gold rush of the 1850s, when miners flooded into the rivers and creeks of the high country. Little remains of the diggings, but the main street still has some Victorian buildings, and nearby Porepunkah, Harrietville and Beechworth have their own gold stories. The Ovens Valley lies under Mount Buffalo, a granite plateau that is a popular spot for hiking, climbing and winter skiing, while the Alpine National Park rises to the south and east.

The Great Alpine Road is the draw for riders. From Bright it climbs and drops in rolling bends through eucalypt forest, past Harrietville, and then pushes up toward Mount Hotham, one of the highest sealed roads in Australia. Surfaces are generally good, with the usual hazards of gravel, wet leaves and wildlife at dawn and dusk. Kangaroos and wombats really do appear on the road. The seasons here are real: snow and ice can close sections in winter, and summer days can be hot with bushfire risk.

Bright has fuel, bakeries and plenty of places to stay, though in autumn weekends rooms are booked well ahead. Myrtleford, about twenty-eight kilometres away, is the next large town on the way back toward the lowlands. Hotham has limited services, so fill up in Bright or Harrietville before climbing, and be prepared for sharp changes of temperature on the mountain.
t.mount hotham@-37.0,147.1:
Mount Hotham stands 1,845 metres above sea level, and the Great Alpine Road crosses its shoulder, making this one of the highest sealed roads in Australia. The terrain is a rolling, wind-bent alpine plateau of snow gums, heath and rock, quite unlike the stereotype of the Australian outback. In winter it is a major ski resort, buried in snow from June to September, and in summer the high meadows burst into wildflowers in December and January.

The area is the country of the Bogong moth, which migrate in huge numbers each spring from Queensland and New South Wales to cool caves in these mountains, where they spend the summer. Aboriginal groups gathered here each year to feast on the moths, in an annual event that was also a time for ceremony and trade. Later, cattlemen drove their herds up to the high plains for summer grazing, and their huts still stand in places. Dinner Plain, a village lower down, was built in the 1980s in a style inspired by those mountain huts.

The road itself is a joy for riders, if a challenging one. On the western side, it climbs from Harrietville in a long series of tight bends, with steep drops and sudden changes of weather. On the eastern side, it eases down through Dinner Plain to Omeo and the wide forests of Gippsland. The surface is good, but ice and snow are real concerns, and in winter chains must be carried on the road. Temperatures at the summit can fall below freezing even in summer. The best time to ride is from late spring to early autumn, with fog and cold wind always a possibility.

Fuel is not available at the top of the mountain, so fill the tank at Harrietville, Bright or Omeo before the climb. The village has cafes and restaurants, which are open longer in ski season, and Hotham Heights, just 2.7 kilometres away, has accommodation. Bring warm gloves and a windproof layer, and take your time on the descent, where brakes work hard.
t.kahuzi biega national park@-2.3,28.2:
Kahuzi-Biega is the place in the world to meet an eastern lowland gorilla, the largest of all the great apes. The park lies in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in South Kivu province, west of Bukavu and Lake Kivu, and it covers a mix of lowland rainforest and the high forested slopes of two extinct volcanoes, Kahuzi at 3,308 metres and Biega at 2,790. Bamboo forest grows on the upper slopes, and the whole mass rises abruptly from the Albertine Rift, one of the richest areas for wildlife in Africa.

Tracking is the main activity, led by Congolese trackers who follow habituated gorilla families through dense undergrowth, and it can be a muddy, humid and rewarding scramble. A silverback may weigh over 200 kilograms, and a group often includes females, infants and a few blackbacks. The park has also been among the most threatened in Africa: it was listed as a World Heritage site in danger in 1997 because of civil war, mining and poaching, and gorilla numbers have fallen sharply over the decades. Local rangers have lost their lives protecting them.

Because of that history, I would not treat this as a casual ride. The security situation in South Kivu has been unstable for years, with armed groups active across the province, and access to the park has been interrupted repeatedly. Check the latest official advice and with reliable local operators before planning anything, and do not rely on old guides. If the way is closed, the Rwandan side of Lake Kivu offers an alternative, with a good tarmac road running along the shore from Gisenyi to Cyangugu through hills of tea and banana, cool lake air and many viewpoints.

Bukavu, the city on the southern tip of the lake, is the nearest centre, with fuel and basic services, though prices are high and supplies are unreliable. Roads in the region can be poor, with potholes, landslides in the rainy season and checkpoints. Carry water, a repair kit and cash in small denominations, and take a local guide.

The dry season from June to August is the usual window, when the tracks are firmer and the forest is a little easier to move through.
t.nyungwe national forest@-2.6,29.2:
Nyungwe is one of the oldest rainforests in Africa and one of the wettest, a block of mountain forest in the south-west of Rwanda that survived the ice ages when so much of the continent dried out. It holds around a thousand square kilometres of dense growth on steep ridges between about 1,600 and 3,000 metres, and it shelters thirteen species of primate, including chimpanzees, L'Hoest's monkeys and large troops of black-and-white Angolan colobus that move through the canopy in loud, tumbling groups. Birdlife is exceptional, with over three hundred species, many found only in the Albertine Rift. Some of the headwaters of the Nile are said to start in its streams.

The road across the forest, which links Huye in the east with Rusizi on Lake Kivu in the west, is one of the best rides in Rwanda. Tarmac is smooth and the road climbs through tea plantations and then into the trees, with long, easy bends, deep green walls on either side, mist drifting across the carriageway and the occasional colobus family crossing. Rain can come at any time, even in the dry season, and cloud can reduce visibility to a few metres, so slow down and use your lights. Temperatures at altitude are cool, and a waterproof layer is essential. Baboons sit by the road at points, and they have learned to grab food from riders, so keep snacks out of sight.

Walking in the forest is arranged through park offices, with guides and fees, and the canopy walkway, a suspension bridge some forty metres above the forest floor, offers a view of the treetops that most visitors do not forget. Chimpanzee tracking begins before dawn and can involve a long, steep and muddy scramble, so plan it carefully.

Small guesthouses near Gisakura, beside a tea estate on the edge of the forest, offer rooms and meals, and the tea itself is excellent.

The drier months, from June to September and from December to February, are the best for walking and riding, though the forest earns its reputation at any time of year.
t.otways rainforest roads photo pull off@-:
Mount Disappointment is the name that matches the mood on a grey day here, and the forest it rises from is an unexpectedly wild patch to find forty-odd kilometres north of Melbourne. The coordinates fall among the places of Eden Park and Wandong, near Whittlesea and the Kinglake Ranges, and not in the Otways at all. The Otways are a long day to the south-west, along the Great Ocean Road, so treat this point as the place where a ride into the green hills begins and ends.

The country is tall wet forest of mountain ash, the tallest flowering plants in the world, with tree ferns, mossy gullies and the occasional lyrebird scratching in the leaf litter. Parts of it were burnt in the Black Saturday fires of February 2009, which swept through Kinglake and the surrounding hills, and the regrowth is now thick and bright green in places, with grey skeletons of dead trees still standing in others. Rhodes is an island that has been fought over for three thousand years, and the walls of its old town still carry the marks. In 1309 the Knights of St John, a crusading order driven from the Holy Land, took the island and spent two centuries turning its capital into one of the strongest fortresses in the Mediterranean. They built the Palace of the Grand Master, a vast castle of pale stone, and the Street of the Knights, a long cobbled lane lined with the headquarters of the order's language groups. In 1522 the Ottoman sultan Suleiman besieged the city with a great army and, after six months, forced the knights to leave.

The old town is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and it is walkable and compact, with mosques, churches and a former synagogue within the same walls. The newer city, with about 56,000 people, wraps around it, with a harbour lined by cafés and a pair of bronze deer on columns marking the entrance, where, according to legend, the Colossus once stood, a giant bronze statue of the sun god Helios, toppled by an earthquake in the third century BC.

Fuel and food are easy. From Rhodes the main road runs down the east coast, past beaches and resorts, toward Lindos, where a white village climbs below an ancient acropolis perched on a cliff above the sea. The road is generally good, with long, gentle curves through olive and pine, and traffic is heavy in July and August. The west coast, battered by wind, is quieter and wilder, and the interior hills have villages where the food is good and the pace is slow.

The weather is warm from April to October, and the sea is at its best in September. Ferries run to nearby islands, and the harbour is a pleasant place to watch them come and go.

Letoon is a sanctuary in a flat green plain, and what you find is mostly water and frogs. The ruins of three temples, dedicated to Leto and her children Apollo and Artemis, stand in the valley of the Eşen river, near the coast of ancient Lycia, and in wet seasons the foundations are flooded, so that the old columns stand in pools full of croaking frogs. According to the story, Leto came here with her twins, thirsty and hunted by Hera, and when local shepherds refused her water, she turned them into frogs.

The sanctuary was the religious centre of the Lycian League, one of the earliest known federations of cities, and it is a UNESCO World Heritage site, together with nearby Xanthos. In 1973 archaeologists found here a stone with an inscription in three languages: Greek, Aramaic and Lycian, a language that was then almost unknown, and it helped scholars decipher the Lycian tongue. A little theatre and a nymphaeum, a fountain house, survive near the temples, and a modest site museum is open at set hours.

The setting is quiet and rural. Greenhouses of tomatoes and peppers cover much of the plain, and the road passes through small villages where farmers sell fruit by the roadside. Kalkan, a pretty coastal town of about 3,000 people, lies roughly twelve kilometres away, and Kaş is farther, so fill the tank before you go, or in Fethiye. The road along this coast is among the most beautiful in Turkey, with turquoise bays on one side and pine-covered mountains on the other, and the bends can be tight and surprising.

Go in spring, when the wildflowers bloom and the water is high, or in autumn, when the heat has eased. In summer the plain bakes, and the site offers little shade. Bring water, a hat and some patience, and take a moment to sit by the pools, listening to the frogs, and imagine the pilgrims who once came here.

The Eşen valley has long been a farming country, and the landscape around the ruins of Xanthos is one of green fields, red earth and bare limestone hills. This stop lies close to the main ruins, among villages and orchards, and the rock tombs and carved pillars of the Lycians stand on the slopes above the road. Lycian tomb builders liked a view: they cut their graves in the cliffs, often in the form of wooden houses, and raised tall pillar tombs, topped with burial chambers, near the city.

The valley has a gentle rhythm. Farmers work among rows of vegetables and fruit trees, and small tractors rumble along the lanes. Kınık, the nearest village, has a few shops and tea houses, but little else. For fuel and a proper meal you need to go to Kalkan, which is about thirteen kilometres away, or to Kaş, which is a good deal farther, so plan your fuel carefully. The coast road is lovely, but it winds through hills, and distances can be deceptive.

Much of the finest sculpture from this region now lies in London. In the nineteenth century, a British traveller, Charles Fellows, removed the carved friezes of the Harpy Tomb and the Nereid Monument and shipped them to the British Museum, where they are displayed today. Casts of some of these works stand on the site, but the originals are far away. It gives the visit a poignant edge, a feeling of something missing from the place it was made for.

The best time to visit is spring or autumn, when the air is mild and the fields are green. In high summer the heat is fierce, and shade is rare. They look down quietly on the valley, as they have for twenty-five centuries.

Xanthos was the greatest city of ancient Lycia, and its story is one of defiance. In 540 BC the Persian general Harpagus attacked it, and according to the historian Herodotus the Xanthians fought to the last, setting fire to their own homes and perishing together rather than surrender. Centuries later, in 42 BC, Brutus besieged the city during the Roman civil wars, and again the people chose destruction over capture. It is a grim record, and the city remains the symbol of Lycian stubbornness.

The ruins stand on a hillside above the Eşen river, and they include a Roman theatre, a Lycian acropolis, a monumental tomb on a tall pillar and an inscribed stone known as the Xanthos obelisk, whose text in the Lycian language is one of the longest known. The site is part of the UNESCO listing shared with Letoon, a few kilometres away. A small team of archaeologists still works here, and the site is usually open in daylight hours.

Kınık, the closest village, is small and simple, and for fuel you need to travel to Kalkan, thirteen kilometres to the south, or Kaş, much farther along the coast. There are tea gardens near the entrance, where a glass of strong tea and a plate of olives is welcome after a walk among the stones. The surrounding hills are dotted with rock tombs, and some of them can be seen from the road, a startling sight on a dry hillside.

The riding in this part of Turkey is excellent. The coast road, with its views of the sea and its long, tight curves, passes through pine forests and past quiet beaches, and the traffic is light outside the high season. In summer the heat is intense, and a cold drink is as valuable as fuel. Come in spring, when the hills are green and the poppies are in flower, and the old city looks as if it had risen out of the grass.

Heraklion is the big, busy, slightly untidy capital of Crete, and it has never tried to be pretty. The old Venetian harbour still holds a fortress, the Koules, whose sea walls were built to keep out the Ottomans, and the long ramparts of the town, with their bastions, enclose a centre of narrow streets and small squares. On one of those bastions lies the grave of Nikos Kazantzakis, the author of Zorba the Greek, with a plain wooden cross and an epitaph that says he hoped for nothing, feared nothing, and was free.

The great attraction is just south of the city. Knossos, the palace of the Minoan kings, was the heart of a civilisation that flourished on Crete about four thousand years ago, with frescoes of dolphins, bulls and young acrobats, and a tangle of rooms and corridors that may have inspired the legend of the labyrinth. The Archaeological Museum in the city holds the finest finds, and is well worth a visit, especially for the delicate gold jewellery and the famous snake goddess figurines.

Heraklion has over 137,000 people, so fuel is plentiful. The city itself is chaotic, with heavy traffic, scooters and double-parked cars, and the best advice is to leave it quickly. The mountains lie within easy reach, with roads climbing through olive groves and villages to high plateaus and gorges, and the coast road to the east leads through resorts to quieter beaches. Cretan food is some of the best in Greece, with thick barley rusks topped with tomatoes and cheese, wild greens, snails and lamb, all washed down with raki.

Summers are hot, and the wind can blow hard on the coast, so a spring or autumn ride is more comfortable. In the evening the harbour fills with strollers, and the old fortress glows in the last light. It is a good place to start a trip, with a coffee in hand and the mountains waiting on the horizon.

For more than two centuries it was the capital of Spanish Central America, a grand colonial town of churches, convents and mansions at the foot of three volcanoes, Agua, Fuego and Acatenango. In 1773 a series of earthquakes shook it so badly that the authorities moved the capital to a new site, now Guatemala City, in 1776. The old city was partly abandoned, and many of its churches stand today as roofless ruins, their arches and walls covered with moss and flowers.

It is now a UNESCO World Heritage site, with cobbled streets, pastel houses and a central square shaded by trees. The Arco de Santa Catalina, a yellow arch across a street, frames a view of the Volcán de Agua. During Holy Week the streets are covered with carpets of coloured sawdust and flowers, made over many hours and then trampled by processions. About 39,000 people live here, so fuel and food are easy to find, though stations are mostly on the edge of town.

The cobbles are the thing to remember. Wet or dry, they are rough and uneven, and a loaded bike can be hard to hold, so go slowly, and look for guarded parking. Fuego, the active volcano that looms to the south-west, regularly puffs smoke and occasionally erupts, and at night the glow of lava can sometimes be seen from the hills. The roads that climb toward San Juan del Obispo and beyond wind through coffee farms and small villages, with views over the city's red roofs.

The best season is the dry months from November to April, when the sky is clear and the volcanoes stand out sharp. The rainy season brings afternoon downpours and slick roads. Early mornings are crisp, and the light is soft on the old walls. Sit in the square with a cup of local coffee, and watch the day begin.

Natchez sits on a high bluff above the Mississippi, the southern end of the long, gentle ribbon that is the Natchez Trace Parkway. About fifteen thousand people live in town now, but in the decades before the Civil War it was among the richest places in the country, home to cotton planters whose mansions still stand along the quiet streets. Many of those houses are open to visitors, and the old river landing at Natchez Under-the-Hill, once a rowdy port, sits below the bluff with a view of the huge brown river and the bridge to Louisiana.

The Trace itself is far older than any of that. It began as a trail used by Choctaw, Chickasaw and Natchez peoples, and later by boatmen who floated goods down the Mississippi, sold them and walked home north along the path. The modern parkway, a national park road that runs some four hundred and forty miles to Nashville, follows much of that route. It is a superb motorcycle road precisely because it is so calm: the speed limit is about fifty, there are no commercial trucks, no billboards, and the road is wrapped in forest of pine, oak and magnolia.

Riding the southern end, you pass old mounds, such as Emerald Mound, one of the largest Native ceremonial mounds in the country, and quiet pull-offs where sunken sections of the original trail are still visible. Deer are the main hazard, especially at dawn and dusk, and the heat in summer is thick and humid. Spring and autumn are ideal, with softer light and cooler mornings. There is little fuel along the Trace itself, so fill the tank in Natchez before heading north.

In town, eat something Southern: catfish, fried green tomatoes, gumbo and pie are all done well here. Sit by the river at sundown and watch the barges push slowly past. It is a place to finish a long ride and stay the night, the sort of town where the pace is set by the water rather than the clock.
