t.rezekne@56.5,27.3:
Rēzekne is the heart of Latgale, the eastern region of Latvia, which has its own language, its own pottery and a strong Catholic tradition that sets it apart from the Lutheran north. The pin lands in the centre of the city, which has about thirty-eight thousand people and is often called the Heart of Latgale. It lies on the river Rēzekne, among low hills and lakes, a short way from the Russian and Belarusian borders.

The roads are quiet, flat and straight, running between forests of pine and birch, fields and small wooden villages, with the occasional long climb over a glacial ridge. The surface varies, and some rural roads are gravel, though main routes are well kept. Traffic is light, and the best time is summer, when the days are long and the lakes are warm, or early autumn, when the forests turn gold. Winters are cold, with deep snow, and fog can be thick.

The city has a long history. The ruins of a castle built by the Livonian Order in the thirteenth century stand on a hill above the river, and the statue called Latgales Māra, a tall female figure holding a cross, stands near the centre as a symbol of the region's unity. It was destroyed by the Soviets and rebuilt in 1992. A modern concert hall, the Latgale Embassy Gors, has become a centre of culture. The Latgalian ceramic tradition produces dark, burnished pots, sold in local craft shops.

t.kibuye@-2.1,29.3:
Kibuye sits on the shore of Lake Kivu in western Rwanda, and the setting is the best argument for coming. The lake is long, deep and hemmed in by steep green hills, with a coast of small bays and peninsulas and islands covered in forest. On a calm morning the water is a sheet of pewter and fishermen paddle out in wooden boats lashed together in threes, their nets draped across long poles. The town, called Karongi in official use, is a quiet place with a small harbour, a few hotels and a handful of lakeside cafes.

Kivu is an unusual lake. It is one of the African Great Lakes, but it has no hippos or crocodiles and no bilharzia, so swimming is safe, and it holds enormous quantities of dissolved methane, which Rwanda now extracts to generate power. Boat trips go out to Napoleon Island, where a colony of fruit bats hangs in the trees, and to other small islands with good views. Rwandan coffee, grown on the surrounding slopes, is excellent, and a cup beside the water is a pleasure.

Kibuye also has a darker past. During the 1994 genocide, many thousands of people were killed in and around the town, including at the church on the hill, and the church is now a memorial where visitors can pay their respects. It is a sombre, quiet place, and visitors are asked to behave with care and respect.

The road along the lake, part of the Congo Nile route, is one of the great rides of East Africa. It twists through the hills in a long run of bends, climbing and dropping past tea plantations, banana groves and small villages, and the tarmac is good by regional standards. Rwanda enforces speed limits and helmets strictly, so stay within the law, and watch for pedestrians, bicycles loaded with bananas and motorbike taxis. Fill the tank at Kibuye or the larger towns. Rain is frequent, particularly from March to May, and the hills can be misty in the early morning.
t.nyungwe@-2.5,29.2:
Nyungwe is the largest surviving block of montane rainforest in East and Central Africa, and the road that crosses it, running from Rusizi on Lake Kivu toward Huye, is one of the most atmospheric rides in the continent. The forest covers about a thousand square kilometres of steep hills, and it is very old, having survived the ice ages when other forests shrank, which is why it holds such an abundance of life. There are thirteen species of primates here, including chimpanzees and large troops of Angolan colobus monkeys, which often sit by the road, and more than three hundred species of birds.

The ride is cold, wet and wonderful. The road climbs from the lakeshore through tea plantations at Gisakura into thick forest, where the trees close overhead and the mist drifts across the tarmac. Elevations reach almost two thousand five hundred metres, and the temperature drops by many degrees, so waterproofs and warm layers are essential. The bends are tight and often hidden in fog, and heavy trucks grind along the grade with little care for bikes. Ride slowly, use your lights and keep clear of the roadside, where monkeys sometimes sit and troops cross.

Walk if you can. The canopy walkway, a suspension bridge strung about fifty metres above the forest floor, offers a view from the tree tops, and trails lead through tree ferns, giant lobelias and orchids to waterfalls. Chimpanzee tracking is possible but needs an early start and a permit, so arrange it in advance. The park is also regarded as one of the possible sources of the Nile, as streams here feed rivers that eventually flow to both the Congo and the Nile basins.

The dry months of June to August and December to February are the best for visiting, though the forest is never really dry. Stay overnight if you can. The dawn chorus of birds and the sound of rain on the leaves are worth the early alarm.
t.high country omeo@-38.1,145.3:
Cranbourne sits on the south-eastern fringe of Melbourne, where suburb gives way to market gardens, horse paddocks and the flat country around Western Port Bay. For anyone returning from the Victorian high country this is the first sign of home, and the last place where the road stops feeling like countryside.

What many riders do not know about Cranbourne is that it holds one of the finest gardens in the country. The Australian Garden, part of the Royal Botanic Gardens Cranbourne, is a landscape of native plants arranged around red sand, dry creek beds and eucalypt groves. It is a fine place to wander on a day off the bike, and its cafe is more reliable than most. The remnant bushland nearby is also home to koalas and, in the quieter patches, swamp wallabies and the occasional echidna.

The riding is mostly straight and fast here, and the South Gippsland Highway and Thompsons Road carry heavy local traffic, so I would treat this as a place to be, not a place to ride. If you want better roads, head south and east toward Tooradin and the lowland edges of Western Port, where flat farmland and wetlands give a quiet half-hour. The Bunurong and Boonwurrung people lived and fished around this bay, and the tidal flats are an international site for migratory birds, particularly the waders that arrive from Siberia and Alaska each spring.

Cranbourne is a big place with nearly twenty thousand people, and fuel, supermarkets and every chain restaurant you could want are within a kilometre. It also has a racecourse that draws crowds on meeting days, so allow for some extra traffic if you pass through then.

If you have had a long day in the mountains and want something gentle, the botanic gardens offer a shady place to wind down. Park, take off the jacket, and let the sound of birds replace the engine.
t.mareeba@-17.0,145.4:
Mareeba is the dry side of Far North Queensland. The town of about eleven thousand lies on the Atherton Tablelands, a plateau behind Cairns, but it sits in the rain shadow, and so the lush rainforest of the coast gives way to open eucalypt woodland, grassland and cattle country. The change is dramatic when you ride up the Kuranda Range from the coast: in an hour you go from wet tropical forest to red earth and dry savannah. The country here was long a tobacco-growing district, and the old kilns are still visible in places, but today the crops are coffee, mangoes, sugar cane and tropical fruits.

The town has a strong frontier flavour. It hosts a rodeo every July, one of the best known in the north, and its main street has a mix of pubs, cafes, a heritage museum and rural supply stores. Coffee is a local pride, and a number of plantations around town offer tastings, which make a good excuse for a stop. The Mareeba Wetlands, a few kilometres outside the town, are a conservation area where jabirus, brolgas and other birds gather in the dry season. Visitors can walk or take a boat on the lagoon.

For a rider, the roads around Mareeba are wide, smooth and fast, with long curves through bushland and rolling hills in the distance. The Kuranda Range Road from Cairns is a winding, forested ascent, and is busy with trucks, but the Tablelands loop is calmer, with plenty of overtaking opportunities, though you should keep to the speed limits. Heat is the main enemy. In the summer wet season, from December to March, storms and humidity dominate, and the roads can flood, while in the dry season, from May to October, the days are warm and the nights cool.

Mareeba has everything: fuel stations, supermarkets, motels and a good selection of cafes. If you are riding the Tablelands loop, it is the sensible place to fill up and eat before heading into the quieter parts. Kangaroos and wallabies are active at dusk and dawn, and they are a real danger, so avoid riding late in the evening. Carry water, and wear a vented jacket, since the air can be fierce.
t.innisfail@-17.5,146.0:
Innisfail is a sugar town, and you can tell from the smell: sweet, slightly burnt, drifting over the cane fields when the mill is crushing. It sits at the mouth of the Johnstone River in the wettest part of Australia, where banana and cane farms run up to the foot of the rainforest, and rainfall is measured in metres rather than millimetres.

The town has an unexpected architectural claim. After a cyclone flattened much of it in 1918, it was rebuilt in the 1920s and 1930s with a distinctive streak of Art Deco, and many of those buildings still line the main street. Later cyclones, including Larry in 2006 and Yasi in 2011, hit the coast hard, and the town's resilience is evident. There is a large Italian and Chinese heritage here, from the cane cutters and market gardeners who settled in the early twentieth century, and it shows in the food: good coffee, good gelato, and Chinese temples tucked in unexpected corners.

The ride in from the Tablelands, down the Palmerston Highway, is the real attraction. The road drops from the cool upland through a succession of bends carved into thick rainforest, with the air getting warmer and heavier as you descend. The Palmerston passes through Wooroonooran National Park, where cassowaries, those large, flightless, blue-necked birds, still roam; road signs warning of them are not decoration, and a slow approach at dawn and dusk is wise. The surface can be damp and slick, leaf litter is common, and fallen branches follow storms. In the wet season, roughly December to April, flash floods can close roads, so check conditions.

Innisfail itself has all the services of a regional town: fuel, supermarkets, takeaway, and accommodation. Nearby, Paronella Park, a Spanish-style castle built in the 1930s by a Catalan immigrant, is a curious ruin among the tropical vegetation and a good place to spend an hour.

Come in the dry months, from May to October, for the best chance of clear skies. Stop for a coffee in town, and watch the afternoon thunderheads build over the ranges.

Epping is a suburb on the northern edge of Melbourne, one of those wide, flat, fast-growing places of shopping centres and fuel stations along the highway, and its job in this ride is simple: it is where you fill up before heading for the coast. Lalor, next door, is the same. Melbourne's suburbs here spread across basalt plains, an enormous flat sheet of old lava that once carried grassland and now carries roundabouts and estates, with the Plenty River skirting the edge.

The Great Ocean Road starts a long way southwest of here. From Epping the usual route is to cross the city on the ring road, join the freeway to Geelong, and then follow the coast through Torquay, where the road proper begins, to Lorne and Apollo Bay and on to the Twelve Apostles. It is a day of about two hundred and fifty kilometres in a single direction if you ride the whole thing. The road itself was built by returned soldiers after the First World War, a work that took more than a decade and was dedicated as a war memorial, so that you are riding through a monument.

Fuel on the coast is available at Lorne, Apollo Bay and Port Campbell but costs more and the stations are far apart on some stretches, so a full tank at the start is sensible. Take note that Victoria has low tolerance for speeding and many cameras, including mobile units on the Great Ocean Road, and that the limit drops through every town. Morning departure matters: get through Melbourne before the traffic builds and you reach Torquay with a clear road.

Weather here changes quickly. Melbourne is known for four seasons in a day, and the coast can be cool and windy when the city is warm. Pack a waterproof layer, and for the early hours in autumn and winter, gloves. Check the forecast for fire danger days in summer, when roads in the Otways can close at short notice. If you are leaving at dawn, a coffee from one of the many cafes near the highway is a fine way to start, and the place is easy to find from the ring road.

Research and Wattleglen are small places on the northeastern fringe of Melbourne, where the suburbs give way to the green wedge of the Nillumbik shire, a hilly, wooded country of orchards, bushland and acreage properties along the Yarra River. Traffic is moderate during the week, but at weekends the roads fill with cyclists, so ride with patience. The surface can be uneven and the gum trees drop branches, bark and leaves on the road, so scan ahead. Speed limits are low and enforced, and wildlife, particularly kangaroos at dawn and dusk, makes night riding unwise.

Warrandyte, a little to the east on the Yarra, has a place in Victorian history: gold was found nearby in 1851, and the diggings were among the first in the colony to be worked. Kangaroo Ground, on the hilltop just north of Research, has a stone memorial tower built in the 1920s as a war memorial, and from its top you look over the ranges, a place that rewards a short climb.

Knoxfield and Scoresby are outer eastern Melbourne suburbs on the flat land at the foot of the Dandenong Ranges, and their label as a high point is the ranges themselves, which rise on the eastern skyline as a long blue-green wall. Mount Dandenong, the highest, reaches about six hundred and thirty metres, which is modest by European standards but impressive from the suburbs, and it is covered by tall wet forest of mountain ash, among the tallest flowering trees in the world.

The ranges are the playground of Melbourne riders, and the roads up the western slopes from Ferntree Gully and Boronia are narrow, twisting and steep, with trees meeting overhead. The surface is mostly good but can be damp and covered in leaves, and weekends bring cars, cyclists and a large crowd of motorcyclists, so the cafes of Olinda and Sassafras fill up. The district has a reputation for police attention, with speed cameras and officers on bikes, so stay within the limits. Weekdays are quieter, and the early hours, when fog sits in the gullies, are the best.

In Sherbrooke Forest you may hear the lyrebird, a ground-dwelling songbird that mimics every sound it hears, from other birds to camera shutters and chainsaws, and the males sing loudly in winter. The One Thousand Steps, a walk up the hillside from Ferntree Gully, is a Melbourne fitness ritual and a memorial to the soldiers of the Kokoda Track. The gardens of the ranges are famous for rhododendrons and tulips, and a spring weekend can be crowded.

Knoxfield and Scoresby have many petrol stations and food outlets along the highways, so nothing is needed from the ranges themselves, where fuel is scarce, and it is best to arrive with a full tank. The ranges can be cool and wet when the plains are warm, so bring a layer. In summer, on days of total fire ban the forest can be dangerous, and visitors should check warnings. In winter mist and cold are common, and some mornings bring frost. A pie from a bakery and a coffee in Olinda is the traditional reward.

Epping is not a place anyone puts on a poster, and I would be misleading you if I said otherwise. It is a suburb on Melbourne's northern edge, sitting beside Plenty Road and the Hume corridor, with big shopping centres, industrial estates and housing built over the old volcanic plains. A ride that has come back from the Great Ocean Road and the Otways has plenty of better places to end, but cities need ways in, and this is one of them.

The ground here is basalt, part of the great volcanic plain that sweeps across western and northern Victoria, and the soil is a heavy, dark clay that grows grass and little else. Before the suburbs, this was grassland dotted with red gums, and a few remnants survive along the creeks, particularly the Darebin Creek and its parks. Wurundjeri people lived in the area, and parts of the creek corridors are carefully managed for both heritage and ecology.

The riding is purely functional. Plenty Road is a busy arterial, the Metropolitan Ring Road and the Hume Highway are wide, fast and heavily policed, and speed cameras are numerous. If you are here at rush hour, accept that you will sit in traffic, and filter carefully, because lane splitting rules in Victoria are specific and not as relaxed as in some other places. Do check what is permitted before you do it.

The upside of a big suburb is convenience. Epping has more than thirty thousand people and every service imaginable: petrol stations, supermarkets, bike shops, and a mix of restaurants shaped by the many communities who settled in this part of Melbourne, including Greek, Italian, Macedonian and Vietnamese families. A good bakery or souvlaki place will do a better meal than any highway roadhouse.

For a more rewarding ride from here, Plenty Road leads north to Whittlesea and on into the hills around Kinglake and the Yarra Ranges. These hills were devastated by fires on Black Saturday in 2009, and the regrowth has transformed the area; the bends are worth a Sunday of their own once you are rested.
t.mornington@-38.3,145.1:
Mount Martha is a bayside town on the Mornington Peninsula, a leafy cluster of beaches, coastal scrub and big houses that rises on the slopes of a low hill between Mornington and Dromana. For a ride described as easy and scenic, it is a fitting place to end: the road runs close to the water, and the sea is rarely out of view.

The peninsula has been a holiday destination for Melburnians since the nineteenth century, when families made the trip by paddle steamer to Sorrento and Portsea. Today it is an affluent area with vineyards, orchards, and cellar doors, and the cool climate produces particularly good pinot noir and chardonnay. The Moorooduc and Tuerong roads inland wind through the wine country, with farm stands selling strawberries in summer and apples in autumn. In Mornington itself, the main street is lively, with good cafés and a weekend market.

The coast is lined with colourful bathing boxes at Mount Martha and Dromana beaches, and the Balcombe Estuary and Mount Martha Park offer short walks through coastal tea tree and banksia. Kangaroos survive in pockets of bush on the peninsula, and koalas are sometimes seen in the manna gums, particularly around Mount Eliza and Arthurs Seat. Arthurs Seat, the highest point on the peninsula, is a short ride away and offers a wide view over the bay and the city skyline, plus a chairlift for those who want it.

Riding conditions are pleasant but busy. On sunny weekends the peninsula's roads fill with cars and cyclists, and the pace is slow, with frequent roundabouts and limits that are enforced by cameras and police. Early mornings and weekdays are best. The Nepean Highway can back up badly on summer Sunday afternoons, so allow for it if you are going back to the city.

With more than seventeen thousand people in Mount Martha, there is no shortage of fuel, food or coffee, and the Mornington township is bigger still. Sunset from the foreshore is often lovely, with the bay going pink and the skyline of Melbourne a faint line in the distance.
t.palm cove@-16.7,145.7:
Palm Cove is the quiet end of the northern beaches north of Cairns, a village of under four thousand people on a curve of sand with a long jetty and an avenue of old paperbark trees along the beachfront, their bark peeling in soft white layers. The paperbarks, or melaleucas, lean over the footpath and give shade to the cafes and restaurants beneath. It is a resort village, calm and a bit upmarket, but small enough that a rider on a road trip can wander in without feeling out of place.

The Captain Cook Highway, which runs along the coast from Cairns to Port Douglas, is one of the loveliest coastal roads in Australia. It leaves Cairns and follows the shoreline, curving between the sea on one side and the dark green rainforest-covered ranges on the other, with the Coral Sea beyond. The road is well surfaced, with wide bends, gentle gradients and plenty of lookouts, though traffic can be heavy, with tourist buses and cars. A steady speed rewards you with a continuous view of beach, headland and cane fields. Speed limits are low in the villages and are enforced.

Swimming here needs care. From about October to May, the box jellyfish and Irukandji jellyfish are present in the tropical waters, and the beaches carry warning signs. Palm Cove has a stinger net enclosure, and the sensible thing is to swim only inside it and to heed any lifeguard's advice. In the cooler months, from June to September, the risk is lower. Crocodiles live in the rivers and estuaries of the region, and signs warn of them, so be sure to follow local guidance. The Wet Tropics hinterland shelters the cassowary, a huge flightless bird, and you may see road signs warning of it.

Fuel is available at nearby Clifton Beach and at Kewarra Beach and the northern suburbs of Cairns, so fill up before heading north. Mornings are the best time to ride, when the light is soft, the air cooler and the traffic thin. The wet season, from December to March, brings heavy rain, humidity and sometimes cyclones, and roads can flood. Winter is dry and warm, and is the high season.
t.moletai@55.2,25.4:
Lithuanians will tell you that Molėtai is where the lakes begin, and the numbers back them up: the district around the town holds well over two hundred lakes, more than any other part of the country, scattered among low wooded hills left by the last glaciation. The town of about seven thousand sits on the shore of one of them, in the region called Aukštaitija, the Highlands, which are not high at all by Alpine standards but give the landscape a rolling shape that flat Lithuania elsewhere lacks. Utena, a bigger town and the nearest with a proper range of services, lies thirty kilometres to the east.

Two unusual institutions are found nearby. The Molėtai Astronomical Observatory, set on a hill outside the town, was opened in the 1960s and benefits from the dark skies of the region, and a museum of ethnocosmology, a short drive away, explores how people through history have understood the stars, with a building designed to look like an observatory. Both give a reason to linger into the evening, when the lakes go still and the sky fills with stars.

The riding in this part of Lithuania is gentle and pleasant. Roads are generally smooth, running between pine forest and birch groves, past farms with wooden fences, wells with long sweeps and storks nesting on poles. Bends are soft and long, with no steep climbs, and the lakes appear as flashes of silver between the trees. Speeds are low and police are active, so keep to the limits. Dusk and dawn bring deer and elk onto the road, and rain makes the surface slick on the older sections. Spring and early autumn have the best colour, though June, with its long light, lasts until nearly eleven at night.

The local food is hearty and a good match for a day on the road. Cepelinai, large potato dumplings stuffed with meat and served with sour cream, are the national dish, and šaltibarščiai, the cold pink beetroot soup, is a summer favourite. Smoked fish from the lakes and dark rye bread can be found in the cafes, along with honey from local beekeepers. Molėtai has fuel stations, a supermarket and a few cafes on the main street, and the shore of the lake is a good place to rest and swim in summer, when the water warms to a comfortable temperature.
t.guatemala city@14.6,-90.5:
Guatemala City sits in a high valley, at around 1,500 metres, ringed by volcanoes. On a clear morning, from a rooftop or a ridge, you can see the cones of Pacaya, Agua, Fuego and Acatenango lined up along the horizon, and Fuego often sends up a white plume of ash. The city has been rebuilt several times after earthquakes, most seriously in 1917 and 1976, and its landscape of gullies and ravines, crossed by high concrete bridges, makes it feel both modern and fragile. At its centre, in Zone 1, stand the cathedral, the National Palace and a big plaza where families come to sit and talk.

The city has an odd, layered history. Before the Spanish, a great Maya city, Kaminaljuyú, stood on the site, and its earthen mounds survive in a park in the western part of town. The modern capital was founded in the 1770s after earthquakes destroyed the colonial capital at Antigua. Today it is a vast, noisy, hard-working metropolis of coffee and corporate towers, with food that ranges from street tamales and tortillas to elaborate dishes in the fashionable Zone 10.

Riding here is intense. Traffic is dense and aggressive, motorbikes weave between lanes, and the streets run in grids that are easy to get lost in. The highways out of town, the CA-1 and CA-9, climb quickly into pine forest and cooler air, and the road toward Antigua and Lake Atitlán is where the riding becomes enjoyable, with long bends and wide views. Ride in daylight, keep your belongings out of sight, and take local advice on areas to avoid. Rain falls heavily between May and October, usually in the afternoon, so aim to start early.

Fuel is plentiful, with stations on every major road and open around the clock in the larger roads, and food ranges from pollo campero to modern restaurants. Choose a hotel with a secure garage, as street parking is risky overnight, and do not leave luggage on the bike. Altitude can give a mild headache for the first day, so drink plenty of water and take it slowly.
t.san cristobal el alto@14.5,-90.7:
San Cristóbal El Alto clings to the hills above Antigua Guatemala, on the road that climbs toward San Juan del Obispo and Santa María de Jesús. The air here is cooler than in the valley, scented with pine smoke and coffee, and on clear mornings the three great volcanoes of the area, Agua, Fuego and Acatenango, stand along the skyline like a drawn curtain. Fuego, the active one, is often puffing a plume of ash into the sky, which makes for a dramatic backdrop.

The history here is Antigua's. The old Spanish capital was founded in 1543 after an earlier site was destroyed by a mud flow from Agua, and it was abandoned after the earthquakes of 1773. Its ruined churches and convents, with their broken arches and carved stone, make it a UNESCO World Heritage Site. San Juan del Obispo, just above, had the bishop's residence, an old house with a handsome courtyard and a small chapel, where the town's bishops once retired from the heat of the valley. The surrounding villages have a Maya character, with women in woven huipiles and small markets where the produce is stacked in bright piles.

The ride up is a joy. The road climbs from Antigua in a series of tight bends, past coffee farms, flower nurseries and roadside stalls, with steep drops and good views down over the city and the valley. Cobbles appear on the village sections and can be slick in the rain, and buses and trucks take the corners wide, so be ready to give way. Dust and ash can lie on the road, particularly after an eruption, and afternoon cloud often rolls in, turning a clear morning into drizzle by three.

San Cristóbal is small and has no major services, but Antigua, only three or four kilometres below, has fuel stations, restaurants and many hotels, including some with secure parking for bikes. Stop on the way for a coffee at a farm or a roadside stall, and try a hot chocolate with spices in one of Antigua's old cafés. Leave before the afternoon rain if you plan to ride the hairpins again.
t.musanze@-1.5,29.6:
Musanze is the town you go through to reach the gorillas. It lies at the foot of the Virunga volcanoes in the north-west of Rwanda, a high, cool town of tidy streets and bustling markets, with the cones of Bisoke, Karisimbi and Sabyinyo rising behind it like props from a film. The mountains are shared with Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and the border lies not far off. The population is large, more than eighty thousand, so Musanze has fuel stations, banks, supermarkets and a whole industry of guides and drivers.

The road from Kigali is well surfaced and runs about a hundred kilometres through a landscape of terraced hills, banana groves and small farms, climbing steadily as it goes. Rwanda is called the land of a thousand hills, and from the saddle of a motorcycle you feel every one. The curves are tight and frequent, the surface good, and the sights endless: people carrying huge loads on their heads, boys pushing bicycles stacked with sugar cane, and women in bright dresses at the roadside. Motorbike taxis, called motos, are everywhere, and their riders are brisk and skilled, so keep your distance and watch for sudden stops. Helmets are required by law, and traffic police are active.

The reason most people come is the mountain gorillas of Volcanoes National Park, which can be visited on guided treks that must be booked in advance and are costly. Dian Fossey, the American primatologist, spent years studying them here and is buried near the research camp she founded on the slopes of Karisimbi. The park has helped the gorilla population to recover, and the revenue supports local communities. If you are not trekking, the lakes Burera and Ruhondo, a short drive away, are lovely, and the lava caves near Musanze are worth a visit.

The climate is cool and often wet, with two rainy seasons, from March to May and from October to November, and the roads can be slippery. The dry months of June to September are best for riding. Musanze is famous for its potatoes, and you will find them everywhere, fried, boiled or stewed with goat. Carry some small notes for the roadside stalls, and fill the tank in town before heading for Gisenyi and Lake Kivu.
t.rusizi@-2.5,28.9:
At the southern tip of Lake Kivu the water squeezes out into the Rusizi river and tumbles down toward Lake Tanganyika, and the Rwandan border town of Rusizi, once and still often called Cyangugu, sits right at the hinge. Across the river is Bukavu, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, close enough that you can see its hillside houses and hear the traffic on a quiet evening. Check the border situation before you plan anything beyond this bank; for most riders, this is the end of the road.

The ride here from the north is a long one, and by the end you know the lake's moods. The Congo Nile Trail follows the shore with a lot of climbing, short sharp hills, and cuts between fishing villages and coffee slopes. Lake Kivu is odd water: deep, calm, with no hippos or crocodiles, but with dissolved methane in the depths that Rwanda now taps to generate electricity. In the evening the fishermen set out in boats lashed together in threes, singing as they paddle.

South of town the road climbs into Nyungwe, one of the oldest rainforests in Africa and home to chimpanzees and a long list of other primates, plus an astonishing number of bird species. The road across the forest toward Huye is among the most beautiful in the country, but it is often damp, misty and cold, with sudden bends and little traffic after dark. Keep your speed down, watch for monkeys at the verge, and carry waterproofs. Fuel is available in Rusizi, which is a town of more than sixty thousand people, but fill up in town before heading into the forest.

Rusizi is also a pleasant place to stop and do very little. The waterfront has small restaurants where you can order grilled tilapia from the lake with fried plantains, and Kamembe, the town up the hill, has the hotels and the airport. The best months are June to September, when the roads are driest and the views clearest.
t.fethiye@36.6,29.1:
Above the harbour at Fethiye the cliff has been carved into a Greek temple front. The tomb that Lycian craftsmen cut for a man called Amyntas in the fourth century BC stares out over the bay from about halfway up the rock, and once you have seen it you start spotting smaller tombs in the hillside all around the town. Fethiye sits on the site of ancient Telmessos, at the western end of the Lycian coast, where the pine-covered Taurus mountains drop into a wide bay full of islets. An earthquake in 1957 flattened much of the town, so the centre is modern, but the setting is lovely: a long waterfront with boats going out to the islands, and restaurants where you can pick your fish from the ice.

For a rider, Fethiye is the place where the coast road begins to show its character. The D400 heads east toward Kaş, Demre and Antalya, and once you pass the last tourist suburbs it settles into a rhythm of long climbs through pine forest and drops to sheltered bays, with views across the Mediterranean that make you want to stop at every layby. Surface quality is generally good, bends are broad and medium-fast, and traffic is lighter outside the summer peak. Be cautious in July and August, when minibuses and tourist cars clog the road and heat hammers the tarmac.

Ölüdeniz, about seven kilometres south, has the famous turquoise lagoon and the paragliders who jump from Babadağ, a mountain that rises nearly two thousand metres above the sea. Butterfly Valley and the ghost village of Kayaköy, an abandoned Greek town left empty after the population exchange of the 1920s, lie nearby, and the contrast between the empty stone houses and the busy beach is hard to forget.

Fethiye has about sixty thousand people, which means fuel, workshops and hotels in every price range. Breakfast at a local place can include honey, olives, cheese and fresh tomatoes, and the fish market near the harbour is a short walk from anywhere. The best months are May, June, September and October, when the sea is warm and the roads are less crowded.
t.kalkan@36.3,29.4:
Kalkan used to be Kalamaki, a Greek village, and the whitewashed houses that tumble down its hillside to a small harbour are the legacy of that older life. In 1923, when Greece and Turkey exchanged their populations, the Greek families left and Turkish families from the islands and mainland arrived to take their place, and the town's name was changed to a Turkish one that means shield, perhaps for the rock face behind it. Today Kalkan is a smart, small resort of about three thousand people, with narrow lanes, bougainvillea over the doorways and roof terraces that look out over the Mediterranean toward the sunset.

The D400 coast road between Fethiye and Kaş is the finest stretch of the Turkish Mediterranean, and Kalkan sits in the middle of it. The road climbs along the cliffs, drops to sandy coves, then climbs again, with views over a sea so blue that it looks like an exaggeration. The surface is generally good, the bends open and the speed limits plausible, though you should watch for lorries, tour buses, and dolmuş minibuses that stop without warning. Wild goats sometimes cross the road. In summer the heat is fierce and the sun low, so wear sunglasses and a light jacket for the evening.

The area is dense with ancient sites. Patara, about fifteen kilometres to the west, has a very long beach of pale sand where sea turtles nest, along with the ruins of a Lycian and Roman city, including a half-buried meeting hall of the Lycian League, an early federal parliament. It is also said to be the birthplace of Saint Nicholas, who became the model for Santa Claus. Further inland, the Saklıkent gorge cuts a dark slot into the mountains, and the ruins of Xanthos stand on a hill above the river valley.

Kalkan has fuel on the main road and a small harbour where fishing boats and gulets tie up. Food is the town's great pleasure: mezes in the evening, fresh fish grilled over charcoal, and the sweet, flaky pastry known as baklava. Kaş, a larger town, lies twenty-one kilometres further east, and it has more of everything. The best months are May, June, September and October, when the sea is warm and the roads are quiet. In midsummer, ride in the early morning and swim in the afternoon.
t.kas@36.2,29.6:
Kaş is a harbour town with a past that sits in plain sight. In the middle of the old town, carved into the rock above the road, is a Lycian tomb, a stone tomb cut like a house with columns and a pediment, some two thousand four hundred years old, and above the town on the hill there are more. The Lycians, a people of southwest Anatolia who spoke their own language and built their own cities, chose to bury their kings in high places so that eagles could carry their spirits away, or so the story goes. The Greek name of the town was Antiphellos, and there is a small Hellenistic theatre by the sea, which still looks over the water as it did in antiquity.

The town today is a laid-back, pretty place of about eight thousand people, with a small harbour, a bazaar of narrow lanes, bougainvillea and wooden balconies, and a good supply of bars and restaurants. Two kilometres offshore lies the Greek island of Kastellorizo, which Turks call Meis, so near that you can pick out the houses on its waterfront, and a daily ferry connects the two. Divers come for the wrecks, caves and clear water, and boat trips run to Kekova, where the ruins of a sunken Lycian city lie in the shallows.

The road in from Kalkan, along the D400, is one of the best in the country, with long curves above the sea, and the road onward toward Demre and Antalya climbs through pine forest and along cliffs. The surface is mostly good, though traffic can thicken in July and August. Wind is common in the afternoon, so keep a firm grip on the bars when the road runs along open stretches. Evenings are warm and the light is soft, a good time to ride.

Kaş has everything: fuel stations on the approach roads, supermarkets, cafes, bakeries and plenty of rooms. Fish restaurants on the harbour serve the day's catch with salad and bread, and a plate of mezes with a glass of rakı is the traditional way to spend the evening. Try the local yoghurt, which is thick and sharp. In the cooler months the town is quiet and charming, and you can have the roads almost to yourself. Mind the sudden rain showers that can turn the road slick.
t.cukurici mound@37.9,27.4:
Most visitors to Ephesus head for the marble street and the big theatre, but a few kilometres away, on the edge of the plain, a low earth mound hides an earlier story. Çukuriçi Höyük is the remains of a village that people began to settle about 8,500 years ago, in the Neolithic, long before Greek colonists came to the river mouth and long before anyone built a temple to Artemis. Archaeologists have found houses of mudbrick, obsidian tools traded from far-off islands, and signs of early farming. It is the kind of place where you have to read the information boards and use your imagination, because there are no towers or columns. What you see is a gentle hump in the ground, olive trees, and a view toward the hills.

That is exactly why it is worth the short detour. The Ephesus area, with its modest town of Selçuk, makes a good base for a day's riding, because so much lies close together. The marble ruins of Ephesus are a short ride away, the huge Basilica of St John stands on a hill above Selçuk, and a lone column is all that is left of the Temple of Artemis, once counted among the Seven Wonders. Storks nest on the old Byzantine aqueduct in town, and you will see them clacking from their nests in spring.

Roads here are flat or gently rolling, running between orchards, fig trees, olive groves and fields of cotton. Surfaces are mostly good, but local traffic includes tractors, scooters and tourist minibuses. Leave early in summer when midday temperatures climb above thirty-five, and take water. West of Selçuk the road leads to the beach towns around Kuşadası, with the Aegean glittering beyond, and in the other direction toward the mountains and the village of Şirince, known for fruit wines and stone houses.

Selçuk has about thirty thousand people, so fuel stations, cafes and pensions are plentiful. Try gözleme, a thin flatbread stuffed with cheese or spinach and cooked on a griddle, and have a glass of tea under the plane trees. April, May and October are the best months, warm and quiet.
t.gordonvale@-17.1,145.8:
Gordonvale lies at the foot of the mountains south of Cairns, in a flat, green valley of sugar cane, and above it rises a peculiar peak. Walsh's Pyramid, a steep-sided, conical mountain of about 920 meters, is claimed to be the highest free-standing pyramid-shaped mountain in the world, and every year runners race to its summit in a local event. The mountain makes a dramatic backdrop to a town that is otherwise a modest working place, with a sugar mill that sends up steam, cane trains and old timber houses.

The town has a place in the history of an unfortunate animal. In 1935, a batch of cane toads, imported from Hawaii to eat the beetles that damaged the cane, was released at Gordonvale, and the toads multiplied beyond all control, spreading across northern Australia. A cane toad statue in town marks the spot, a wry monument to ecological error. The Mulgrave River runs through the valley, and the green hills behind hold rainforest.

For motorcyclists, Gordonvale is the base of the Gillies Range Road, the Gillies Highway, which climbs to the Atherton Tablelands in about nineteen kilometers, with some two hundred and sixty tight bends, hairpins and steep grades. It is among the best known twisty roads in Queensland, winding through dense rainforest, with tree ferns, vines and glimpses of the coastal plain far below. At the top, the Tablelands offer a different world, cooler and drier, with lakes, farms, waterfalls and the village of Yungaburra, where you may see platypus in the creek at dusk.

Gordonvale has fuel, a supermarket and cafes, and Cairns, about twenty-five kilometers north, has everything. Fill up before climbing, as the range has no services. The best months are May to October, the dry season, with warm, sunny days, while the wet season, from December to March, brings heavy rain, landslips and occasional cyclones that can close the road. Trucks use the range road, so take care on blind corners, and watch for cassowaries, large flightless birds that sometimes cross the road in the rainforest.
t.ravenshoe@-17.6,145.5:
Ravenshoe is the highest town in Queensland, at about nine hundred and thirty metres, and you feel it the moment you climb out of the tropical coast: the air thins and cools, the cane fields give way to cattle pasture and tall eucalypt forest, and in winter there is a morning chill that surprises people who have come from Cairns in shorts. The town sits on the volcanic soils of the Atherton Tableland, red and rich, with remnants of rainforest on the edges. It began as a timber settlement, and was named after the novel Ravenshoe by Henry Kingsley, which a local timber getter was fond of, according to the story.

The surroundings repay a visit. Millstream Falls, a few minutes from town, is a broad curtain of water that is said to be the widest single-drop waterfall in Australia, spilling over a basalt lip into a pool. On the hills above town a wind farm, one of the first in the country, turns slowly in the steady air from the Coral Sea. Tully Falls, further south, is a long white fall in the forest, best in the wet season. The forests here are home to tree kangaroos, platypus in the creeks, and cassowaries, the big flightless birds that can be dangerous if they are surprised, so slow down in rainforest sections where signs warn of them.

For riders, the Palmerston Highway is the attraction. It climbs from the coastal plain near Innisfail through rainforest, with tight bends, a rolling climb and lovely shaded corners, and arrives at Ravenshoe in cool air. The surface is generally sealed and decent, but wet leaves, mud and damp patches are common, and mist can cut visibility. Beyond the town, the roads across the Tableland towards Atherton are smoother, with sweeping views over farmland.

Fuel is available in Ravenshoe, and Atherton, thirty-eight kilometres away, is the next sizeable town. A cafe or bakery in the main street is a good place to warm up. The dry season, from May to October, offers the best riding, with clear days and cool nights, while the wet season brings heavy rain and flooding.
t.ligatne@57.2,25.1:
Līgatne is a small town on the Gauja river in the heart of Latvia's biggest national park, and it has an unusual double character. On one side is its past as a company town, built around a paper mill that has been making paper here since the early nineteenth century and which gave the town its rows of tidy workers' houses and its handsome old buildings. On the other is its present as a gateway to nature, with forest trails and a nature park where wild animals live in large enclosures and can be seen from walkways. Bears, wolves, lynx and elk, all native to Latvia's forests, can be watched in surroundings that look more like the wild than a zoo.

There is also a surprise under the hills. Near the town stands a Soviet-era bunker, built in secret in the Cold War as a refuge for the Latvian Communist leadership in case of nuclear attack, and now open to visitors on guided tours. It is an eerie place, with long corridors, offices, a bakery and a command room, all preserved as they were when the Soviet Union collapsed. Tours should be booked in advance, and they are a good way to understand what life was like behind the Iron Curtain.

The Gauja valley is a landscape of sandstone cliffs, caves, pine forest and a winding river, and the best way to see it is slowly. A small cable ferry crosses the river here, pulled across by the current, and is a charming reminder of an older way of travel. The valley's cliffs, often covered in graffiti from centuries of visitors, are reached by short walks, and a stretch of the river is popular for canoeing in summer.

The riding is pleasant, with smooth roads through forest and farmland, gentle bends and light traffic. The roads along the valley offer views across the river and the cliffs, and cyclists are common in summer. Elk and deer can cross at dusk, so keep your speed sensible. Autumn is spectacular, when the forest turns red and gold and mist fills the valley in the mornings. Avoid gravel roads after heavy rain, since they can be soft.

For services, Līgatne has a shop, cafes and guesthouses, but the larger town of Sigulda, about fourteen kilometres away, is the main stop for fuel, restaurants and supermarkets. Sigulda also has a castle, a cable car across the valley and a bobsleigh track used in international competitions, and makes a good complement.

Plan to spend a few hours here. The nature park and the bunker are worth the time.
t.valmiera@57.5,25.4:
Valmiera is the biggest town in northern Latvia, a river city of nearly twenty-seven thousand people on the Gauja, and it feels like a place with its own life rather than a waystation. Its history goes back to the thirteenth century, when the Livonian Order, the German crusading knights who controlled much of the Baltic, built a castle here, and the ruins still stand on a hill above the river. The Church of St Simon, a tall Gothic building with a brick tower, is one of the oldest in Latvia, and its bells ring across the town. The town was heavily damaged in the Second World War, and much of the centre has a plain look, but it has been rebuilt with parks, riverside paths and a lively market.

The modern town is known for industry and education. Valmiera makes glass fibre, and the factory is one of the biggest employers, and a university college adds a young population. Local beer is a point of pride, and a brewery in the area offers tastings. The town is also strong in sport, with basketball a particular passion, and the arena is a social centre on match days. Parks and a stretch of the Gauja with sandstone cliffs, a short walk from the centre, offer a quiet place to relax.

For a rider, Valmiera is a good base for exploring the Gauja National Park, which begins a short way south. The roads here are generally good, with smooth surfaces, gentle bends and light traffic, and the scenery is a pleasant mix of forest, river valley and farmland. Elk and deer are a risk at dusk, and in winter the roads can be icy, with snow from November to March. Summer evenings are long and warm, and the riding in June and July is a delight, with light until late.

The town has everything you need. Fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants are plentiful, with Latvian dishes such as grey peas with bacon, rye bread soup and smoked fish on offer, and cafes along the main street. Hotels and guesthouses are easy to find, and prices are lower than in Riga. Strenči, about eighteen kilometres to the north-east, is a smaller town on the road to Estonia.

Take a walk by the river in the evening, when the light is soft and the town is quiet.
t.winding stair mountain@34.7,-94.7:
Winding Stair Mountain is a long, forested ridge in southeastern Oklahoma, and the Talimena Scenic Drive follows its crest like a thread along a hem. The Ouachita Mountains are unusual in the United States because they run east to west, not north to south, folded into long parallel ridges with broad valleys between them, and from the top you can see row after row of blue ridges receding into Arkansas. The elevation is only around 800 metres, but in this flat part of the country it feels like a proper mountain range.

The road was built in the 1960s as a scenic route, and its name is a blend of two towns: Talihina in Oklahoma and Mena in Arkansas, fifty-four miles apart. On a motorcycle it is a gentle, rewarding ride. The curves are easy and well banked, the surface is smooth and the traffic is light, especially on weekdays. Pull-outs appear every few miles, each with a view over a wooded valley, and the ridge-top forest of oak, hickory and shortleaf pine creates a green tunnel in summer. The ride is at its best in October, when the maples and sweetgums turn red, and in early spring, when the redbuds and dogwoods bloom.

Weather is the main thing to watch. Thunderstorms in spring and early summer can be violent, and the ridge is exposed to wind, so keep an eye on the radar. Winter ice can close the drive, and the road is not maintained as a priority route. There is wildlife, with white-tailed deer, wild turkeys and, in places, black bears, and at dusk the deer are a real hazard.

The country's history is mostly that of the Choctaw, who were forced here from the south-east on the Trail of Tears in the 1830s, and the area still carries many Choctaw place names. Further west, Heavener Runestone Park has a stone carved with symbols that some people believe to be Norse runes, a legend as stubborn as it is unproven.

Talihina at the western end, Heavener and Poteau to the north, and Mena to the east all have petrol, and the pit stops of choice are small-town diners serving chicken-fried steak and pie. Carry water and a layer, and tell someone your route, because mobile coverage is patchy along the crest.
t.queen wilhelmina state park@34.7,-94.4:
A mountaintop state park named after a Dutch queen is the sort of fact that needs explaining, and the explanation is a railway. In the 1890s Dutch investors in the Kansas City Southern line, which ran through the nearby town of Mena, built a grand hotel on the crest of Rich Mountain and named it for their young queen, Wilhelmina. The original hotel did not last, but the name did, and the present lodge, rebuilt in the 1960s, sits on the same ridge with a view that spreads over Arkansas and, on a clear day, a long way beyond.

At around 800 metres the summit is the highest point in the area, and the park feels like a small island above the forest. A miniature train runs in season, a few trails wander through the oak and pine woods, and the little campground gets busy at weekends. The air is cooler than in Mena, and the lodge has a restaurant that is popular for its view across the valley.

The road up is part of the Talimena Scenic Drive, the high route along the Ouachita ridges that runs west into Oklahoma. From Mena, Highway 88 climbs from the valley in a series of easy, flowing bends, and the surface is generally good. The gradient is steady, the curves are gentle, and the road is quiet outside peak seasons. Mist often fills the valleys on cool mornings, and autumn brings brilliant colour in the hardwoods, with red from the maples and gold from the hickories. In winter, ice and snow can close the road, and fog can be dense.

Mena, about sixteen kilometres away, is a small town with petrol, shops, cafes and motels, and it is the place to stock up before climbing. The park has its own picnic areas and a small gift shop, and the lodge is open most of the year, though hours vary. Evenings on the ridge are lovely, with a long, orange light over the hills and crickets in the grass. Keep an eye out for white-tailed deer on the road, and in summer for the wasps and ticks that thrive in the woods.
t.sulphur@30.2,-93.4:
Sulphur is the working front door of Louisiana's Cajun coast, a refinery and chemical town in Calcasieu Parish a few minutes from Lake Charles. It may not look like the start of a nature trail, and that is part of the point. The industrial flares and stacks give way, a short ride south, to marsh, bayou, and open Gulf, and the contrast is the story of this corner of Louisiana.

The town takes its name from the sulphur deposits found deep underground in the late nineteenth century. The mineral was too deep and too hot to mine in the usual way, and the engineer Herman Frasch devised a method of pumping superheated water down to melt it and bringing it up as liquid. That innovation made Louisiana a major source of sulphur for decades. The town still feels like a place built by industry, with plain roads and practical buildings, and it deserves a little respect for that.

For a rider, Sulphur is a practical stop, and a good one. This is the last place with a full range of services before the Creole Nature Trail heads south into the marsh. Fill the tank, buy water, and eat something solid, because the villages farther on are small and sometimes thin on offerings. A bowl of gumbo or a plate of boudin, the spicy rice sausage that Cajun country takes very seriously, is easy to find around here. The nearby town of Carlyss is smaller, and Lake Charles is the larger city to the east, with everything a traveller could want.

South of town, the riding changes completely. The land flattens, the road runs dead straight for long stretches, and the sky grows large. Wind off the Gulf can push a bike around, especially on exposed causeways and bridges, and summer brings heat, humidity, and sudden storms. Mosquitoes in the marsh are a fact of life, so keep a visor closed when you stop. The best seasons are spring and autumn, when migrating birds crowd the wetlands, and winter days can be clear and mild. Hurricanes are the great risk of late summer, and in recent years they have reshaped this coast more than once.
t.peterhof@59.9,29.9:
Peterhof is Peter the Great's answer to Versailles, built on the south shore of the Gulf of Finland, and for a few weeks of the year it is the only place in Russia where the fountains outshine the architecture. The palace stands on a bluff above the sea, and from its terrace the Grand Cascade tumbles down toward the canal, with golden statues and a central figure of Samson wrestling a lion, the symbol of Russia's victory over Sweden at Poltava in 1709. A straight canal runs from the cascade to the Gulf, and the park is full of lesser pavilions, fountains and shaded avenues.

Construction began in the 1710s, as Peter founded Saint Petersburg and wanted a country residence near the sea, and it was expanded by later rulers, especially Elizabeth. Monplaisir, the small pavilion by the water, was Peter's own favourite, simple and low, with a view of the gulf, and it is a good counterweight to the splendour of the main palace. The estate was almost completely destroyed in the Second World War, when the German army occupied the site and burned the buildings, and the restoration that followed is one of the great postwar achievements. The fountains run from about May to early October, and the water is gravity-fed, without pumps, from springs on the higher ground.

For a rider, Peterhof is a stop on a coastal route, and the approach is less romantic than the destination, with urban roads, traffic lights, and heavy traffic on weekends. Expect crowds, parking restrictions, and coach parties in summer, and plan to arrive early or late. The road along the shore has some pleasant stretches between the town and Saint Petersburg, with views of the gulf, though speed limits and cameras are common. Wind off the water can be chilly even in July, and autumn brings rain and fog.

Fuel and food are no problem. Peterhof is a large town, with petrol stations on the main roads, cafés and restaurants around the park, and plenty of hotels. Tickets for the palace and the lower park are separate, and the lines can be long, so book in advance if you can.

Walk down the canal to the sea, and look back at the golden cascade in the afternoon sun. It is theatre on a grand scale.
t.izborsk@57.7,27.9:
Izborsk claims to be older than Russia, which is a bold thing for a village of a thousand people. The Primary Chronicle records that in 862, the Varangian prince Truvor, brother of Rurik, took up residence in Izborsk, and so the site is counted among the oldest settlements in the country. Whatever the truth of that story, the hill is certainly ancient: a limestone ridge above a valley, topped by a stone fortress whose first walls date from the fourteenth century and whose long, towered curtain still stands, grey and lichened, among meadows and birches. It guarded the western border against the Livonian knights, and it was rebuilt, besieged and burned repeatedly.

You walk up through a gate and find yourself in a space that is mostly empty, with grass, a small church, and a wide view across the valley toward Estonia. Below the fortress, a road winds down to a group of springs known as the Slovenian Springs, which gush from the foot of the hill and feed a stream, and which have been regarded as holy for centuries. The cold water tastes of minerals, and people fill bottles at the troughs. In spring, the valley is covered with flowers, and in autumn, it turns gold.

The ride from Pskov is a pleasure in the way that quiet, rolling countryside can be. The roads run through fields, birch woods and small villages, with long gentle curves, gravel verges and wide views. The surface is patchy in places, with frost heave and repairs, and you should watch for tractors, cattle and the odd pothole. Traffic is light, and the best seasons are late May to early October. In July, the heat can be considerable, and thunderstorms roll in during the afternoon. Remember that you are close to the Estonian border, and a border zone applies, so carry your documents, and avoid wandering off toward the frontier.

Fuel is not available in the village, and the nearest sizeable town is Pechory, about nineteen kilometres away, where several stations and shops can be found. Izborsk has a few small cafés and guest houses, and a hot meal of soup and pies is a good idea after a morning on the road.

Stay for the evening if you can. The light on the walls is warm, and the swallows circle the towers.
t.pechory@57.8,27.6:
Pechory has a monastery that never closed, which in Russian history is nearly a miracle. The Pskovo-Pechersky Monastery, founded in 1473 around a set of caves in a sandstone ravine, has been in continuous use for over five hundred years, even through the Soviet period. The reason is an accident of geography. Between 1920 and 1940, the town belonged to independent Estonia, under the name Petseri, and the monastery stayed open under a government that did not persecute it. By the time the Red Army arrived, in 1940, and later when Stalin turned a blind eye after the war, it had become too well known to close, and it survived the anti-religious campaigns.

The caves are the heart of it. Monks carved galleries into the soft sand, and for centuries buried their dead in niches along the walls, so that the passages are lined with hundreds of simple graves, each marked with a name. Visitors can go down with a candle and a guide, and the air is cool and still. Above ground, the monastery is a compact fortress, with whitewashed walls, golden domes, and a church built into the cliff, and it is a lively place, with pilgrims, monks, and a bookshop. Dress modestly, with covered shoulders and knees, and women need a headscarf.

The town lies in the westernmost part of the Pskov region, a few kilometres from the Estonian border, and the area has a distinctive character, with Estonian-built houses from the interwar period, the Setu people, a small Finno-Ugric community that straddles the frontier, and a feel of an end of the line. Because it is a border zone, you should carry your passport, and be cautious about riding off toward the frontier.

The riding is easy and rural. The road from Pskov runs through farmland and small villages, with long straights and gentle rises, and a surface that is mostly decent. Summer is the main season, and May to September is the sensible window. Rain is frequent, and the land is green.

Fuel and food are easy, since Pechory is a town of thirteen thousand with several stations, shops, cafés and a few hotels. It is the best place for supplies for miles around, and you should fill up before heading to Izborsk or the villages. Go down into the caves, if you can, and notice how the sound changes. Outside again, the bells will seem louder.
t.yagodnoye@62.5,149.6:
Yagodnoye means berry place, a sweet name for a town that grew out of one of the hardest chapters of Soviet history. It stands on the Kolyma Highway in the heart of Magadan Oblast, in the gold and tin country that was developed in the 1930s by the Dalstroy organisation using the labour of prisoners. The road itself, nicknamed the Road of Bones for the people who died building it, passes right through, and many older residents have family stories that stretch back to the camps. About four thousand people live here now, in a settlement that has been shrinking since the end of the Soviet period.

For a rider, reaching Yagodnoye is a major achievement. The Kolyma Highway is a long, remote and demanding route, with sections of good asphalt interrupted by gravel, mud, and frost heave that can throw a bike off line. Traffic is light, but trucks are heavy and fast, so give them room, especially on blind bends. The weather is changeable, with cold mornings and warm afternoons in summer, and snow and ice at either end of the season. July and August are the most practical months, though early September can be beautiful with golden larch. Winters here are among the coldest in the inhabited world, with temperatures that regularly fall below minus forty.

Fuel, food and basic accommodation are available in Yagodnoye, which is the main supply point for a very long stretch of road. Fill the tank, check the bike, stock up on food and water, and be prepared for the next distances, because the next real services may be many hours away. Local cafes serve hearty dishes, usually soup, meat and potatoes, and the people are used to travellers who arrive tired and dusty.

The land around is taiga and mountain, with larch forest, bog and rivers that run clear and cold, and it is wild country with bears, wolves and elk. Look for the traces of the gold mining past, from old dredges to abandoned settlements, and remember that these places have a human story that deserves respect. At the right moment, in the long light of a July evening, the larch forest turns warm and soft, and the road seems to belong to a quieter and less violent age.
t.main component@-17.2,145.8:
Inland from the cane fields south of Cairns, the land rears up into a wall of rainforest so dense that the ridgelines seem to steam after every shower. These coordinates sit in the heart of the Wet Tropics of Queensland, the World Heritage forest that runs along the coastal ranges of the far north, here in the country between the Mulgrave and Russell rivers. Gordonvale lies about fourteen kilometres to the north, Babinda a little further south, and the tableland town of Yungaburra up over the range to the west.

This forest is old in a way few places are. It holds lineages of plants that date back to Gondwana, when Australia was still joined to Antarctica, and it shelters creatures you will not see elsewhere: the cassowary, a flightless bird as tall as a person that should be given the road and plenty of room, tree kangaroos, musky rat-kangaroos and electric blue Ulysses butterflies. Above it all stands Bartle Frere, Queensland's highest mountain, usually wrapped in cloud. The Aboriginal rainforest peoples of this country, among them the Yidinji, have lived here for many thousands of years and still hold the land's stories.

For riders, the nearby Gillies Range Road is the headline act: a climb from the coastal flats near Gordonvale up to the Atherton Tableland, with a famously long sequence of tight bends packed into a short stretch. It is a joy on a dry morning and a slippery, leaf-strewn test after rain, which here is often. Watch for caravans crawling uphill, cyclists, and wildlife at dawn and dusk. The Bruce Highway along the coast is flat, busy and dull by comparison, so use it only to link the good bits.

Gordonvale has fuel, a bakery or two and a pub, and Babinda is known for its Boulders, a swimming hole in clear mountain water, though signs warn that the currents there have claimed lives and should be taken seriously. The dry season from about May to October is by far the most comfortable time; in the wet, cyclones and flooded causeways can shut roads for days. Bring rain gear whatever the forecast says.
t.izhorsky bench@59.7,29.9:
South of St Petersburg, the flat marshy plain of the Neva lowland suddenly steps up onto a limestone plateau. Geologists call the edge a glint or bench, and here, near Russko-Vysotskoye and Kipen, it forms a low but noticeable escarpment, the northern edge of the Izhora plateau. It is one of the natural features included in the wide UNESCO listing of St Petersburg and its surroundings, which recognises not only palaces and canals but the landscape the city was built against.

The plateau is made of ancient Ordovician limestone, and water filters through it and bursts out in springs at the foot of the bench, feeding clear streams and small lakes. These springs were once vital for the imperial palaces and villages, and many are still visited by locals filling bottles. In spring the woods along the bench are full of wildflowers that like the lime-rich soil, and in summer the fields above are thick with grain and hay. Nearby, the Duderhof heights rise above the plain, the highest ground in the St Petersburg area, with views across to the city on a clear day.

This is gentle country to ride, with long straight roads across fields, birch woods and villages of wooden houses, punctuated by towns with Soviet apartment blocks. Road quality varies a lot, from smooth highway to patched secondary roads with deep potholes, and traffic around the city can be heavy and impatient. Summer nights here are very short; around the white nights of June it barely gets dark at all, and you can ride late in a soft silvery light. Winters are long, dark and icy, and motorcycle season effectively runs from May to September.

At the time of writing, many governments advise against travel to Russia, and entry, insurance and payment can be complicated for foreign visitors, so check the current situation carefully before planning a visit. Fuel stations are frequent along main roads, and Gorbunki and the villages nearby have shops and cafés. The palace parks of Peterhof and Ropsha are close by, and Fort Totleben out in the Gulf of Finland marks the far edge of the old defences of the capital.
t.memorial sites of the genocide nyamata@-:
This is a place to arrive quietly. The label names Nyamata, the church in the Bugesera district south of Kigali where thousands of people who had sought refuge were killed in April 1994, but the coordinates sit in the southern highlands near Nyamagabe, the former Gikongoro, close to Murambi, another of the memorial sites. Both belong to the group of four genocide memorials, Nyamata, Murambi, Gisozi in Kigali and Bisesero, that UNESCO inscribed on the World Heritage list in 2023, recognising them as places of remembrance of the genocide against the Tutsi, in which some eight hundred thousand to a million people were murdered in about a hundred days.

At Murambi, a technical school on a hilltop became a killing site when tens of thousands of people who had been told they would be protected there were attacked. At Nyamata, the church still holds the clothes of the victims piled on the pews, and the walls and roof bear the marks of grenades and bullets. Both memorials are harrowing, and visitors should be prepared for what they will see. Guides, many of them survivors or relatives of victims, explain the history with great dignity. Photography is often restricted, and respectful dress and behaviour are expected.

The journey to the south of Rwanda takes you through a landscape of extraordinary beauty, which makes the history all the harder to grasp. The country is known as the land of a thousand hills, and the roads wind endlessly up and down steep slopes covered in terraced fields, banana groves and tea plantations, with views over valleys and ridges in every direction. The main roads are generally well paved and well maintained, though they are busy with minibuses, trucks, bicycles carrying heavy loads and pedestrians walking along the edges.

To the west of Nyamagabe lies Nyungwe National Park, a vast mountain rainforest home to chimpanzees and many other primates, with a road crossing the forest that is one of the most spectacular in East Africa. Nyamagabe and Huye, the former Butare, have fuel, food and accommodation. Rwanda has strict rules on plastic bags and on speed limits, which are enforced by cameras and police. Ride carefully, take time to absorb what you have seen, and remember that the people you meet live with this history every day.
t.ropshinskoe highway@59.8,29.9:
Ropshinskoe Highway is the road that leaves the Gulf of Finland behind at Peterhof and climbs gently south towards Ropsha, and for a ride that starts and ends here it is a good place to look at a map and understand the ground. You are on the edge of the Izhora upland, a low limestone step above the coast. It never looks like much from the saddle, a few tens of metres of rise through birch and pine, but in this flat country that step decided who could see whom, and that mattered enormously in the last century.

The road itself is simple riding: two lanes, long straights broken by soft bends, villages with dachas behind green fences, and the occasional bus stop where people wait with shopping bags. The surface varies from fresh asphalt to patched sections that rattle the mirrors, so keep your eyes open after rain and in spring, when frost heave leaves ridges across the lane. Weekend traffic out of St Petersburg can be thick in summer as everyone heads for the dacha, and slow lorries are common. Early on a June morning, under the white nights, the light lies low and gold across the fields and the whole thing feels very far from the city.

Ropsha at the far end has a dark footnote. In July 1762 the deposed Emperor Peter III was held at the palace there after his wife seized the throne as Catherine the Great, and within days he was dead, officially of colic, almost certainly at the hands of his guards. The palace is now a ruin. Closer to the coast, Peterhof and its fountains were the Romanovs' showpiece, and between 1941 and 1944 this whole belt was front line, with the German siege ring of Leningrad running close by. Trenches and memorials are scattered through the woods if you look.

Practically, Peterhof is the town with everything: fuel stations on the main road, cafes, shops and the crowds of the palace park. Ol'gino and Gorbunki nearby have the basics. Out on the highway itself services thin quickly, so leave with a full tank. Mosquitoes in the forest edges in July are no joke; keep the visor down when you stop.
t.oranienbaumsky springboard@59.8,29.7:
The Oranienbaum Springboard is not a single building but a piece of ground, and once you know the story the low woods and fields south of the Gulf of Finland look entirely different. In September 1941, as German and Finnish forces closed the ring around Leningrad, a pocket of coast around Oranienbaum, today's Lomonosov, held out. It was cut off from the city by land, supplied across the water and under the guns of Kronstadt, and it never fell. In January 1944 the Second Shock Army broke out of this pocket as one jaw of the offensive that finally lifted the siege.

Riding here today, you are on quiet regional roads between Gostilitsy, Lomonosov and Petrodvorets, through mixed forest, peat bogs and small farms. The country is gently rolling, with the Izhora plateau rising to the south, and the roads are a mix of decent asphalt and rougher village stretches. Corners are few and friendly; the pleasure is in the space and the light rather than in lean angle. Watch for tractors, loose dogs and unmarked potholes, and in autumn for wet leaves on the bends under the trees.

Memorials mark the old perimeter at intervals, often a gun, a tank on a plinth or a simple obelisk with fresh flowers at its foot. Locals still come on Victory Day and on the January anniversaries. The siege cost the city something like a million civilian lives, and the soldiers who held this pocket did so in cold and hunger not much better than inside the city. It is worth stopping, switching off and simply listening; the woods are very quiet.

Nature has long since taken the trenches back. Birch and alder grow out of the shell craters, cranes cross the fields in spring and autumn, and elk are not unusual at dusk, which is a good reason to keep the speed down on forest stretches late in the day. Gostilitsy is small; for fuel, food and a proper meal, Petrodvorets and Lomonosov on the coast road are the places, each with filling stations, shops and cafes. From Lomonosov you can also see the long dam to Kronstadt across the water, the fortress island that kept this coast alive.
t.component around russell river@-17.3,145:
Rain is the first fact of life along the Russell River. The river drains the eastern slopes of the Bellenden Ker Range, south of Cairns in far north Queensland, and these mountains, including Bartle Frere, at 1,622 metres the highest peak in the state, catch the moist trade winds off the Coral Sea and wring out some of the heaviest rainfall in Australia. The result is a dense, steaming tropical rainforest that tumbles down the mountains to the coastal plain, part of the Wet Tropics of Queensland World Heritage Area, listed in 1988. It is one of the oldest continuously surviving rainforests on earth.

The forest is alive with strange creatures. The southern cassowary, a huge flightless bird with a blue neck and a horny casque on its head, roams the forest floor and occasionally the roadside; give it plenty of room, because it can be dangerous. Tree kangaroos, musky rat-kangaroos, brilliant blue Ulysses butterflies and a dazzling array of birds and frogs live here. Near Babinda, the Babinda Boulders are a series of pools and granite boulders in a clear, fast creek, beautiful but deceptively dangerous, with a long list of drownings; heed the warning signs. Josephine Falls, on the slopes of Bartle Frere, has natural rock slides and swimming holes.

The coastal plain below is sugar cane country, with small towns built around sugar mills, narrow-gauge cane railways crossing the roads, and the smell of burning cane and molasses during the crushing season from about June to November. Babinda is a classic example, a small town that grew up around its mill, with the cane trains rattling past the end of the main street.

The Bruce Highway runs north to Cairns and south to Innisfail through the cane fields, flat and busy with trucks. For better riding, head inland: the Gillies Range Road from Gordonvale climbs to the Atherton Tableland in a famous series of hairpins, popular with riders, with dense rainforest on either side and views across the plain. On the tableland, Lake Eacham and Lake Barrine are crater lakes surrounded by rainforest. Watch for cassowaries, wet roads and slow cane trucks. Babinda has fuel and basic shops; Gordonvale and Innisfail are larger. The wet season, from December to April, brings torrential rain, floods and cyclones; the dry season is warm and pleasant.
t.component around malaan@-17.6,145.6:
Up on the Atherton Tableland, behind Cairns in far north Queensland, the land rises from the hot coastal plain to a cooler plateau of volcanic soil, rolling farmland and patches of dense rainforest. Near Ravenshoe, which claims to be the highest town in Queensland, the forest around Malaan is one of the components of the Wet Tropics of Queensland World Heritage site, a long strip of tropical rainforest along the coast and the Great Dividing Range that contains some of the oldest continuously surviving rainforest on Earth. The forests are home to tree kangaroos, possums, rare frogs and birds, and, in the lowlands, the cassowary, a large flightless bird with a bony crest that is best admired from a distance.

The tableland is a land of waterfalls. Millstream Falls, near Ravenshoe, is one of the widest single-drop waterfalls in Australia, especially impressive after the wet season, and the famous waterfall circuit around Millaa Millaa takes in several more, cascading over basalt into pools surrounded by ferns. The volcanic lakes, Lake Eacham and Lake Barrine, are great places for a swim in clear, cool water, and the giant curtain fig tree near Yungaburra, with its roots hanging like a curtain, is a sight not to be missed.

The riding is some of the best in Queensland. The Palmerston Highway descends from Millaa Millaa through the rainforest of Wooroonooran National Park towards Innisfail on the coast, with plenty of bends, and the Gillies Range Road from Gordonvale to Yungaburra climbs hundreds of metres in a long, tight sequence of curves, one of the most famous motorcycle roads in the region. The Kennedy Highway links Ravenshoe with Atherton and Mareeba. Roads can be slippery in the wet season, roughly December to April, and cattle and wildlife, including wallabies, can appear at any time.

Ravenshoe has fuel and a few shops and pubs, and Atherton, the main town of the tableland, has everything you need.
