Try the local produce, which is excellent: tropical fruit, coffee grown on the tableland, cheese from the dairy farms around Malanda, and avocados. The tableland can be surprisingly cool in winter, so bring a warm layer for the evenings.
t.historical centre of the town of peterho:
Peter the Great wanted a palace by the sea that would rival Versailles, and he chose this stretch of the southern shore of the Gulf of Finland, about thirty kilometres west of Saint Petersburg. What became Peterhof is a town built around an imperial residence: the Grand Palace on a terrace above the sea, the Grand Cascade of gilded statues and fountains falling toward a canal that runs straight to the water, and parks full of pavilions, including Peter's own small Dutch style house, Monplaisir, right on the shore. The fountains run on gravity, fed by springs on the higher ground inland, a feat of eighteenth century engineering.

The town itself grew around the palace, with churches, barracks, villas and a nineteenth century cathedral of Saints Peter and Paul in red brick. During the Second World War Peterhof was occupied and badly damaged, and much of what you see today was painstakingly restored after 1945. The Prioratsky Park, nearby, contains a curious palace built for the Order of Malta in the late eighteenth century, made of compressed earth.

The road from Saint Petersburg runs along the coast, busy with traffic, buses and tourists, especially in summer. It is not a great ride in itself, but the views over the gulf are lovely, and Kronstadt, the naval fortress town on an island, is reachable via the dam that crosses the gulf. Further west, Lomonosov, formerly Oranienbaum, has another palace and park.

Arrive by boat if you can bear to leave the bike for a few hours: hydrofoils run from the city centre in summer and land at the pier at the foot of the canal, which is how many people first see the cascade, framed by the palace above.

Practical matters for foreign riders in Russia are complicated at present, with travel advisories, insurance and payment restrictions to consider, so check the current situation carefully before planning any trip. Fuel and services are plentiful in Peterhof and the surrounding towns. The fountains generally run from late spring to early autumn, and the parks are busiest on weekends and holidays; early morning is the best time to visit.
t.nyungwe national park@-2.6,29.2:
Nyungwe is one of the oldest rainforests in Africa, a mountain forest spread over the ridges of south-western Rwanda between Lake Kivu and the Burundi border. It is high, wet and green in a way that makes the rest of the world feel dry: tree ferns taller than a house, orchids on the branches, mist pouring through the valleys in the morning, and the sound of water everywhere. The ridges here form part of the great divide between the Congo and Nile basins, and Rwanda proudly claims one of the remotest sources of the Nile in these hills.

For a rider, the gift is the road. The main highway from Huye in the east to Rusizi on Lake Kivu crosses the whole park, and it is well paved, beautifully engineered and absolutely full of bends, climbing and falling through the forest for the best part of an hour. There are few villages, little traffic beyond buses and trucks, and baboons and monkeys sitting at the verge. The weather is the main challenge: rain can arrive any afternoon, the road gets slippery under leaf litter, and fog can drop visibility to a few metres. Drive on the right, keep speeds sensible, and expect speed checks on the approaches.

The park is home to chimpanzees and a dozen or so other primate species, including the acrobatic L'Hoest's monkeys and large troops of Angola colobus. A canopy walkway near Uwinka lets you walk out over the treetops. On the western edge the forest gives way to the tea estates of Gisakura, emerald terraces cut into the hillsides, a striking frontier between wild and cultivated.

Rwanda's history is impossible to ignore, and one of these rides connects Nyungwe with the genocide memorial at Nyamata, one of the most harrowing places you will ever visit. Seeing the country's calm, clean and orderly present afterwards puts the scale of what was rebuilt into perspective.

Fuel is the thing to plan. There is nothing inside the park, so fill up in Huye or in Rusizi, Cyangugu as it used to be called, on the lake, about forty kilometres from here, before you enter. Bring warm and waterproof layers even on a hot day, because the higher sections of the road are surprisingly cold. Park entry and activities require permits arranged in advance.
t.component around edmund kennedy@-18.2,14:
North Queensland has the oldest rainforest on the planet, and it stands beside the Great Barrier Reef, with the two meeting in a few places where the trees come down to the sea. Edmund Kennedy National Park lies on the coast near Cardwell, between the Bruce Highway and the Coral Sea, and it protects a lowland strip of tropical rainforest, mangroves and swamps. It is named after the explorer Edmund Kennedy, who landed in the nearby Rockingham Bay in 1848 on an expedition to Cape York, and died after months of hardship, speared by Aboriginal men near the northern tip. Only three of his party of thirteen survived, thanks in part to Jackey Jackey, an Aboriginal guide who stayed with him.

The park is part of the Wet Tropics of Queensland, listed by UNESCO in 1988, which are among the oldest continuously surviving rainforests, with plants whose lineage goes back well over a hundred million years. The cassowary, a huge flightless bird with a blue neck and a casque like a helmet, lives here, and warning signs along the road ask drivers to slow down. In tidal creeks, saltwater crocodiles are present, so it is not a place to swim, and from November to May, box jellyfish, the stingers, make the sea dangerous.

The Bruce Highway runs through Cardwell and Tully, and the road is long, straight in places, and at other points, particularly the Cardwell Range, a winding climb with views over Hinchinbrook Island. Speed limits are enforced, traffic includes road trains and tourist buses, and wildlife on the road, from wallabies to cassowaries, requires care at dawn and dusk. Remember to keep to the left. The wet season, from December to March, brings heavy rain and the occasional cyclone, and Cardwell and Tully were hit hard by Cyclone Yasi in 2011.

Cardwell, a small seaside town, has fuel and a good seafront, and Tully, which claims to be the wettest town in Australia, has more shops. Murray Falls, up a side road, gives a pleasant walk through rainforest. Carry water, wear insect repellent and keep an eye on the clock, because daylight ends quickly in the tropics, and the best months for riding are May to October.
t.the lugovoy@59.9,29.9:
Peterhof is the work of a tsar who wanted his own Versailles on the Gulf of Finland. Peter the Great began the palace and its gardens in the early eighteenth century, and by the time of his daughter Elizabeth and later of Catherine the Great, the Great Cascade, with its gilded statues and its fountains, was one of the most extravagant waterworks in Europe. Behind the formal gardens, the Lugovoy, meaning the meadow park, is a larger, quieter landscape of open lawns, ponds, tree-lined paths and old oaks, a place where Petersburgers come to walk dogs and push prams on weekends.

The twentieth century was brutal here. Peterhof was occupied by German forces from 1941 to 1944, and the palace was burned, the statues carried off or smashed, and the park cut down. After the war, restorers rebuilt it piece by piece, and the central statue of the Great Cascade, Samson wrestling a lion, which had been taken, was recreated in 1947. The whole complex is part of the UNESCO listing for Saint Petersburg and related monuments.

Across the bay, the fort of Krasnaya Gorka and the other coastal batteries are part of the wartime story, as they held out against the invaders. The town of Peterhof, with about seventy thousand people, has fuel, restaurants and plenty of shops, though in summer the roads to the palace fill with tour buses. Ol'gino, a little east, is smaller.

For a rider, the old Peterhof Highway from Saint Petersburg is an easy run, wide and fast, with traffic lights and heavy trucks. The park itself is for walking, not riding, and the gardens are best seen on a weekday morning, before the crowds. The fountains run from May to early autumn, and the water, moving through the park on gravity alone, is a wonder. In October the leaves turn gold and the fountains are switched off with a ceremony.
t.the water bringing system of peterhof@59:
The fountains of Peterhof run without a single pump, and that is the cleverest thing about them. When Peter the Great planned his gardens in the 1710s and 1720s, engineers led by Vasily Tuvolkov worked out that the water of the Ropsha hills, about twenty kilometres to the south, stood high enough above the Gulf of Finland to feed the fountains by gravity alone. They dug canals, built ponds and laid pipes, so that the water flows from the heights to the Upper Garden and down to the Great Cascade, where it shoots high into the air. The system, still essentially the same, is part of the UNESCO listing for Saint Petersburg.

The landscape around Ol'gino, where this system passes, is quiet and rural: meadows, birch groves, drainage channels and small ponds, with the water slipping through stone-lined canals. It is not a showpiece, so do not expect a visitor centre at every corner, but there is real satisfaction in following a canal that has run for three hundred years. Fishermen like the ponds, and herons stand in the shallows.

The nearest town is Ol'gino, small, and the large town of Peterhof has fuel and shops. The Gulf coast, with the coastal fort Shanets and the old batteries, lies not far from here, and it forms part of the defensive line that held during the siege of Leningrad. The monuments of the Blockade Ring are on the same route and connect the engineering of the eighteenth century with the war of the twentieth.

The roads in this area are flat and straight, with rural lanes between fields and woods. Surfaces are mixed, with patches of broken asphalt, and rain turns the verges to mud. It is peaceful riding, with light traffic outside the weekend rush. Late spring and early summer, when the meadows are in bloom and the evenings are long, are the best times, and in autumn the birch and aspen turn yellow along the canals.
t.malia@35.3,25.5:
Malia is two things in Crete at once: a beach resort known for loud nights, and the site of a Minoan palace that is nearly four thousand years old. The first palace was built around 1900 BC, destroyed by an earthquake or invaders, rebuilt about 1650 BC and then destroyed again around 1450 BC, the same wave of disasters that ended Minoan power across the island. It was excavated by French archaeologists from the 1920s, after a local scholar, Joseph Hatzidakis, had begun work in 1915. It is the third in size of Crete's great palaces, after Knossos and Phaistos.

What you see today is a maze of low walls, storerooms and big pithoi, the huge storage jars, with a wide central court once used for ceremonies. In the west court stands a strange stone disc, the kernos, with hollows around the rim, perhaps used for offerings of grain or oil, and its purpose remains a mystery. The setting is a flat plain between the mountains and the sea, planted with olives, so you can almost hear the sea from the ruins.

Malia town itself, with about four thousand permanent residents, swells in summer with holidaymakers, and has fuel, supermarkets, tavernas and bars. The old town, a short walk from the beach, is quieter, with traditional houses and cafés. Agios Nikolaos, to the east, is a prettier town with a lake in the middle, and Heraklion, the capital, is about thirty-five kilometres west. Order Cretan food, such as dakos, a rusk with tomato and cheese, and lamb with wild greens.

The roads are excellent for riding. The old national road along the coast is busy, but inland, the road climbs toward the Lasithi Plateau, a high plain ringed by mountains and once dotted with white-sailed windmills, which used to pump water for crops. The climb is a series of hairpins through olive and almond groves, with huge views. Summer is hot, so ride early, while spring brings wildflowers and autumn gives warm, soft light. Meltemi winds in July and August can be strong on exposed ridges, so keep a firm grip.
t.gostilitskoe highway@59.9,29.8:
Peterhof is famous for its fountains, and the road called Gostilitskoe runs along the high ground behind the palace, where the water begins. When Peter the Great decided in the early eighteenth century to build a rival to Versailles on the southern shore of the Gulf of Finland, the engineers had a problem, because the ground at the shore is flat, and a fountain needs a head of water. They found springs and ponds on the Ropsha heights, a few kilometres inland, and built a system of canals, reservoirs and pipes that carried water downhill to the palace by gravity alone, without a single pump. That system, the Water-bringing system of Peterhof, still works, and it is a marvel of its time.

The fountains themselves, which number in the hundreds, include the Samson, a golden figure tearing open a lion's jaws in front of the Grand Palace, which commemorates the Russian victory at Poltava on St Samson's day in 1709. The park runs down to the sea, and the Maritime Channel, a straight canal, brings the water to the gulf. During the Second World War the palace was gutted by German forces, and it was rebuilt from photographs and memory. It is one of the great restoration stories of the century.

This is gentle country, a plain of fields and birch woods rising slowly to the Izhora uplands, with old estates and small villages along the road. The soil is poor and the winters are long, but in June the meadows are loud with insects and the light is high and clear. Oranienbaum, now called Lomonosov, is a short ride along the coast, and has a palace of Prince Menshikov, Peter's favourite, that survived the war intact.

The road itself is straightforward riding: broad, flat and fairly fast, with a decent surface in summer and potholes after the thaw. Traffic is heavy on summer weekends with tourists heading for the fountains, so go early. Peterhof, Petrodvorets and Lomonosov have fuel, supermarkets and cafés, and Saint Petersburg is half an hour away. Entry conditions can change, so check what applies to you. The fountains run from late spring to early autumn, and are switched off for the winter.
t.the historic centre@37.3,26.6:
Patmos is a small island, only about thirteen kilometres long, in the Dodecanese, and it is famous for one reason. Tradition holds that the apostle John was exiled here by the Roman authorities in the first century and received the visions recorded in the Book of Revelation in a cave on the slope below the town. The Cave of the Apocalypse, with its rock cleft where the voice of God was said to speak, is still a place of pilgrimage. Above it, the fortress-like Monastery of Saint John the Theologian was founded in 1088 by the monk Christodoulos, with a charter from the Byzantine emperor, and it rises over the white houses of Chora like a castle.

Chora, the old town, is the true historic centre. Its narrow lanes, steps and whitewashed walls were laid out around the monastery for protection against pirates, and its mansions were built in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries by captains and merchants who grew rich from trade. UNESCO listed the town and monastery in 1999. Walking it at dusk, when the day trippers have gone back to the boats and the light turns gold, is the best time, with the Aegean spreading in every direction and the neighbouring islands floating in a haze.

A motorbike is exactly right on Patmos. The roads are few and short, winding between low, bare hills, small bays and stone walls, with the whole island a ten-minute ride in any direction. The climb to Chora is steep, with a few tight bends, and in the old town itself the lanes are too narrow for vehicles, so leave the bike at the edge and walk. The meltemi, the strong north wind of summer, can blow hard in July and August, and sand and gravel gather on corners. Spring and autumn are the loveliest seasons, with fewer visitors.

Skála, the port, has most of what a rider needs: the fuel station, cafes, bakeries and tavernas by the water. The ferries arrive here, and the connection to the mainland takes many hours, so plan your timings carefully. A plate of grilled octopus, a Greek salad and a glass of local wine at a harbour table make an unhurried end to the day. The ride goes across the water, in thought at least, to Ephesus in Turkey, where tradition places the House of the Virgin Mary.
t.the mordvinov s estate@59.9,29.8:
Peterhof's fountains get the attention, but the coast road west of it, running along the Gulf of Finland toward Oranienbaum, is the better introduction to the landscape. The Mordvinov estate, named for a family of Russian statesmen and naval officers, belongs to the string of country houses that nobles built along this shore in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, when Peter the Great's new capital pulled the whole aristocracy to the Baltic. A famous Admiral Nikolay Mordvinov, a liberal economist and president of the Admiralty Board in Catherine's and Alexander's time, is the best-known bearer of the name, though I cannot swear that he is the owner meant here.

The setting is flat and wooded, a low coastal plain with sandy soil, birch and pine, and a shoreline of reeds and shallow water. The roads are straight and well maintained, with heavy traffic near the city and in summer, and the surface is generally good, though the edges can break up after winter. Riding in the early morning or evening, when the light slants through the trees and the gulf glows pale, is far better than at midday, when the roads fill with day trippers. The white nights of late May to July, when it never gets fully dark, give this region a distinctive, dreamy atmosphere.

Petrodvorets, the modern name of Peterhof, has about sixty-two thousand people and Lomonosov, the old Oranienbaum, over forty thousand, so fuel and food are easy. Petrodvorets has the Grand Cascade and the palace that Peter intended as a Russian Versailles. Lomonosov has Menshikov's palace, a gaudy, handsome relic of Peter's favourite, and a park along the sea. Both were badly damaged in the Second World War and painstakingly restored.

Conditions can change quickly in the gulf, with fog or sudden rain. Winter is long and cold, and the snow season runs from November to March or April. If you stop by the water, notice how shallow the gulf is, and how far the reeds reach, and how the whole coast seems to be waiting for the next season.
t.s k grieg s estate sans ennui@59.9,29.7:
Samuel Greig was a Scottish naval officer from Inverkeithing who rose to become an admiral in Catherine the Great's navy, and in 1788 he fought the Battle of Hogland against the Swedes in the Gulf of Finland, a few weeks before dying of fever at Reval. He is the S.K. Greig of the label, Samuil Karlovich in Russian style, and an estate on this coast called Sans Ennui is associated with the family, French for without boredom, a charming name for a country house. The site lies near Bolshaya Izhora, west of Lomonosov, where the land is flat, wooded and close to the water, and the Izhora river flows toward the gulf.

Riding here is straightforward. The roads follow the coast through birch and pine woods and low fields, with a good surface in most places and moderate traffic, rising in summer when dachas fill up and day trippers head for the beaches. There are few bends to speak of, but the changing light on the water makes the ride pleasant, particularly in the long evenings of early summer. In winter the roads ice over and the whole district falls silent under snow. You will also find the Troitse-Sergieva Pustyn, the Trinity-Sergius Hermitage, which stands near Strelna, a monastery founded in the early eighteenth century and revived after the Soviet years.

Bolshaya Izhora is a small place of under four thousand people, so fuel and services are best found in Lomonosov, about six kilometres away. The town has over forty thousand inhabitants and the fine palace and park of Oranienbaum, which survived the siege of Leningrad because the front line stopped nearby, and the area was held by Soviet troops as a bridgehead for years. That fact gave the old estates a lucky survival rate that many neighbours did not enjoy.

Pull up somewhere with a view of the gulf and think of the Scottish admiral, who built a career and a country house on the far side of Europe from his birthplace. Russia in the eighteenth century drew in sailors, doctors, engineers and gardeners from across the continent, and the shoreline here is dotted with their stories.
t.house of virgin mary@37.9,27.3:
High above Ephesus, on Bülbül Dağı, the Nightingale Mountain, there is a small stone house in a pine wood that Christian tradition, and a certain amount of nineteenth-century detective work, links with the last years of Mary. The story goes that John the Apostle brought her to Ephesus after the crucifixion. In the 1800s a German nun, Anne Catherine Emmerich, described the house in visions, and a French priest set out to find it and identified the ruins. The Catholic church has never officially declared it authentic, though several popes have visited, and both Christians and Muslims, who honour Mary as Meryem Ana, come to pray here. A wall outside is covered with folded notes and strips of cloth bearing wishes.

The building is small, with a chapel, and the air is cool and fragrant with pine. A spring nearby is said to heal, and pilgrims queue at its taps. It is a gentle, quiet place, in pleasing contrast to the crowds below at the ancient city.

The approach from Selçuk is a short climb of about five kilometres on a well-surfaced road, with a handful of hairpin bends and views over the Aegean plain. It is a lovely little ride, particularly early, before coaches arrive, or late in the day when the light is low and the valley is gold. In midsummer, expect heat and congestion, with a one-way flow for buses, and be prepared to park well. In winter the road is quiet and the air is clear, though rain can bring slippery leaves.

Selçuk is a friendly town with fuel stations, bakeries, cafés and a weekly market, and a good place for a long lunch of grilled meat or fish. Kuşadası, a little further to the coast, is bigger and busier, with plenty of services. Down in Selçuk you will also find the remains of the Temple of Artemis, one of the ancient wonders, of which just a single column stands, and the Basilica of St John. A small entrance fee is charged at the house, and modest dress is expected. Carry water and some small change for the donation boxes.
t.cairns@-16.9,145.8:
Cairns sits in the tropical far north of Queensland, with the Coral Sea on one side and a wall of rainforest mountains on the other, and the whole town is organised around the idea of being a launch pad. Boats leave daily for the Great Barrier Reef, small planes head for Cape York, and the road north runs up to the Daintree, where the oldest rainforest on earth meets the beach. The town was founded in the 1870s as a port for the goldfields at Hodgkinson River and later became a sugar and tourism centre. It is not especially pretty in the old-town sense, but the Esplanade, with its saltwater lagoon, mudflats full of waders and cheerful backpackers, has a relaxed tropical air.

The reason a rider starts here is the Tablelands. From Cairns you climb the Kuranda Range, or take the Gillies Highway, which twists up through some hundreds of bends in a few kilometres of forest, and then reach the cool, dairy-farm plateau around Atherton, with crater lakes, waterfalls and volcanic soil. It is tremendous motorcycle country, with smooth asphalt, good camber and generally respectful traffic, and the contrast between sweaty coast and cool upland is part of the pleasure. Look out for cassowaries on the roads in the rainforest, which are big, dangerous birds, and for tour buses on the narrow bends.

The wet season, roughly December to April, brings humidity, cyclones and flooded roads, and the stingers, box jellyfish, make swimming in the sea inadvisable then. From May to October the weather is dry and mild, which is the ideal riding time. Mornings are the freshest and clearest, and the mountains can be shrouded in cloud by afternoon.

Everything is easy in Cairns, from fuel stations to repair shops, hotels and restaurants. The pedestrian-friendly night markets and the Rusty's Markets in the daytime sell fruit like mangosteen, rambutan and custard apples, and there is good seafood, including barramundi and Moreton Bay bugs. Once you leave town the stations thin out in the hills, but Kuranda, Mareeba and Atherton all have fuel, so just keep an eye on the gauge. Pack a rain jacket whatever the forecast, and sunscreen for the lowlands.
t.the zubov s estate otrada@59.9,29.7:
Oranienbaum is the old name of Lomonosov, and the story of the town begins with a man who liked to build on a grand scale. Alexander Menshikov, one of Peter the Great's closest friends, laid out a palace here on the south shore of the Gulf of Finland in the early eighteenth century, and the place became a favourite residence of the imperial family. Today its park and palaces are part of the Saint Petersburg ensemble that UNESCO listed in 1990.

The Zubov estate, called Otrada, which means delight or comfort, belongs to the quieter side of Lomonosov. It is one of the manor houses that grew up along this coast, built for the nobility who followed the court. The sea is close, the park is shaded, and the sense of a country retreat is still strong. Detail matters less than atmosphere here: birch avenues, ponds, and the long light of a northern summer evening.

Oranienbaum's biggest surprise is how much survived. Unlike the palaces of Peterhof and Tsarskoye Selo, it was not occupied by German troops in the Second World War, because the Oranienbaum bridgehead held out through the siege of Leningrad. The Chinese Palace, built for Catherine the Great, escaped with little damage, and its painted rooms are among the most delightful in Russia. Nearby, the little fortress of Peterstadt belonged to Peter III, Catherine's husband, who played at soldiers here before his overthrow in 1762.

The road along the coast from Saint Petersburg to Lomonosov is a ride of about forty kilometres, mostly flat and fairly fast, with plenty of traffic near the city and quieter stretches beyond. Summer is the season, with long evenings and warm light, but the sea breeze can be cool. Winter brings ice and snow, and the coast road can be treacherous. There are speed cameras on many sections, and local drivers are not always patient.

Lomonosov is a town of forty-two thousand people with pumps, shops and cafés, so supplies are no problem. A walk in the lower park, with the sea at the end of the avenue, is a good way to spend an hour.
t.the park alexandria@59.9,29.9:
Alexandria Park is one part of the great Peterhof estate that most visitors skip, which is a good reason to visit it. Peterhof is known for its Grand Cascade and golden statues, the fountains that Peter the Great designed to rival Versailles, and for the crowds that pack the Lower Park in summer. Alexandria, on the other side of the road, is quieter, with winding paths, ponds, old oaks and a collection of small romantic buildings set among the trees.

It was created in the 1820s as a gift from Emperor Nicholas I to his wife Alexandra Feodorovna, a Prussian princess who loved Gothic fantasies, and the name is hers. The centrepiece is the Gothic Chapel, a miniature cathedral of white stone designed in a German Gothic style and standing on a rise in the park. The Cottage Palace, built as a summer home for the imperial couple, is a rambling, asymmetrical house in an English cottage style, far from the grandeur of the formal palaces. The royal family loved it for its informality, and it was the favourite summer retreat of Nicholas.

The park is also a place of rest after the formal fountains. Visitors wander through avenues of lime and oak, along an artificial lake and past pavilions, many of them being restored. It lies along the Kronstadtskoe Highway, the road that leads from Peterhof toward the coast and the Dam, so it is an easy place to stop on a longer ride.

Riding to Peterhof from Saint Petersburg means about thirty kilometres of busy road along the south shore of the gulf, with traffic jams in summer, but the road itself is wide and decent. The gulf is just out of sight to the north. A quieter ride is early morning or evening, when the light is low and there are fewer cars. In winter snow and ice can make the road difficult.

Peterhof, with seventy-three thousand people, has fuel, cafés and supermarkets, only two and a half kilometres from the park. There is a modest entry charge, and opening hours change by season, so check ahead.
t.bisesero@-2.2,29.3:
Bisesero is a place where the story is carried by the hills themselves. In April 1994, in the first weeks of the genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda, thousands of people from the surrounding area fled to the steep, wooded ridges of Bisesero, above Lake Kivu, and held out for weeks against armed attackers with sticks, stones and whatever they could find. They were eventually overwhelmed, and tens of thousands were killed in the area, in one of the worst massacres of the genocide. Today a memorial site stands on the hillside, with mass graves and a small museum, and survivors and guides are on hand to explain what happened.

It is a place that asks for quiet and a sober attitude. Visitors should come with respect, dress modestly, avoid taking photographs of human remains and follow the guidance of the staff. It is not a stop to fit in between two other things.

The road to it is among the finest in Africa. The route along Lake Kivu, from Gisenyi in the north to Kibuye, now called Karongi, and on to Cyangugu in the south, follows the shore with steep forested slopes above it, and the road clings to the hillsides in constant bends. Lake Kivu lies at about 1,460 metres, so the climate is mild, and the water, which is one of the African Great Lakes, is deep and calm. The surface of the main roads in Rwanda is notably good, with clear markings and few potholes, and traffic is light, though motorbike taxis, buses and trucks are common. Rain is heavy from March to May and in the autumn, and the mud on side tracks can be treacherous.

Rwanda enforces helmet laws strictly, speed limits are monitored, and plastic bags are banned, a policy that has made the country remarkably clean. Fuel is available in Karongi, a town of nearly fifty thousand people, and the main towns along the route, but is sparse in the countryside. The road onward leads south to Nyungwe National Park, one of the oldest rainforests in Africa, where chimpanzees and colobus monkeys live in the canopy.

Eat simply in Karongi, at a lakeside restaurant with a fish brochette, a local speciality, and take a moment to think.
t.sestu kalns ziestu@56.8,25.6:
Somewhere in the Latvian countryside, on a modest rise above the Daugava, stands a marker that was once part of the most ambitious measuring job of the nineteenth century. Sestukalns is one of the stations of the Struve Geodetic Arc, a chain of triangulation points that runs for nearly three thousand kilometres from Hammerfest on the Arctic coast of Norway to the Black Sea. The astronomer Friedrich Georg Wilhelm Struve, working out of the observatory at Dorpat, now Tartu, led the survey between 1816 and 1855 to find the size and shape of the Earth, and the result was accurate to a degree that astonished geodesists. It is on the World Heritage list, with a few dozen of the stations that still survive across ten countries.

Nothing about the landscape is dramatic, and that is exactly why the arc worked: Latvia is gentle, with low ridges, pine woods, farms and slow rivers, and its sky is wide. The Daugava, the great river that runs from Russia past Daugavpils and Jekabpils to Riga, has been dammed in several places, and the stretch near Koknese and Plavinas was drowned by reservoirs in the twentieth century, so the old rapids lie beneath the water. The ruins of the medieval castle of Koknese stand on a promontory above the reservoir. The rides that use this stop link the Struve station with the old town of Jekabpils, known in German as Jacobstadt after Duke Jacob of Courland, and with the historic centre of Riga.

On a motorbike, Latvia is easygoing rather than dramatic. The main road along the Daugava, the A6, carries trucks and cars at speed, so the quiet side roads are more pleasant, with gravel in places, farmsteads, storks nesting on poles in summer and long straight avenues of birch. Police patrol, and speed limits drop sharply near villages. Expect long summer evenings in June, when the sun barely sets, and flat, golden light in September, with mushrooms for sale along the verges. Winter is cold and dark, with snow and ice.

Aizkraukle, some thirty-five kilometres away, is the nearest sizeable town, with fuel stations, shops and cafes, and Jekabpils on the other bank has a similar range. Out in the villages, services are scarce, so top up when you can. Try rye bread, smoked fish, pirags, the bacon-filled bread rolls, and a glass of kvass or a local beer at a roadside cafe. Riga is about a hundred and twenty kilometres to the north-west, an easy ride on the main road.
t.ayasuluk hill@37.9,27.4:
The hill of Ayasuluk is where old Ephesus went to live when the harbour silted up. As the sea retreated from the ancient city and the Cayster river filled the bay with mud, the people drifted north-east to this ridge, which already held a shrine to St John, and a new town grew around it. Tradition says that John the Evangelist spent his last years in Ephesus and was buried here, and in the sixth century the emperor Justinian built a huge domed basilica over the supposed tomb, with a marble floor and a nave of great length. The ruins stand on the slope today, with fragments of columns and arches, and you can walk among them in the shade of cypresses.

Above the basilica, a fortress crowns the summit, its walls Byzantine in origin and later rebuilt by the Seljuk Turks and others, and the view from the ramparts is wide, taking in the town of Selcuk, the plain, the ruins of Ephesus in the distance and, on a clear day, the sea. At the foot of the hill, the Isa Bey Mosque, built in 1375, is one of the oldest mosques in Anatolia, a calm courtyard with a dark prayer hall. Nearby, a single reconstructed column marks the site of the Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, which once stood here with more than a hundred columns and now lies mostly under reeds and standing water.

Selcuk is an easy town to enjoy. It has about thirty thousand people, a Saturday market, storks nesting on old Roman arches, and small restaurants where you can eat grilled meat and salad in a courtyard. The ride visits the Lydian burial mounds of Bin Tepe, far to the east, and the Greek island of Samos, across the water, reached by ferry from Kusadasi. Heading east, the roads cross the fertile valley of the Kucuk Menderes river, past fig orchards, cotton fields and olive groves, then rise into the hills, with plenty of curves and pleasant views.

Fuel stations are along the main roads, and there is no need to worry. Summer is hot, with temperatures often above thirty-five degrees, so early starts are sensible, and the best months are April to June and September to October. Be careful in town, where the streets are narrow and the drivers impatient, and watch for tour buses near the main sites. Climbing the hill takes half an hour, and the fortress is usually open in the day, with a small entry fee, so bring water and a hat.
t.ephesus@37.9,27.4:
Ephesus once had a population of a quarter of a million, a harbour that brought in ships from across the Mediterranean, and a temple counted among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. Today it has the best-preserved street plan of any Roman city in the east, and a crowd of visitors who walk down its marble roads each morning. The most photographed building is the Library of Celsus, whose two-storey facade, with its columns and statues of the virtues, was built in the early second century as a tomb and a library for a Roman governor, and rebuilt from the fallen stones in the twentieth century. The Great Theatre, carved into the slope of Mount Pion, held about twenty-five thousand people and is where, according to the Acts of the Apostles, the silversmiths of Ephesus rioted against Paul for threatening the trade in souvenir shrines of Artemis.

Walk down the Marble Street and the Curetes Street, with their ruts from carts, mosaic floors, public toilets with seats in a row and the terrace houses of the rich, with their painted walls and heated floors, and the city comes alive. Ephesus was also an early centre of Christianity, and a council held here in 431 declared Mary to be the Mother of God. The harbour has silted up, and the sea is now several kilometres away, so the city that lived by the water died when the water left.

Getting there is simple, since Selcuk lies three kilometres away, and the road is flat. The challenge is the crowds, with coaches arriving from the coastal resorts and cruise ships at Kusadasi, so be at the gate when it opens, and expect the heat to build rapidly. In summer, the stones become very hot, and there is little shade. Spring and autumn are better, with softer light, and winter is quiet, with the chance of rain. The ride goes on to Samos in Greece, which you reach by ferry from Kusadasi, a short crossing that takes the bike and gives views of the coast.

Selcuk has plenty of fuel stations, mechanics, cafes and guesthouses. The village of Sirince, in the hills above, is known for fruit wines, olive oil and stone houses, a pleasant place for lunch. Bring water, sun protection and comfortable shoes with a good grip, since the marble is slippery. A local guide can add a lot to the visit, and a small fee is usual.
t.omeo@-37.1,147.6:
Omeo sits at the end of a long, empty road in the high country of Victoria, and for a long time it was a place people passed through on their way to somewhere else. In the 1850s, that somewhere else was gold. Prospectors poured in, and for a while Omeo was a rough, bustling frontier town, with a reputation for lawlessness that earned it the nickname of the Wild West of Victoria. Then the gold ran out, and the town settled into a quieter life as a service centre for cattle farmers and, later, for skiers heading for the mountains.

The land around is rolling grazing country with the Alps rising behind, and the town sits in a valley at about six hundred metres. A serious earthquake in 1885 damaged many buildings, and the rebuilding gave the main street its present, solid look. A few old buildings survive, including the courthouse, and a small museum tells the story of the goldfields. Snow gums, granite boulders and wide skies set the tone.

For riders, Omeo is a milestone on the Great Alpine Road, which runs from Wangaratta to Bairnsdale over the highest sealed road in Victoria. The section south from Omeo, through Cassilis and down to the coast, is a long, twisting descent through eucalyptus forest, while to the north, the road climbs through Dinner Plain to Mount Hotham, at around 1,800 metres, with long sweeping views, wide bends and a surface that is generally good. In winter, snow and ice are serious, and chains may be required, so late spring to autumn is the best time. In summer, bushfire can close roads, so check conditions before you leave.

There is fuel in Omeo, and a few cafes, a pub and a bakery, but hours are limited, especially out of season. Dinner Plain, about thirty kilometres up the road, has fewer services. Take a warm layer, as the high country can be cold even in January.
t.wangaratta@-36.4,146.3:
Wangaratta stands where the Ovens and King rivers meet, on the flat plains at the foot of Victoria's north-eastern ranges, and it is the gate to the high country. The Great Alpine Road starts here, and for many riders, the day begins with a coffee on the main street before the long climb into the hills. The town has about eighteen thousand people, a wide central square, and a mix of old brick buildings and newer shops.

The country around is rich in history. The famous bushranger Ned Kelly was captured at Glenrowan, a short distance to the west, in a shoot-out in 1880, and the area is full of Kelly sites. The nearby town of Beechworth, a gold-rush settlement with well-preserved stone buildings, is a short ride to the east. Rutherglen, to the north, is known for its fortified wines, especially muscats and tokays, aged in old barrels and sweet as syrup.

Wangaratta is also known for its music. Every November, the Wangaratta Festival of Jazz and Blues fills the town with musicians and visitors, and the cafes and pubs have live bands. If you arrive then, book a bed well in advance.

For riding, the highlight is the road itself. The Great Alpine Road heads south-east along the Ovens Valley, through Myrtleford and Bright, with beautiful farmland and tall poplars that glow in autumn, then climbs through the forest to Mount Hotham, one of the highest sealed roads in Australia. The first stretch is easy and flat, and the bends tighten later. Autumn is lovely, but can bring early morning frost. In summer, bushfire is a risk, and in winter, snow.

Fuel is easy in town, and the supermarkets and cafes are good. This is the place to fill the tank, check your tyres and buy water before heading into the hills, because services become fewer farther on. Take a layer, as the mountains are cold, even on a sunny day.
t.component around lake eacham@-17.3,145.6:
Lake Eacham is a hole in the ground filled with water. About ten thousand years ago, magma met groundwater beneath the Atherton Tablelands and the ground blew apart in a steam explosion, leaving a deep, round crater that gradually filled with rain. Today it is a lake about sixty-five metres deep, ringed with rainforest and clear enough that you can see turtles in the shallows. It is part of the Wet Tropics of Queensland, a World Heritage Area inscribed in 1988.

The forest around the lake is dense and ancient, with giant trees, strangler figs, ferns, orchids and palms. Southern cassowaries, huge flightless birds with blue necks, still live in this area, and signs warn drivers to slow down for them. Platypus can sometimes be seen at dusk in the creeks nearby, particularly around Yungaburra, the small village about five kilometres away, and the Curtain Fig Tree, an enormous strangler fig with aerial roots hanging like a curtain, is a short drive from the village.

Swimming in the lake is popular, with a path around the shore and picnic tables under the trees. The water is cool, clear and soft, and there are no crocodiles. Early in the morning, mist rises off the surface and the birdsong is loud.

Reaching the Tablelands from the coast is part of the fun. The Gillies Range road, which climbs from the lowlands near Gordonvale to the plateau, is famous among riders for its 263 bends, tight and well surfaced, through rainforest. It can be wet and slippery, with leaf litter on the road, and trucks are a hazard. The tablelands themselves are green, rolling farmland with dairy herds, lakes and small towns.

Yungaburra has a few cafes and a pub, and Malanda and Atherton, both larger, have fuel and supermarkets. The wet season runs from December to April, with heavy rain, while the dry season, from May to November, is the best time to visit. Evenings are cool at altitude.
t.the colonizer s park@59.9,29.9:
Peterhof sits on the south shore of the Gulf of Finland, about half an hour's ride west of central Saint Petersburg when the traffic behaves, and the Colonists' Park is one of its quieter green corners. Most visitors come for the Grand Cascade and the gilded fountains of the Lower Park and never notice that the wider Peterhof estate is a patchwork of separate gardens laid out by different tsars over a couple of centuries. This one belongs to the later, more relaxed layer: lawns, big trees, ponds and paths meant for strolling rather than for impressing ambassadors.

The ride out is flat, and I mean properly flat. The land here is a low coastal plain, a terrace left behind by the retreating Baltic, so there are no corners worth the name, only long straight roads, tram-straight avenues and a lot of traffic lights. The Peterhof highway out of the city is busy at commuter hours and on summer weekends, when half the city heads for the fountains, so go early or accept a slow crawl. What you get in return is a very particular light: pale, low, silvery, and in June the white nights stretch the evening almost to the next morning.

Peterhof itself is a proper town of some seventy thousand people, so petrol, food and coffee are all easy within a kilometre or two, and there is no need to plan around it. Parking a bike near the park is simple compared with the palace crowds, and the paths under the trees are cool when the main avenues are baking. Mosquitoes in midsummer are real, so do not sit by the ponds at dusk in a T-shirt.

The history here is the history of Peter the Great's ambition to turn a swampy Baltic shoreline into a window on Europe. He founded the palace complex in the early eighteenth century as a seaside answer to Versailles, and the estate was nearly destroyed during the Second World War, when the occupation left the palaces gutted and the fountains' pipework wrecked. Restoration took decades and in some respects is still going on, which gives the whole place a slightly scrubbed, recently reborn look that is rather moving once you know the story.

If you have the choice, come on a weekday in May or September. The trees are doing something worth looking at, the fountain queues are shorter, and the park is the sort of place where you can park the bike, buy a coffee in town, and take a slow hour with the gulf only a few minutes away.
t.gisenyi@-1.7,29.3:
Two countries share one shoreline here, and the border runs between the beach bars. Gisenyi, now officially Rubavu, is Rwanda's lakeside resort on the northern shore of Lake Kivu, and the Congolese city of Goma starts a few kilometres across the line, under the dark cone of Nyiragongo. The volcano is the dominant fact of the landscape: its 2002 eruption sent lava through Goma, and its crater holds one of the world's largest lava lakes, glowing red at night when the sky is clear. Cross-border crowds, market women with baskets on their heads and boda riders weaving between them give the town a restless energy.

The road that leads here is among the most beautiful in central Africa. The Congo-Nile Divide road runs along the ridge above Lake Kivu, a spine of high hills that separates the watersheds of the two great rivers. It rolls through tea plantations, terraced banana groves and eucalyptus, and every few kilometres the lake appears below, a hammered silver sheet scattered with islands. The Rwandan roads are well surfaced, clean and lined with people walking, cycling and carrying loads, so a rider needs to be alert, slow and generous with the horn. Motorcycle taxis are everywhere, and helmets are the law.

Lake Kivu is odd. It is one of the African Great Lakes, and it contains huge quantities of dissolved methane and carbon dioxide trapped in its deep water, a hazard that scientists monitor and that Rwanda taps for power. The surface is safe and calm, and because the lake is free of bilharzia, as locals say, swimming from the town beaches is popular on weekends. Fresh fish, grilled tilapia and the small sambaza, are the staples at lakeside restaurants, usually with a cold local beer and a plate of plantain.

Gisenyi is a proper town, with fuel stations, banks, hotels and plenty of food, and it is the place to stock up before heading anywhere else in the region. Fuel is easier to find on the Rwandan side than in the remote hills. The border post is close, but the Congolese side is another matter, and the situation in the eastern Congo has been unstable for years, so take advice before crossing.

Volcanoes National Park, home of the mountain gorillas, lies about an hour to the east, and the road to it is a good ride too. The weather is mild at this altitude, with rain most afternoons in the wet seasons and clear, bright mornings.
t.yarra valley and black spur@-37.7,145.3:
Chirnside Park, with nearly ten thousand people, is just over a kilometre away, and Lilydale, a bigger suburb of sixteen thousand, three kilometres, so this is the eastern edge of Melbourne, where the city dissolves into the Yarra Valley. The ride starts here with a fill of fuel, and everything ahead is better than the suburbs behind.

The Yarra Valley is one of Victoria's great wine regions, specialising in cool-climate chardonnay, pinot noir and sparkling wines, and the vineyards roll across gentle hills with the Great Dividing Range blue beyond. Cellar doors, cafes and farm stalls appear every few kilometres, and good bakeries are everywhere. Lilydale has a history of its own, since the singer Dame Nellie Melba grew up in the district and is buried in the cemetery there, and she took her stage name from Melbourne.

The star of the ride is the Black Spur, a stretch of the Maroondah Highway between Healesville and Narbethong. The road winds through a cathedral of mountain ash, the tallest flowering trees on Earth, which tower above tree ferns and moss. The light is green and dim, the air cool and damp, and the smell of eucalyptus and wet bark is rich. The road is smooth, with long, flowing bends, and it is a favourite among Melbourne riders, so it can be busy at weekends. Take care of damp patches and fallen bark, and watch for cars cutting the corners.

Nearby Healesville has a wildlife sanctuary where you can see koalas, wombats and platypuses, and it works in the care of injured animals. The Great Dividing Range lies beyond, and the road toward Marysville and Lake Mountain climbs into cool, forested country. The 2009 bushfires devastated parts of this region, and the regrowth, with young green shoots on dark trunks, is a quiet reminder of that.

Fill the tank here, since the stations thin out as you head into the hills. Early mornings are crisp, even in summer, and fog can hang in the valleys. Pack a layer, since the weather in the Dandenongs and Yarra Ranges can be changeable, and sudden showers are common. A coffee in Healesville is a good way to start.
t.mornington peninsula easy scenic@-38.3,1:
Mount Martha, a seaside suburb of nearly eighteen thousand, and Mornington, a bigger bayside town of twenty-three thousand, are the closest places, four and a half kilometres away, so this fuel gate sits on the eastern shore of the Mornington Peninsula, which curls like a hook into Port Phillip Bay south of Melbourne. It is the holiday coast of Melburnians, with long sandy beaches, shaded foreshores and a gentle, relaxed air.

The most photographed things here are the beach boxes, tiny, brightly painted timber huts lined up along the sand at Mount Martha, Dromana and Brighton, some of which have sold for the price of a house. Mornington's main street has a long row of cafes and bookshops, and the pier is a pleasant place for a stroll and a view across the bay to the city towers on a clear day. The calm water of the bay is good for swimming and for children, and boats bob in the harbour.

The ride is an easy scenic loop, which suits the relaxed character of the area. Roads wind along the shore and over the low hills, past orchards, vineyards and horse paddocks, and the peninsula is known for its cool-climate wine, particularly pinot noir and chardonnay, and for its farm gates, selling strawberries, cherries and apples in season. The corners are gentle, the surface mostly smooth, and the speed limits generally low, and police do patrol, so keep it sensible.

Traffic is the catch. On summer weekends and holidays, the main road down the peninsula crawls, with cars queuing for the beaches, and a bike can filter only where it is legal and safe. Go early, on a weekday if you can, or in autumn, when the water is still warm and the crowds have gone.

Fill up here, since this is a good place for fuel and coffee, with plenty of stations. Fresh seafood, fish and chips and good coffee are everywhere, and the evening light on the bay, with the sun going down behind the Bellarine across the water, is lovely. Pack sunscreen, as the Australian sun is strong, and keep a light jacket, because a southerly can bring a sudden chill.
t.kuranda@-16.8,145.6:
Kuranda sits above the tropical lowlands of Far North Queensland, a village of about three thousand people in the rainforest on the Great Dividing Range, reached from Cairns by one of the most unusual commutes in Australia. The Kuranda Scenic Railway, built by hand in the 1880s and 1890s, climbs the range through fifteen tunnels and across high bridges, past the Barron Falls, and the Skyrail cableway glides above the canopy. By road, the Kuranda Range Road winds up through forest in steep bends.

The village is a market town for visitors. The Original Rainforest Markets, which began in the 1970s, sell crafts, leather, jewellery and food, and the little streets are crowded with stalls and cafes. Behind this, the place has a quieter side, with walks in the forest, a butterfly sanctuary and a bird aviary. The Barron Gorge National Park, a section of the Wet Tropics World Heritage Area, protects some of the oldest rainforest on Earth, a living relic of the ancient forests that covered the continent when it was part of Gondwana.

This is cassowary country. The cassowary, a large flightless bird with a blue neck and a helmet of bone, lives in the forests of the region, and warning signs show where they cross the road. They are rare, powerful and shy, and a close encounter is both thrilling and dangerous. Slow down in signed zones. Other wildlife includes tree kangaroos, spectacular butterflies and, at night, frogs and flying foxes.

For a rider, the Kuranda Range Road is a good twisty climb, with tight corners, a steady gradient and dense forest on both sides. The humidity is high, the road surface can be wet or greasy, and sudden tropical downpours are common, especially in the wet season from about December to March, when the roads can also flood. The dry season, from May to October, is the best time, with warm days and cool nights.

The village has basic services, including a petrol station, but Cairns has the widest choice, so fill up there before the climb. Behind Kuranda lies the Atherton Tableland, a cooler, greener upland of dairy farms, crater lakes and waterfalls, which makes for a lovely day's riding. The air smells of damp earth, flowers and woodsmoke, and the morning mist hangs in the trees.
t.high country omeo weekend@-38.1,145.3:
Cranbourne East and Cranbourne, towns of sixteen and twenty thousand people, sit right here on Melbourne's south-eastern fringe, and this fuel gate marks the start of a long weekend ride to the Victorian high country around Omeo. It is a long way, about three hundred and fifty kilometres to the east, and the early going is a matter of leaving suburbia behind and finding the open road.

Cranbourne is known for its Royal Botanic Gardens, a branch of the Melbourne gardens devoted to Australian plants, with a huge sand-and-rock garden that shows the country's diversity. The surrounding land is flat and market-garden country, with Westernport Bay to the south, and the Dandenong Ranges visible to the north. Once clear of the city, the road swings east through Gippsland, a long green province of dairy farms, forest and lakes between the Great Dividing Range and the sea.

Omeo is a small town in the high country that grew in the 1850s when gold was found, and it became a centre for miners and later for cattlemen who drove their animals up to the summer pastures on the high plains. The Great Alpine Road, which passes through, is one of the best motorcycle roads in Australia, with long climbs and descents through alpine forest, over Mount Hotham, a ski area at about 1,800 metres. The road can be icy in winter, and snow may close sections, so check conditions and carry chains if needed.

Fill the tank here. Stations are plentiful on the Princes Highway in Gippsland, but the roads in the high country are long and sparsely served. Carry water, wear layers and allow time, because the distances are bigger than they look. The weather is changeable, with snow possible on the high plains even in late spring and cold nights at any time.

The best seasons are late spring and autumn, when the air is cool and clear. In autumn, the poplars and elms in the valleys turn gold, and the mountain ash forests are tall and green. Smoke from bushfires can affect summer riding, and fire bans apply in hot weather, so look at current local advice before planning a long trip.
t.high country omeo weekend@-37.1,145.4:
Yea is the nearest town, eight kilometres from this spot, a small place of about fifteen hundred people on the Yea River in the foothills of the Great Dividing Range, in the Murrindindi district north-east of Melbourne. It is a food stop, and Yea has been feeding travellers on the road to the high country for a long time. Its main street holds bakeries, cafes and a pub, and the town is known for its pies, its antiques shops and its wetlands, where a boardwalk leads through reed beds full of birds.

The surrounding country is rolling and green, with cattle, sheep and some forestry. The Cathedral Range, a jagged ridge of rock rising steeply above the forest, lies to the east, and its state park offers fine walks and climbs. In February 2009 the Black Saturday fires swept through the region, causing great loss of life and destroying many homes, and the recovery is visible in the regrowth and the memorials. Locals are proud and welcoming, and talk about it only when they want to.

The Great Victorian Rail Trail, a long cycling and walking route on an old railway line, passes through Yea and Alexandra, and it gives an idea of the old transport links, the railway that once carried timber and farm produce to Melbourne. Lake Eildon, a large reservoir built in the 1950s on the Goulburn River, lies a short ride away and is popular for boating and fishing, with houseboats moored in sheltered bays.

For the rider, the road here is a mix of gentle highway and winding secondary routes. The Goulburn Valley Highway and the Melba Highway are smooth and fast, while the smaller roads through the hills offer corners, forest and views. Wildlife is a hazard at dusk, with kangaroos and wombats on the verges, and trucks use the main roads, so give them space.

Yea has fuel and basic services, and Alexandra and Seymour, a town of six thousand about twenty-seven kilometres away, have more. A pie and a coffee in the main street is the standard stop. Weather can be cool in the hills, even in summer, and frost is common in winter, so pack layers and watch for ice on shaded corners in the morning.
t.melbourne victoria@-37.4,146.1:
This pin falls in the forested ranges of Victoria's high country, about forty kilometres south of Mansfield and Alexandra, in the headwaters of the Goulburn River country, so the label of a swim and a return refers to a trip's end rather than a town. The rivers here, the Goulburn and its tributaries, the Howqua and the Jamieson, run clear and cold from the mountains, and the pools along them are good for a dip on a hot day.

The Goulburn is the longest river in Victoria, and it rises in the Great Dividing Range north of the Yarra Ranges before flowing north-west toward the Murray. Along its upper reaches lie small settlements that started as gold-mining camps in the 1850s and are now quiet villages with pubs and camping grounds. Lake Eildon, a large reservoir built in the mid-twentieth century, backs up the river and offers swimming beaches, boating and fishing.

Swimming in the high country needs a little common sense. The water is cold even in summer, because it comes from the mountains, and the current can be strong after rain, so choose slow, shallow pools with a clear exit. Snakes, especially tiger snakes and brown snakes, live in the river banks and wet grass, and a stick tapped on the ground before sitting down is a reasonable habit. Wear sandals for slippery rocks.

The riding is lovely. Roads wind through mountain ash and messmate forest, over low saddles and along river valleys, with a good surface and plenty of bends. Many are narrow, and logging trucks use some of the forest roads, so be wary on blind corners. Wildlife is common at dusk, with kangaroos, wombats and wallabies on the road. Fog and frost can linger in the shade, so take care on cold mornings.

The nearest towns for fuel are Mansfield, a town of about five thousand, and Alexandra, with fewer, so fill the tank in either before heading in. Take water, food and a layer, and let someone know your route, since mobile coverage is patchy. On a warm afternoon the forest smells of eucalyptus and dry leaves, and the sound of cicadas is loud.
t.mornington peninsula easy scenic@-37.4,1:
Alexandra is thirty-five kilometres away, and this food stop lies in the forested hills between the Goulburn valley and the Victorian high country, not far from Mansfield. The nearest place for a proper lunch is one of those two towns, and either is a good choice, since this part of Victoria has a rich tradition of country food and a long history of hospitality for travellers on the road to the snow.

Mansfield, a town of about five thousand at the foot of the mountains, is the gateway to Mount Buller, a ski resort where Victorians have skied since the 1930s. The town's main street has bakeries, cafes and pubs, with a lively atmosphere on winter weekends. It also has a place in the folklore of the outlaw Ned Kelly. In 1878, at nearby Stringybark Creek, the Kelly gang shot three policemen, an event that turned them into the most wanted men in the colony, and the story is told in local memorials and museums.

Local produce is a pleasure. The high country produces beef and lamb, cool-climate wines, trout, cheese and honey, and the cafes make good use of them. A hot pie with a cold drink on a bench in the sun is a country classic, and a proper bakery will have sausage rolls, vanilla slices and fresh bread. In autumn, walnuts and chestnuts appear at roadside stalls, and berry farms open in summer. Many places close early, particularly midweek, so plan for a late-morning or early-afternoon meal.

The road between towns runs through forest, over low ranges and across river valleys, with long, easy bends and smooth surfaces. Traffic is light, apart from weekends and ski season, when it increases noticeably. Wildlife, especially kangaroos and wombats, is active at dawn and dusk. Winter brings frost, ice and occasional snow to higher parts, so check conditions and carry warm gear.

Fuel is available in both Alexandra and Mansfield, and the stations on the main roads are modern. The weather in the hills can be unpredictable, so pack a rain jacket and a warm mid-layer. The air smells of eucalyptus and woodsmoke, and a meal after a long morning in the saddle tastes better than it has any right to.
t.jackson mississippi@32.3,-90.2:
Jackson, the state capital of Mississippi and a city of nearly two hundred thousand people, sits on the Pearl River, and the Natchez Trace Parkway skirts it along the shore of the Ross Barnett Reservoir, a big artificial lake to the north and east. It is a southern city of broad avenues, heavy heat and deep history, and it is not an obvious tourist destination, but it rewards a curious visitor. The state capitol, a grand building finished in 1903 with a copper dome, is a good place to start, and it still stands over the downtown.

The city's history is complicated. It was named for Andrew Jackson and founded as the state capital in the 1820s, and during the Civil War it was attacked and burned so often that Union soldiers reportedly called it Chimneyville, after the brick chimneys left standing. In the twentieth century, Jackson was a centre of the civil rights movement. Medgar Evers, the state's field secretary for the NAACP, was murdered in his driveway here in 1963, and his house is now a memorial, and the Freedom Riders arrested in 1961 were taken from here to Parchman prison. A civil rights museum in the city tells the story with care.

For a rider, Jackson is a place to rest and refuel, and the Parkway makes a lovely approach. North of the city, the Trace passes through Ridgeland and along the reservoir, with its marshes and cypress, and a craft centre beside the road sells local pottery, quilts and baskets. The roads in the city are wide and busy, and the heat from May to September is serious, with high humidity and storms. In the shoulder seasons, the weather is mild and the azaleas bloom in spring. Watch for potholes and heavy traffic on the interstates.

Fuel, food and hotels are plentiful, and you will not go hungry. Mississippi cooking is a good reason to stop: fried catfish, collard greens, cornbread and a very sweet pecan pie are standard fare, and barbecue and soul food restaurants fill the older neighbourhoods. The writer Eudora Welty lived in the city for most of her life, and her house is open to visitors, with its garden and its books. If you finish your ride here, give yourself time for a slow evening, because Jackson is a place that repays attention.
t.cesis@57.3,25.3:
Cesis has the look of a place that has been fought over, and it has. The old castle, a ruin of grey stone on a low hill above the town, was begun in the early thirteenth century by the Livonian Order, the German crusading knights who conquered this part of the Baltic, and for three centuries it was one of their strongest seats, with towers, walls and the residence of the order's master. It was destroyed in the Great Northern War in the early eighteenth century, and the ruins stand beside a later manor house that now holds a museum. In summer, you can climb the round tower with a candle lantern, a pleasantly gloomy experience.

The history of the town is tied to Latvia's own struggle. In June 1919, in the battle of Cesis, Latvian and Estonian troops defeated a German force and helped to secure the independence of both nations, and Estonians still honour the date as Victory Day. The town sits within Gauja National Park, Latvia's oldest, established in 1973, and the river Gauja, which runs through a deep valley of red sandstone cliffs, caves and pine forest. The Gauja is the longest river that lies entirely in Latvia, and in summer, canoeists paddle along it for days.

Cesis has a brewery, which has been making beer since the late sixteenth century according to its own history, and the product is sold across Latvia. A glass of the local lager or a dark beer with a plate of smoked fish, rye bread and grey peas with bacon is a Latvian classic. The old town, with its cobbled streets, wooden houses and a church with a tall brick spire, is pleasant to wander. Cafes are small and friendly, and prices are low.

The town has about eighteen thousand people, enough for fuel, supermarkets and rooms. The road to Cesis from Riga, the A2, is a straight run through forest and farmland, and is easy riding, though trucks are many and overtaking needs care. Roads in the park are narrower, with sandy edges and sudden bends, and the surface is mixed. Sigulda, with its castles and cable car, is a short ride away to the south-west. In summer, the light is long and the nights short, with dusk lasting past eleven in June, while in autumn the forest turns gold and the air smells of mushrooms and damp leaves. Be prepared for cool nights even in summer.
t.thredbo@-36.5,148.3:
Thredbo is a ski village tucked into the upper valley of the Thredbo River in the Snowy Mountains of New South Wales, and in summer it has the slightly stunned air of a place waiting for snow. The chalets are built steeply on the hillside, the lifts stand idle, and the main street is quiet until the mountain bikers arrive. It sits inside Kosciuszko National Park, and Mount Kosciuszko itself, at 2,228 metres the highest mountain in Australia, is only a few kilometres away on foot.

The ride in from Jindabyne along the Alpine Way is one of the best in the country. The road follows the Thredbo River upstream through snow gum forest, with bends that tighten as the valley narrows, and the surface is generally well kept, though the park's wildlife is a hazard. Wombats, kangaroos and wallabies come out at dusk and dawn, and an unlucky collision with one of them can end a day. Watch your speed, and look well ahead through the corners, where animals can stand just beyond the apex.

Thredbo has a history that is part sad, part inspiring. It was established by Czech and Slovak engineer Tony Sponar and others after the Second World War, and its alpine style, with timber lodges and hearty cooking, reflects those European roots. In 1997 a landslide destroyed two ski lodges, and eighteen people died, with one man pulled alive from the wreckage after more than three days. The village remembers it quietly, and the community is proud of how it recovered.

Practical matters need a little thought. Entry to the national park is charged by vehicle, so expect to pay a fee at the gate, and in winter snow chains may be required on the road. Cold fronts can arrive quickly, even in summer, and rain at this altitude is cold. Thredbo has cafes, restaurants and a general store, and the village can feed you well, but fuel is a different matter: Jindabyne, thirty kilometres away, is the town with proper services, and it is wise to arrive here with a full tank.

If you have time, take the chairlift to the top station in summer for a walk toward the summit of Kosciuszko, and breathe in air that smells of eucalyptus and cold stone.
t.dead horse gap@-36.5,148.3:
Dead Horse Gap is a saddle on the Alpine Way, high in the Snowy Mountains, where the road crests the ridge between the Thredbo valley and the country that drains toward the Murray. At about 1,580 metres it is the highest point on this road, and it feels like the edge of something. The trees thin out, the snow gums are bent and silvery, and the wind arrives straight from the Southern Ocean with very little to slow it.

The name belongs to a story, and like many such stories it is told in different ways. The version most often repeated is that a group of brumbies, the wild horses of the high country, were trapped by a blizzard here and died, and their bones gave the gap its name. Whether it happened exactly like that or not, it gives a fair sense of the climate. Snow can fall in any month, and in winter the gap is cold, white and unforgiving, with the road often closed or restricted to vehicles carrying chains.

From the car park at the gap, walking tracks head out in several directions, including a route toward the main range and Mount Kosciuszko. It is a place for hikers more than motorcyclists, but a short walk on the open slopes gives a feel of the alpine environment, with tussock grass, tiny wildflowers in summer and views over the ranges. The air is clear and thin, and the silence is broken only by wind.

The riding is the real treat. On the Thredbo side, the road climbs in generous bends through eucalypt forest, and on the western side it drops toward the Khancoban end in a long run of curves, with views of ridges folding away to the horizon. This is a road where traffic is light, the surface is mostly good, and the scenery changes every few kilometres. It rewards a steady pace, and you should still keep an eye out for animals, especially in the early morning and evening.

Jindabyne, about thirty-four kilometres away, is the proper town. Carry extra layers, check the forecast, and tell someone your route if you are riding alone, because the weather turns rapidly and mobile coverage is patchy.
t.millaa millaa@-17.5,145.6:
Millaa Millaa is a dairy town on the southern Atherton Tablelands, about seven hundred metres above the Coral Sea, and it has the look of a place that grows grass for a living. Paddocks roll away in all directions, a deep, volcanic red where the soil shows, and Friesian cows stand in them with the placid air of animals who know how good they have it. The cloud often sits low on the ridges here, and mornings can be damp and cool, a surprise after the heat of Cairns.

The town is best known for its waterfalls. Millaa Millaa Falls, a short drive from the centre, drops in a neat, wide curtain into a round pool, and you may recognise it because it has appeared in a famous shampoo advert. It is also the best known stop on the so-called Waterfall Circuit, which links Zillie and Ellinjaa falls along a loop of country lanes, each with its own pool and viewing path. Swimming is allowed at some of them, in water that is cold, clear and slightly tea-coloured, though you should check conditions after heavy rain.

The ride is a sequence of gentle country roads, with the occasional steep descent into a creek valley and a climb out through rainforest and cane. The Palmerston Highway to the coast is a sharper road, with sweeping bends through the Wet Tropics rainforest, and it is a good reason to extend the day. The surface is mostly good, though the wet season, from about December to March, brings downpours, washouts and slippery patches. In the dry months the air is clear and the ranges look blue.

The Tablelands have a long history as farmland, but they were cleared first for timber, and then for dairy and maize. Ravenshoe, the highest town in Queensland, is nearby and has a different, cooler feel. Some of the country was originally cloaked in rainforest, and patches remain, thick with vines, strangler figs and birdlife. Look out for cassowaries in the rainforest edges, large, flightless and not to be messed with, and for the occasional tree kangaroo in the canopy, though those are almost impossible to see.

Millaa Millaa is small, but it has a fuel station and a couple of cafes serving good coffee and cake. Atherton, about thirty kilometres away, is the larger town with workshops and supermarkets, and Ravenshoe is another option to the west. A visit works best on a weekday morning, before the tour buses arrive.
t.rex lookout@-16.6,145.6:
Rex Lookout is a pull-in on the Captain Cook Highway, high on the headland between Cairns and Port Douglas, where the road leaves the cane fields and clings to a steep, green coastline. From the platform you look straight down onto a succession of bays, long white beaches, scattered islands and a sea that goes from pale green to deep blue. On a clear morning you can see all the way along the coast to the north, with the rainforest hills of the Daintree fading into haze.

The road itself is the reason to come. The highway between Cairns and Port Douglas is one of the finest coastal rides in Australia, cut into the side of the range with the sea on one hand and the jungle on the other. Bends are long, banked and open, the surface is generally good, and the views change at every corner. The range section, known as the Rex Range, climbs and descends in tight sweeps before dropping to the flat, palm-lined sections near Port Douglas. It can be busy with tourist traffic, particularly in the dry season, and the speed limits are lower than a rider would like. Police do patrol it.

At the lookout, you may see hang gliders and paragliders drifting off the ridge in the afternoon, using the sea breeze to hold them up. Wind at the headland is persistent, with gusts across the road, and you may find the bike twitching in the stronger puffs. Sunscreen and water are sensible, because the tropical sun here is fierce, even in the cooler months.

The land is part of the Wet Tropics World Heritage Area, a stretch of rainforest that is among the oldest in the world, with plants whose ancestors go back to the age of the dinosaurs. The sea beneath is the Coral Sea, with the outer Great Barrier Reef some distance off the coast. Beware of the warnings along the beaches: this is crocodile country, and also home to stingers, the box jellyfish, from roughly October to May. Take notice of any signs and do not swim without checking.

For fuel, Port Douglas has stations, as does Craiglie, about fifteen kilometres from the lookout, and Cairns is the larger city to the south. There are cafes and food stalls along the highway at some of the beach settlements. The best times for the ride are early morning, when the light is soft and traffic is light, and the dry season from about May to October.
t.ignalina@55.3,26.2:
Ignalina is a small town on a lake in the north-east corner of Lithuania, close to the borders with Latvia and Belarus, and it is the starting point for Aukštaitija National Park, the oldest of Lithuania's national parks. The landscape is glacial: the ice sheets that retreated ten thousand years ago left behind a rumpled country of hills, hollows, kettle lakes and long ridges, with more than a hundred lakes in the park alone, linked by streams and surrounded by pine forest. The air smells of resin, and in summer, of hay and wild berries.

Ignalina has a slightly unusual history for a rural town. The Ignalina Nuclear Power Plant, a Soviet-built station with the same type of reactors as Chernobyl, stood nearby on the shore of Lake Drūkšiai, and the town of Visaginas was built next to it to house the workers. Lithuania agreed to close the plant as a condition of joining the European Union, and the last reactor was shut down in 2009. The plant's decommissioning continues, and the district has had to find a new way of making a living, with tourism and forestry taking up some of the slack.

The riding here is quiet, flat to gently rolling, and often along roads that run between lakes and forest with long, easy curves. It is not a place for adrenaline, but it is a lovely region for a leisurely day. The surface is generally good on the main roads, with some patched sections, and the side roads can be gravel, particularly in the national park. Elk, roe deer and wild boar cross the roads, especially at dawn and dusk, so keep your speed down. In summer the evenings are long, with light lasting past ten, and the winters are cold and snowy.

The region has its own customs and food. The local cuisine is Lithuanian, with potato dishes such as cepelinai, the large stuffed dumplings, along with smoked fish from the lakes, dark rye bread, and cold beetroot soup in summer. Beekeeping is a strong tradition in the area, and a small museum in the nearby village of Stripeikiai shows the old hollowed-log hives. Honey and mead are on sale in the town and at roadside stands.

Ignalina is a real town of about six thousand people, with fuel stations, shops and cafes, so there is no difficulty in stocking up. Prices are modest, and card payments are widely accepted. Summer is the best season for riding, though late May and September are quieter and the forests are beautiful, with mushrooms for sale along the roadside.
t.palus@55.4,26.1:
