Palūšė, the village on the map as Palus, sits on a narrow strip of land between two lakes in the heart of Aukštaitija National Park, and the setting is the whole charm. The water is on both sides of the road, dark blue in the sun and slate grey under cloud, with pines on the shores and the shapes of small islands in the distance. The village is quiet, with wooden houses, gardens and the occasional boat pulled up on the bank.

What makes Palūšė well known is its wooden church, one of the oldest in Lithuania, built in the mid-eighteenth century in the traditional local style, with a pitched roof, a separate wooden belfry and a simple interior. Wooden churches like this once stood in every village in the country, and many were lost to fire and war, so the survivors are treasured. The church stands on a rise above the water, and the churchyard, with its old crosses and trees, is a calm place to stop for a few minutes, even if you are not a keen visitor of churches.

The park's visitor centre is nearby, and a walk to the Ladakalnis hill, a short climb through the forest, gives a view over a string of lakes that is the best way to understand the shape of the land. The lakes were formed by glaciers, and the long, narrow ones follow the old tunnel valleys where meltwater ran under the ice. In autumn the forest turns gold, and in winter the lakes freeze and become a place for skating and ice fishing.

The riding is easy and atmospheric. The road follows a gently winding path through forest and farmland, with the lakes appearing and disappearing through the trees, and traffic is light. Some of the surfaces are old and patched, and in the park there are gravel tracks leading to hamlets and campsites. Wildlife, from deer to foxes, is common and the evenings are long in summer. Mosquitoes and horseflies are a nuisance in the warm months, so carry repellent and a little patience.

Ignalina, about eleven kilometres away, is the nearest town and has everything you need, so it is sensible to arrive in Palūšė with a full tank. Some guest houses and farm stays offer simple meals, with smoked fish, potato pancakes and dark bread, and the beer and kvass brewed locally are cool and refreshing. Early morning, when mist lies on the water and cranes are calling from the shore, is the best time to be here.
t.kolga@59.5,25.6:
Kolga Bay is shallow and full of boulders, which is how the whole Lahemaa coast looks if you ignore the trees. The name Lahemaa means the Land of Bays, and in 1971 this was declared the first national park in the Soviet Union, a minor miracle in an era that did not care much about protecting land from factories. It covers about seven hundred square kilometres of low coast, with pine forest, bogs, limestone cliffs, fishing villages and old manors strung together along a series of long, flat peninsulas that point out into the Gulf of Finland.

Kolga itself is a quiet village at the head of its bay, and the thing you notice first is the manor. Kolga Manor was the seat of the Stenbock family, Swedish-Baltic nobles who owned much of the land here in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Like many Estonian manors, it was nationalised after independence in 1919, then abused by the Soviets and left to decay. In recent years it has been restored and opened to visitors, and the grounds are pleasant for a walk. The bay beyond is dotted with small islands and reefs, and in spring it fills with migrating birds.

The riding along the coast is flat, quiet and green. Roads in Lahemaa run between pine woods and meadows, and often turn to gravel on the smaller routes toward the peninsulas. Corners are few and gentle, and the main pleasure is the sense of space and the long northern light, which in midsummer lingers until nearly midnight. You will see boulders everywhere, left by the last ice age: giant granite erratics sit in the fields and in the sea, some of them as big as a room. Take care on gravel, and watch for elk at dawn and dusk, which can be dangerous on the road.

Fuel is not on offer in the village. Loksa, about ten kilometres east, has a station and a supermarket, and Tallinn, about fifty kilometres west, has all you need. Estonian food tends to be hearty, with dark rye bread, smoked fish, soups and boiled potatoes, and the local cafés serve simple food with dill and sour cream.

Aim for a calm evening in June, when the bay is flat and the sky stays pale until bedtime.
t.vosu@59.6,26.0:
Võsu is a seaside village in Lahemaa National Park where a long sandy beach, a pine forest and a few wooden villas make up the best of the Estonian summer. The beach is broad and shallow, the water warms up slowly, and in July the place fills with families from Tallinn and Tartu, who come to spend a week or two in their summer houses or in guesthouses along the shore. Reed beds line the nearby river mouth, and the sunsets over the Gulf of Finland are long and gentle.

Behind the beach, the village has a small centre with a handful of shops and cafés and a pleasing collection of old wooden houses with carved verandas, painted in dark red, yellow and green. Many were built in the early twentieth century as summer residences for city people, and the carved trim is a reminder of how the Baltic coast was once a fashionable retreat. The pine forest behind the dunes is full of paths, and in autumn it is full of mushroom hunters, an Estonian passion that borders on the obsessive.

The riding here is gentle and flat. Roads through the park run between woodland, fields and coastal meadows, with long straight stretches and a handful of bends, and they are quiet outside the holiday season. A short ride east or west brings you to some of the park's best sights. Palmse and Sagadi manors, a few kilometres inland, are among the finest in Estonia, and the fishing village of Altja has thatched net sheds, a swing and a small tavern right at the water's edge. The coastal road to Käsmu is a particularly pretty drive. Be prepared for gravel on some of the smaller roads and for sudden fog on cool mornings.

There is no big fuel stop in Võsu, so Loksa, about thirteen kilometres away, is the sensible place to fill the tank, and Rakvere farther inland has larger shops. The village has a few places to eat, serving fried fish, smoked salmon and rye bread. In midsummer, locals light bonfires on the beach for Jaanipäev, the Midsummer festival, and the whole coast glows.

Come in late June or early July for the long light, or in September for empty beaches and mist.
t.kasmu@59.6,25.9:
Käsmu is known as the Captains' Village, and it has the proportions of a place that produced a lot of sailors for a small population. In the nineteenth century, this tiny settlement on a peninsula in Lahemaa trained and sent out so many ship's captains and mariners that a maritime school was founded here, and the old captains' houses still stand in neat rows along the shore, with tall roofs and carved porches. Today the village has fewer than a hundred permanent residents, and the old school building is part of the maritime museum, which tells the story of the village and its sailors.

The bay itself is one of the most beautiful on the coast, dotted with boulders that rise out of the shallow water like the backs of grey whales. Käsmu has an extraordinary number of erratics, huge stones left behind by the glaciers, and a walk along the shore brings you past dozens of them, some as big as houses. A path loops around the peninsula through pine woods and along the beach, and takes about an hour.

Its other claim to fame is smuggling. In the 1920s, when Finland had banned alcohol, the people of Käsmu loaded boats with spirits and sent them across the Gulf of Finland to the Finnish coast, a run of well under a hundred kilometres. The trade was dangerous but profitable, and many of the local houses were built with the proceeds. The Finns, not the Estonians, were the ones breaking the law, but the tale is told in the village with a certain pride, and there is a small exhibit about it in the museum.

The roads out here are narrow, quiet and partly gravel, running through pine forest and past old farmsteads. They are very easy to ride, with almost no traffic and a surface that is generally good, but loose stones appear on corners. Elk and deer cross the road at dawn and dusk, and the light in the forest is soft and green. A few guesthouses and a café in the village provide meals, with smoked fish and dark bread as the staples.

In the evening, with the sun setting behind the pines and the boulders glowing in the shallows, the village has the unhurried air of a place where nothing has needed to happen for a long time.
t.lake bunyonyi@-1.3,29.9:
Bunyonyi means place of little birds, and the name is accurate: kingfishers, herons and cormorants work the water, and the hills around ring with birdsong in the early morning. The lake lies in the Kigezi highlands of south-western Uganda, close to the Rwandan border, at nearly two thousand metres, and it is one of the deepest lakes in Africa. Its shore is a tangle of narrow arms and bays, with some two dozen islands scattered across the surface, and green terraced hills drop right down to the water on every side.

Those terraces are the thing you notice first. Farmers have shaped nearly every slope into steps, growing potatoes, beans, sorghum, peas and maize, and the pattern gives the whole district a sculpted look. The climate is cool and mild, with a fresh smell of wood smoke and wet earth, and mist often fills the valleys at dawn. The lake is also known as one of the few in the region where people can swim without much worry about crocodiles or hippos, though locals warn about parasites in the shallows, so check before you dive in. Travellers paddle out in dugout canoes to the islands.

One of those islands has a sad story. Punishment Island is a tiny patch of land where, in earlier times, unmarried girls who became pregnant were left to die or be rescued, a custom that vanished a long time ago but that locals still recount. Another island was home to a leper colony. The lake is beautiful, but its history is not all light.

The ride from Kabale to the lake is short, along a road that climbs a ridge and then drops steeply toward the water. Most of the main roads in the area are paved, but the lanes down to the shore are rough, with ruts and loose stones, and rain can turn them to mud, so take care. The best time is the dry seasons, roughly June to August and December to February. Morning light over the water is magical, and evening brings cooler air, so a jacket is useful. Watch for pedestrians, boda-boda motorbikes and cattle on the road.

Kabale, eight kilometres away, is a sizeable town with fuel, shops and restaurants, and you should fill the tank before you come. Around the lake there are camps and guesthouses, with simple meals of fish, rice, beans and matoke, the green banana stew that is the staple here. Bring cash, as card machines are rare.
t.kisoro@-1.3,29.7:
Kisoro sits in the far south-west corner of Uganda, in a pocket between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo, and the first thing you notice is the row of volcanoes. Muhabura, Gahinga and Sabinyo stand on the skyline like a set of upturned bowls, their slopes green and their summits often hidden in cloud. They are part of the Virunga range, a chain of volcanoes that straddles three countries, and the town sits at the foot of them, on a high plateau where the air is cool and the land is cultivated to the last metre.

It is a town built on borders. The frontiers with both neighbours are close, so the market is a mixing place where traders from three countries sell produce, clothing and everything else, and the language you hear shifts between Rukiga, Kinyarwanda and Swahili. Gorilla tourism has also shaped the area, because Mgahinga Gorilla National Park, a short way up the road, protects part of the Virunga forest, home to mountain gorillas and the rare golden monkeys. Visitors arrive here to track them, and the town has grown guesthouses, craft shops and cafés around that trade.

The ride from Kabale is a highlight of southern Uganda. The road climbs through terraced hills, over the Kanaba Gap, where a viewpoint looks out across the volcanoes, and descends through patches of forest and fields, with a smooth tarmac surface for most of the way. Traffic is light, but trucks, minibuses, bicycles and cattle share the road, and the bends can be sharp, so watch for blind corners. Mist and rain are common, particularly in the wet seasons, and temperatures can be surprisingly cold, so bring a warm layer and waterproofs. The best months are the dry seasons from June to August and December to February.

Kisoro has petrol stations, shops, banks and a good selection of simple restaurants, and it is the last proper stop before the national park. Local food includes potatoes, beans, matoke and grilled meat, along with strong sweet tea. The volcanoes are the real pleasure, and a clear morning, when they stand sharp against the sky, can make the whole journey feel worthwhile.

If you are heading to the park or the border, make sure you have your documents ready, and give yourself time, because the area runs at its own pace.
t.vacherie@30.0,-90.7:
Vacherie is a small community on the west bank of the Mississippi, and it is a village of cows and plantations, as the name suggests: vacherie is the old French word for a cattle farm. This reach of the river is where Louisiana's sugar-planting history survives in its most concentrated form, and within a few kilometres you can visit three large plantations that each tell a different part of the story.

The most photographed is Oak Alley, famous for its avenue of twenty-eight live oaks that run from the house to the river, planted long before the mansion was built. The oaks are enormous, their branches meeting overhead in a tunnel of shade, and the white-columned house at the end of the avenue is one of the best-known images in the American South. Nearby, Laura Plantation tells the story of a Creole family, with a focus on the women who ran it and the enslaved people who worked it, and its colourful buildings reflect French and Caribbean influences. Whitney Plantation is different: it is a museum devoted to the experience of slavery, with memorials, restored buildings and the names of those who were enslaved on the estate. It opened in the 2010s and has become a major site for historical understanding.

The region is also the heart of Louisiana's Creole and Cajun culture, and the local food is excellent. Gumbo, jambalaya, boudin and andouille sausage appear on local menus, and the sugar cane harvest in autumn fills the air with a sweet, smoky smell from the mills. The land is flat and green, the sky wide, the river hidden behind its levee, and the pace slow.

The ride on the River Road is easy, with long straight stretches, low speed limits through small communities and light traffic, though sugar trucks are heavy in harvest season. The surface is generally decent, but gravel and mud may collect at the verge. Summer is hot and humid, with thunderstorms, and the pleasant months run from late autumn to spring. Watch for the occasional ferry crossing and railway line.

Fuel is available in Lutcher, a few kilometres away, and in larger places such as Gramercy and Chackbay, so fill the tank and bring water. Small cafés near the plantations serve lunch, and a stop under the oaks with a cold drink is a fine way to pass the afternoon.
t.donaldsonville@30.1,-91.0:
Donaldsonville sits where Bayou Lafourche meets the Mississippi, and that confluence has shaped its fortunes ever since the French and Spanish colonial period. It is one of the oldest towns on the river, laid out in the early nineteenth century by a man named Donaldson, and for a short time, in 1830 and 1831, it served as the capital of Louisiana. Today it is a quiet town of about eight thousand people with a historic district of wooden and brick buildings, iron balconies and live oaks, and a slightly faded, thoughtful atmosphere.

The town stands on the edge of Cajun country, where the Mississippi plantation world meets the bayou communities to the south, and you can feel the shift in the music, the food and the accents. Bayou Lafourche, which once carried a share of the Mississippi's water south to the Gulf, still runs through the town, lined with houses, and old steamboat landings and wharves recall the days when the river was the main highway. A fort stood here during the Civil War, and the town saw fighting in 1863. The levee, as everywhere on this road, hides the Mississippi from view until you climb up, and then it appears suddenly, huge and brown and slow.

The riding is easy and slow-paced. The River Road along the levee is flat and mostly smooth, with long straight runs, low speed limits through settlements and little traffic outside harvest time, when sugar cane trucks roll through. A bridge crosses the river nearby, and ferries operate in places. Heat and humidity are heavy from May to September, with sudden storms, and the cooler months are much more pleasant. Watch for loose gravel on the shoulders and for slow farm machinery.

Donaldsonville is a good place for a proper stop. It has petrol stations, groceries, small restaurants and cafés, and some local places serve classic Louisiana dishes such as gumbo, red beans and rice, fried catfish and smothered pork chops. Boudin, a spicy sausage of rice and pork, is sold in shops and eaten with crackers, and you will find it everywhere.

Take a stroll in the historic quarter, where the buildings and gardens have a calm that comes with age. The best time is late afternoon, when the light is low and gold.
t.zakros@35.1,26.3:
The far east of Crete runs out of road at Zakros, and that is exactly its charm. The village sits on the very edge of the island, below the Sitia mountains, and the way here from Sitia, about nineteen kilometres, leaves the tourist belt behind and climbs through olive terraces and rocky hills that smell of thyme and dust.

For a rider, this corner of Crete has the best sort of roads: not a motorway, not a goat track, but a quiet ribbon with enough bends to keep you busy and enough views to make you slow down. Beyond Palekastro, the landscape opens into dry hillsides, small chapels, and the odd view of a bright blue sea. The surface is mostly decent, though gravel in corners and the occasional goat are part of the deal. Wind can be strong on the eastern ridges, particularly in the meltemi months of July and August, and the sun is hard; April, May and October are the sweet spots.

Zakros is famous for its Minoan palace, one of the four great palatial centres of Bronze Age Crete, lying a short way down a gorge towards a small shingle bay. It was a trading port facing Egypt and the Levant, and when it was excavated in the 1960s it still held a wealth of untouched objects, including that rock-crystal vessel which now stands in the museum at Heraklion. Above the palace runs the Gorge of the Dead, called that for the Minoan burial caves in its walls, and you can walk it down to the sea if you have the shoes and the patience. The village itself is little more than a handful of tavernas under plane trees, shaded places where you can sit with a plate of grilled fish or lamb and a small carafe of local wine.

For practical purposes, remember that the nearest real fuel is in Sitia, a harbour town of nearly nine thousand people, so top up there before you come. Palekastro, closer, is a village with limited services, and nothing should be assumed after dark. Bring cash, a bottle of water, and a bit of time. The reward is being at the end of Europe's southern frontier, with the hills behind you and the Libyan Sea in front.
t.izmir@38.4,27.1:
Izmir is where Turkey faces west. It sprawls around a deep bay on the Aegean, with hills behind it and a seafront promenade, the Kordon, along which people stroll, eat and argue until late. The city is ancient Smyrna, claimed by Homer's admirers as his birthplace, and it carries a layered, cosmopolitan past of Greek, Ottoman, Levantine and Jewish communities that still shows in the old bazaar quarter of Kemeraltı.

As a starting point for a ride, Izmir is both generous and demanding. Generous because within an hour you are out of the metropolis and among vineyards, olive groves and the cotton plains of the Gediz and Küçük Menderes valleys. Demanding because the first twenty minutes involve a very large city with fast, assertive traffic, sudden lane changes, scooters and taxis, so it pays to leave early on a weekend morning, when the ring roads are quiet. Summer is hot, with an afternoon sea breeze called the imbat that cools the coast. Spring and autumn are better for the legs and the helmet.

The old agora of Smyrna sits on the hillside above the bazaar and is worth a quiet half hour, with its vaulted arcades and Roman columns. Kadifekale, the hill fortress, has a view that explains why a city was founded here at all, over the harbour and the whole bay. Food is a pleasure. Look for boyoz, the flaky pastry of Sephardic origin eaten with a boiled egg and strong tea at breakfast, and for kumru, a toasted sandwich eaten on the seafront. Figs, fresh fish and salty cheese show up everywhere.

There is no shortage of anything practical in a city of two and a half million people. Fuel stations are everywhere, including on the ring road out towards Çeşme and the Manisa highway, and repairs, parts and tyres are easy to find. Parking in the centre is trickier, so look for an enclosed car park near the waterfront and leave your gear in a secure place. If you need to rest, the park around the Alsancak district is full of tea gardens, and the evening light across the bay, when the ferries slide past, is what the day was built for.
t.viljandi@58.4,25.6:
Viljandi is built around a lake and a castle, and it makes a pleasant job of both. The town sits on steep slopes above Lake Viljandi, a long narrow lake that fills a glacial valley, and the ruins of the Order castle, built by the Livonian Order in the thirteenth century, stand on the hill above it. A footbridge, a graceful suspension bridge built to look like the one that once stood here, crosses the valley between the castle hills, and from it you can see the old town, the lake and the church spire in one view. With about twenty thousand people, it is a university town of sorts, home to a well-known academy for traditional culture.

The town is the centre of Estonian folk music, and every July it hosts a folk festival that draws crowds from across the country, with concerts on the castle hill and in the streets. Viljandi was a Hanseatic town in the Middle Ages, and the old ruins, fragments of red-brick walls and defensive towers, are scattered through the park. The old water tower, the lakeside promenade and the wooden houses on the slopes add to a feeling of calm and creativity. Local food runs to pork, potatoes, rye bread, dark beer and sweet dishes with berries.

Riding in the area is easy and pleasant. The roads wind between wooded hills, farmland and small lakes, with a good surface on the main routes and gravel on the lesser ones. The corners are gentle, and there are many fine views from the high ridges, though the landscape is never dramatic. Traffic is light, and in summer the long days give you generous time to ride into the evening. Wildlife, especially elk, roe deer and foxes, can appear on the road at dusk, so keep your speed sensible after the sun begins to drop.

Fuel is plentiful in Viljandi, with several stations and supermarkets, and you will find cafes with good cakes and coffee in the centre. Smaller places like Viiratsi have limited services, and Suure-Jaani, about twenty kilometres away, is smaller still, so fill up in town. The smell of the place after rain is a mix of birch, wet grass and woodsmoke. Take a slow walk over the suspension bridge and look back at the town; it is well worth the ten minutes.
t.dorpat tartu observatory@58.4,26.7:
The old observatory in Tartu sits on Toome Hill, a leafy mound in the middle of the town beside the river Emajõgi, and it was once one of the most important scientific instruments in the world. The university was founded in 1632 by the Swedish king Gustavus Adolphus, and the town was then known by its German name Dorpat. In the early nineteenth century the astronomer Friedrich Georg Wilhelm Struve built the observatory here, equipped with a remarkable refractor made by Joseph von Fraunhofer in Munich, which was the best telescope of its day. Struve used it to measure double stars, and he also led a great surveying project that ran a chain of triangulation points from the Arctic Ocean to the Black Sea.

The chain, now known as the Struve Geodetic Arc, was created to measure the size and shape of the Earth, and it was one of the first reliable measurements of that kind. UNESCO listed it in 2005, with points in ten countries, and the observatory is one of the Estonian sites. The neoclassical building, painted in soft yellow, is now a museum, and the grounds around it are a pleasant park with views toward the rooftops and the church towers. The hill also has the ruins of the cathedral, a vast medieval brick shell where the university library was later housed.

Tartu is a lively student city of about a hundred thousand people, and its streets are full of bicycles and cafes in the old wooden houses. Riding in is easy, with a good surface and clear signs, and traffic is moderate. Parking a motorbike near the hill is usually straightforward, but cobbled lanes call for care in rain. The surrounding country is gentle, with fields, birch woods and lakes, and the roads outside the town are quiet and well kept. Be ready for gravel on minor roads in the countryside.

Fuel stations are plentiful on the edges of town, and the centre has a large choice of places to eat, from simple Estonian dishes to student-friendly cafes. The air on the hill smells of lime trees in early summer and fallen leaves in autumn. The stones of the old observatory are a good place to pause: in a small, quiet room beneath its dome, a very big idea about the shape of the planet once began.
t.struve geodetic arc@59.1,26.3:
It sounds like a dry thing, a surveying line, but the Struve Geodetic Arc is one of the great quiet adventures of nineteenth-century science. Between 1816 and 1855 a team led by the astronomer Friedrich Georg Wilhelm Struve laid out a chain of triangles stretching about 2,800 kilometres from Hammerfest in Norway to the Black Sea, measuring the angles between hilltops with tremendous care so that the shape of the Earth could be calculated. In the flat, forested north of Estonia, where hills are rare, the surveyors built stone cairns and wooden towers to serve as sighting points, and some of them survive as marked sites along minor roads.

The ground here belongs to the Pandivere upland, a modest limestone plateau in Lääne-Viru County that rises only a little above the surrounding plain but feels like a country of its own. The soil is thin over limestone, with big fields, patches of woodland and old farmsteads, and springs rise in many places along the edges. Väike-Maarja, the nearest town of any size, has about two thousand people, and Rakke and Tamsalu are small too, which tells you how sparsely populated the region is. Roads are generally empty, a mix of good asphalt and fine gravel, and they connect villages scattered across the plateau.

For a rider, the interest is in solitude and space rather than in drama. The bends are gentle and the gradients mild, but the sense of distance and the openness of the sky are striking. Evening light is superb, long and low, turning the fields to gold. Summer nights are short and pale in this latitude, so an evening ride can last until very late. Watch for elk and deer, especially at dawn and dusk, because collisions are a real hazard on Estonian rural roads, and be ready for dust on gravel in dry weather.

Fuel is the thing to plan for. Väike-Maarja has stations and shops, but outside the towns they are rare, so fill up when you can. Bring water and a snack, since the villages are small and the cafes few. The air smells of cut hay and pine in summer, and of damp earth in autumn. Standing by one of the markers, you feel the quiet satisfaction of a place where careful people once measured a whole continent from one hilltop to the next.
t.woibifer voivere@59.1,26.3:
Võivere is a village in the middle of the Pandivere upland, and it gives its name to one of the old triangulation points of the Struve Arc, which Struve's team knew by the German name Woibifer. Today the spot is quiet, a place of fields, farm buildings and a small marker explaining what happened here two centuries ago. The surrounding landscape is the real subject: an open plateau of limestone and glacial deposits, where the ground is just high enough to see across the plain and where villages are strung along the road at generous intervals.

Pandivere is also a sensitive area for groundwater. The limestone is porous, and rainwater drains straight through it into the aquifer below, which feeds springs and rivers across northern Estonia, so farming here is carefully regulated. You might notice a number of boulders in the fields, erratics dragged here by the ice sheets and left behind when they melted, and some of them are huge. In spring the meadows fill with wood anemones and cowslips, and in summer the cornfields wave in the wind. This part of Estonia is quiet in every sense, and the loudest sound you are likely to hear is a cuckoo.

The roads around Võivere are a mixture of narrow asphalt and gravel, and they are often empty. Riding here is a matter of gentle rhythm, with long views and a lot of sky, and it is best in dry weather, when the gravel is firm. After rain, clay and mud can make the minor lanes slippery, so be cautious. The distances between towns are long, and mobile signal can be patchy in places, so carry a map or an offline route. Elk, hares and roe deer cross the roads at dusk, and the cycle of light in the long northern summer allows a late and unhurried ride.

Väike-Maarja, about nine kilometres away, is the nearest place with a shop, a fuel station and a cafe, and Tamsalu and Rakke have smaller facilities. Fill the tank in town and do not count on finding it in the countryside. Rye bread with smoked fish, sour cream and potatoes is a typical meal in local cafes. The smell of the place is of hay and woodsmoke, and on a calm evening the horizon seems very far away.
t.karischki gireisiai@55.9,25.4:
This stop sits in north-eastern Lithuania, in the Aukštaitija highlands near the town of Rokiškis, about twelve kilometres away, and not far from the Latvian border. The name on the map is a mixture of an old German-era spelling and a local village, and the specific site is hard to pin down, so the useful thing is to describe the country around it, which is quiet, gently rolling and full of lakes and woods.

Rokiškis is the local centre, a town of about sixteen thousand people, known for a manor complex that belonged to the Tyzenhaus and later Przezdziecki families. The manor now houses a museum of regional history and an art collection, and its park is pleasant for an hour. The town is also known for its dairy and cheese, and a visit to a local shop turns up good dairy products. Obeliai, to the south, is small and sits on a lake with a pretty old bridge.

The riding is relaxed. Roads are straight and low-traffic, running between fields of rye, potatoes and flax, and pine and birch woods, past wooden farmhouses and wayside crosses carved by hand, a Lithuanian tradition. Bends are gentle, with the occasional pothole, and storks nest on poles in the villages in summer. Mornings can be foggy over the lakes, and autumn colours are fine. Winter brings snow and ice, so late spring to early autumn is the right season.

Lithuania's border with Latvia is open, with no checks inside the Schengen area, and the roads cross without fuss, so side trips are easy. Rokiškis has fuel stations and a handful of restaurants serving cepelinai, big potato dumplings stuffed with meat, and cold beetroot soup in summer. Smaller villages have little, so fill up in town. Take your time on the back roads, and do not be surprised if you meet a horse cart.
t.daugavpils@55.9,26.5:
Daugavpils is Latvia's second city, standing on the Daugava river in the south-east, closer to Belarus and Lithuania than to Riga. About a hundred thousand people live here, and the mixture is unusual: most are Russian speakers, with Latvians, Poles and Belarusians among them, and Old Believers, followers of a seventeenth-century Russian church tradition, have their own communities in the region of Latgale. The city's temperament is quieter and more provincial than the capital's.

Its landmark is the fortress, a vast nineteenth-century complex of earth ramparts, brick barracks and arched gates built by the Russian Empire to guard against Napoleon's armies, which never reached it, although it served in later wars. Today it houses artists' studios, galleries and the Mark Rothko Art Centre, named for the painter who was born in the city in 1903 and emigrated to the United States as a child. The art centre displays reproductions and hosts exhibitions, and the setting is atmospheric, with long brick corridors.

Streets in the city centre are wide, with trams, wooden houses and Soviet blocks sitting side by side. A river path runs along the Daugava and the area around it has pine woods and a few lakes to the north, with the Daugavas Loki nature park downstream offering views of the river's meanders. Riding here is calm, with straight roads and modest traffic, and routes lead west along the river toward Jekabpils, or north into Latgale's lake district. Winters are long and cold, and ice can linger on the roads into spring.

Services are good. Fuel stations are plentiful, and the city has cafes and restaurants serving Latvian grey peas with bacon, rye bread, smoked fish and Russian dishes such as pelmeni. Beer from local breweries is cheap. Parking for bikes is easy near the fortress, and if you have time, allow a slow afternoon in its galleries and an evening on the river bank. Summers are warm and long, with light until late.
t.lydian tumuli of bin tepe@38.6,28.0:
Bin Tepe means a thousand mounds, and the name is only a mild exaggeration. On a low ridge north of the Gediz river plain, a few kilometres from the shore of Lake Marmara, the kings and nobles of ancient Lydia were buried under hundreds of earth tumuli, some of them enormous. Lydia, with its capital at Sardis, was the kingdom of Croesus, whose name became a byword for wealth, and the first state in the world to mint coins from electrum, the natural gold and silver alloy washed down from the mountains. The mounds date mostly from the seventh to the sixth centuries BC, and they were the funeral monuments of a rich, confident civilisation.

The largest is the tomb of Alyattes, the father of Croesus, which Herodotus described in the fifth century BC, noting its great stone base and the stone markers on top that listed the contributions of tradesmen, craftsmen and, he said, girls who worked as prostitutes, who had paid for the largest share. It is some three hundred and fifty metres across and stands more than sixty metres high, one of the biggest burial mounds in the world, a rounded hill of grass and thorn that you could mistake for natural if it were not so regular. A tunnel dug by looters in the nineteenth century leads to the stone burial chamber, and archaeologists have since explored it. The site, with other mounds spread around, is on the World Heritage list.

The riding is in the Gediz country, a broad fertile plain of cotton, vines, sultanas and tobacco, with low mountains on either side and straight roads with long views. The surface is generally good on the main roads and rougher on farm tracks, and tractors, trucks and farm workers on bicycles share the lanes. Summer is very hot, with the hills pale and dry, and spring has green fields and red poppies. Dust can rise in the heat of the day, and an early start is a sensible idea.

Ahmetli, about eight kilometres away, has fuel and cafes, and Salihli, the bigger town to the east, has services of every kind and is the gateway to the ruins of Sardis, with its huge Temple of Artemis and a restored synagogue and gymnasium. The lake nearby attracts birds, and a picnic on top of the mound at sunset gives a wide view across the plain.
t.pythagoreion of samos@37.7,26.9:
Pythagóreio is a small fishing harbour on the south-east coast of Samos, a Greek island that lies so close to Turkey that the strait between them is barely two kilometres wide at its narrowest. The village sits on the site of the ancient capital, which in the sixth century BC was one of the richest cities of the Aegean under the tyrant Polycrates. He built a great mole to protect the harbour, a temple of Hera that was among the largest of the Greek world, and a water tunnel that astonished the ancient world. The island was also the birthplace of Pythagoras, the philosopher and mathematician, and a statue of him stands on the waterfront.

The tunnel of Eupalinos is the thing to see. About a kilometre long, it was dug through the base of a hill by two teams starting from opposite ends, to carry spring water to the city, and they met in the middle with only a small error in height. The engineer, Eupalinos of Megara, used geometry, and Herodotus counted the tunnel among the three greatest engineering works of the Greeks. Part of it is open to visitors, who bend and shuffle through a narrow passage lit by lamps. A few kilometres west, at the Heraion, a single standing column marks the sanctuary of Hera in a flat marshy plain, among fields of olives and vines.

The riding on Samos is a surprise to people who expect only beaches. The island is mountainous, with Mount Kerkis rising to about 1,430 metres in the west, and the roads climb through pine forest and past terraced vineyards, with views of the sea and Turkish mountains. The local sweet muscat wine is made in the villages on the northern slopes. The surface is generally good, but there are goats on the road, gravel in corners and the occasional blind bend, and in summer the heat is strong, with the meltemi wind blowing from the north.

Pythagóreio is small, so you will find cafes and tavernas on the harbour, but for full services and a choice of fuel stations the larger towns of Vathy and Karlovasi are the places. Fill up before heading into the mountains. Grilled fish by the harbour in the evening, with a carafe of local white, makes a good end.
t.bodrum@37.0,27.4:
Bodrum sits on a peninsula on the south-west coast of Turkey, facing the Greek island of Kos across a short stretch of blue water, and its history is longer than its reputation as a holiday town suggests. In the ancient world it was Halicarnassus, a city of Caria, and the birthplace of Herodotus, who has been called the father of history. In the fourth century BC the local ruler Mausolus began a huge tomb for himself, finished after his death by his wife and sister Artemisia, and the structure became one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. The word mausoleum comes from his name. Earthquakes toppled it, and the Knights of Saint John, who took the site in the fifteenth century, used its stones to build the castle that now dominates the harbour.

The Castle of Saint Peter, begun in 1402, stands on a rocky promontory between two bays, with towers named after the nations of the Knights, and it holds an excellent museum of underwater archaeology, with wrecks of Bronze Age and Byzantine ships recovered from the sea floor. The town below is white and low, with bougainvillea over the walls, a lively marina and a long strip of bars and restaurants that stay open late in summer. Fishermen still mend their nets at the quay in the morning.

The peninsula around has good riding if you avoid the weekend crush. Roads wind up and down between bays, through pine hills and groves of olive and tangerine, with views of the sea and islands around every other corner. The surface is generally good, with some patched sections, and in summer the traffic is dense, with minibuses, taxis and hire scooters on the roads. The meltemi wind can blow hard in July and August, and the rock and pine hills look beautiful in the evening light. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with warm sea and uncrowded roads.

Bodrum has fuel, repairs and every kind of shop, and the small resorts of Yalıkavak and Turgutreis, about fifteen kilometres away, also have supplies. Fresh fish, mezes and a glass of raki on the harbour, as the castle lights come on, is a good evening. Parking near the harbour is difficult in summer, so ask your hotel.
t.monastery of nea moni of chios@38.4,26.1:
Nea Moni sits in a fold of the pine-covered mountains above Chios town, on the Greek island of Chios in the eastern Aegean, and it is among the finest surviving Byzantine monasteries. The tradition says that in the eleventh century three monks found an icon of the Virgin hanging in a myrtle bush and had a vision, and that they won the support of the emperor Constantine IX Monomachos, who paid for the building of a church. Its great treasure is the mosaics, made of glass and gold tesserae by craftsmen from Constantinople, which show scenes from the life of Christ against shimmering gold backgrounds. Together with the mosaics of Daphni and Hosios Loukas, they are the most important of their period in Greece, and the monastery is a World Heritage site.

The history of the place has darker passages. In 1822, during the Greek War of Independence, Ottoman troops landed on Chios and massacred much of the population, and many people had sought refuge in the monastery, which was burned. The skulls of the victims are kept in a small ossuary in the grounds, and the event was the subject of a painting by Delacroix. Then in 1881 a violent earthquake damaged the church and the dome, and the building was patiently restored in the twentieth century. The mosaics, though patchy, are still a splendid sight, and the light inside the church changes with the hour.

The road up from Chios town winds through scrubby hills and pine forest, with fine views over the sea, and is a pleasant ride at an easy pace. The surface is mostly good, with tight bends and the occasional goat. In summer the heat is strong, and the mountain air is cooler, and it is wise to stay with the road and not push the speed. The island is also famous for the mastic tree, a small shrub from which a resin is harvested in the south, and the medieval villages of Pyrgi, with walls decorated in black-and-white geometric patterns, and Mesta are worth a visit.

Vrontados and Chios town, about six kilometres away, have fuel, tavernas and shops, and the monastery has no services, so fill up and carry water. Dress modestly, with covered shoulders and knees, and check opening hours.
t.bairnsdale@-37.8,147.6:
Bairnsdale is the gateway to East Gippsland, a handy market town of about eight thousand people on the Mitchell River flats, and it marks one end of the Great Alpine Road. That road climbs about three hundred kilometres from here to Wangaratta, crossing the Victorian Alps by way of Omeo and Mount Hotham, and in places it is spectacular. At Bairnsdale itself, the scenery is flat and the pace relaxed, so it makes sense as a place to refuel and rest before or after the mountains.

One thing to see is St Mary's Catholic Church, which holds a remarkable set of murals painted in the 1930s by Francesco Floreani, an Italian-born artist who had settled in Australia, and the paintings have given the church a reputation far out of proportion to the size of the town. The surrounding district is dairy and farming country, and further south lie the Gippsland Lakes, a huge system of coastal lagoons with fishing villages such as Paynesville, where a small ferry runs across to Raymond Island, known for its koalas.

The riding in the mountains is the point. After Omeo, the Great Alpine Road crosses the high country with long climbs, hairpins and wide views, reaching about 1,850 metres at Hotham Heights, one of the highest sealed roads in Australia. Surfaces are generally good but frost, ice and sudden fog can appear any time of year, and in winter snow chains must be carried on the upper sections. Wildlife, from wombats to wallabies, wanders across the road at dusk. Take care on the descent toward Bright, where the road is tight and steep.

Fuel is available in Bairnsdale at several stations, and the road has gaps, so plan on filling in Omeo, Hotham or Harrietville. Cafes and bakeries in Bairnsdale are generous and cheap, and many riders stop here for a hearty breakfast before heading into the hills.

Late spring is a beautiful time, with wildflowers in the high plains and a fresh green on the lower slopes. In autumn the poplars and oaks around Bright turn gold, and the days are mild and settled.
t.new orleans@30.0,-90.1:
New Orleans exists because of a bend. The French founded the city in 1718 on a crescent of high ground in the Mississippi River, a spot that gave them a portage to Lake Pontchartrain and control of the great river's mouth, and the bend still shapes everything, from street names to the way people give directions by river and lake rather than by compass. The city is mostly below sea level, kept dry by levees and pumps, and after Hurricane Katrina in 2005 the whole country learned how fragile that arrangement can be. People here talk about it plainly and carry on.

The French Quarter, on the high ground, has survived with much of its Creole architecture intact, the iron balconies and courtyards actually dating mostly from the Spanish period after fires in the late eighteenth century destroyed the original wooden town. Louisiana passed to the United States in 1803, and the mix of French, Spanish, African, Caribbean and American influences produced a culture unlike anywhere else on the continent. Jazz was born in these streets, brass bands still march in funerals and celebrations, and you can hear live music most nights on Frenchmen Street without a cover.

The food is serious. Beignets and chicory coffee at Café du Monde are almost a ritual, though the queue can be long, and gumbo, jambalaya, red beans on Mondays, po' boys and oysters are everywhere. Take your time with at least one proper sit-down meal, because lunch here is an event.

As a place to ride, New Orleans is flat, hot, humid and rather chaotic, with potholes that could swallow a front wheel, so city streets demand attention. Beyond the city, the River Road follows the levee upriver past old sugar plantations, oil refineries, small towns and big skies, a strange and moving ride that holds both beauty and a painful history, since the plantations were built on enslaved labour. Some of the houses are museums that now tell that story more honestly than they once did.

Fuel and food are no problem within the city and the suburbs. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, while summer is steamy, with thunderstorms most afternoons, and hurricane season runs from June to November. Carnival, ending on Mardi Gras, fills the streets with parades and crowds, so book ahead and expect closures.
t.talihina@34.8,-95.0:
Talihina is a very small town in the Ouachita Mountains of southeastern Oklahoma, with just over a thousand people, and it is the western gate of one of the best ridge roads in the middle of the country. The name comes from the Choctaw language, and is often translated as iron road, a reference to the railroad that arrived here in the 1880s. This is Choctaw Nation land, and the tribe's presence is visible in the town signs, the language and the cultural centres. The Choctaw were forced here from Mississippi on the Trail of Tears in the 1830s, a history that gives the landscape a sombre depth.

The Ouachitas are unusual among American mountains because their ridges run east to west, instead of north to south like the Appalachians, a result of ancient folding when continents collided. The long parallel ridges are covered in shortleaf pine, oak and hickory, and valleys between them are wooded and quiet. The Talimena Scenic Drive, whose name joins Talihina and Mena, climbs onto the crest of Winding Stair Mountain and Rich Mountain and follows it for about eighty-seven kilometres into Arkansas.

The road is a national scenic byway and was built in the 1960s as a showcase for the region's forests. It is a gently curving road with a low speed limit, and it has no real challenges apart from weather and wildlife. The views are long, over forested valleys that roll out to the horizon, and pull-offs along the way let you stop and look. In October and early November the hardwoods turn crimson, orange and gold, and the road fills with visitors, so mid-week is best.

Fuel is in Talihina, but it is wise to fill up and to check what is open, since towns here are small and shops close early. The nearest bigger towns are some distance away, and services on the ridge are essentially nil, so bring water and snacks. Mobile signals are patchy in the hollows.

Weather changes quickly on the ridge, with fog in the mornings and thunderstorms in summer, and ice in winter can close the road. Spring brings dogwood and redbud, which light the hillsides in white and pink. Watch for deer and for the occasional loose dog or cattle near the edge of the road.
t.mena@34.6,-94.2:
Mena is a small Arkansas town at the foot of the Ouachita Mountains, near the Oklahoma border, with a little over five thousand people and an old railroad main street. The story goes that Dutch investors who backed the railway named the town after the wife of one of their number, and the Dutch connection has stuck, so that the state park on the mountain above is named for Queen Wilhelmina of the Netherlands.

Queen Wilhelmina State Park sits on top of Rich Mountain, at one of the highest points in the range, reached by the Talimena Scenic Drive. The lodge there, built in the style of a mountain retreat with a tower, has a restaurant and a view over the forested ridges. It was originally built in the 1890s by the railroad hoping to attract tourists to a mountain resort, and later rebuilt. A narrow-gauge train for children runs in the park in the warmer months.

For riders, the Talimena Scenic Drive starts just outside the town and climbs onto Rich Mountain through a series of bends, a road that runs for about eighty-seven kilometres along the crest to Talihina in Oklahoma. It is a road for a slow, easy rhythm, with curves that follow the contours of the ridge and views over forested hills to the north and south. In autumn, when sweetgum, maple and hickory turn bright red and gold, it is among the most visited roads in the region, and the best light comes in the late afternoon.

Mena has fuel, groceries and a handful of diners and family restaurants, and the sort of friendly main street where strangers get a nod. The nearest larger towns are some distance away, so it makes sense to stock up before heading up the mountain, as services on the ridge are limited. Mobile signal fades in the valleys.

The best seasons are spring and autumn. Summer brings heat, humidity and thunderstorms, and winter can bring ice, with the upper road sometimes closed. Deer are common, so ride carefully near dusk. The night sky on the mountain is very dark, and on a clear evening the stars are impressive.
t.hot springs@34.5,-93.1:
Hot Springs is the only city in America with a national park running down its main street. The springs are the reason: forty-seven of them rise at the foot of Hot Springs Mountain, carrying rainwater that fell thousands of years ago and heated deep underground. Congress set the area aside for federal protection in 1832, decades before Yellowstone, and the elegant bathhouses along Central Avenue, known as Bathhouse Row, were built in the early twentieth century when visitors came from across the country to soak away their ailments.

You can still fill a bottle for free from public jug fountains around town, and the water is hot, clean and slightly mineral. The town also has a long reputation for gambling, gangsters and horse racing. Oaklawn Park, a short ride north, remains a major track, and Hot Springs was a pit stop for a number of famous mobsters in the 1930s. Bill Clinton grew up here, and the town has a certain faded grandeur that makes it worth a slow walk.

For a rider, the start of Highway 7 is a major draw. The road leaves downtown and climbs into the Ouachita Mountains, one of the few ranges in America that run east-west, with long ridges covered in shortleaf pine and oak. Within minutes you are on bends that tighten and ease around hollows, passing quiet lakes and the occasional roadside produce stand. Lake Hamilton and Lake Ouachita spread out to the south and west, and the road goes through Ouachita National Forest in places where there is little but trees on both sides.

Practical life is easy here. The town has fuel stations, plenty of diners and a good supply of motels, and on a weekend you may need to book ahead, especially during the racing season in spring and during the autumn colors. Mornings are cooler and calmer. Summer afternoons are hot and heavy, with thunderstorms that can drop a lot of water quickly.

If you have time before leaving, walk up the hillside behind Bathhouse Row. The paths wind through old forest and finish at an observation tower with a broad view over the valley and the Ouachitas beyond.
t.lake charles@30.2,-93.2:
Lake Charles is the gateway to the Creole Nature Trail, an All-American Road that loops south from the city across the marshes of southwest Louisiana to the Gulf. It is a flat, low, watery place where the horizon is mostly sky and the road often runs on a raised bank between bayou and rice field. This is Cajun country, and you notice it first in the language on the radio and the boudin sold at gas stations, a rice-and-pork sausage that locals eat on the way to work and consider a proper breakfast.

The city itself has about seventy thousand people and a history tied to timber, rice and later to petrochemicals along the Calcasieu Ship Channel. Its lakefront is pleasant at sunset, and the casinos on the edge of town draw a large share of visitors from Texas, a short drive west. Hurricanes have shaped the recent story. Laura in 2020 and Delta soon after damaged a huge number of buildings, and recovery has been slow in places. The old downtown has some fine architecture, and the Mardi Gras here is a big local tradition, with a rural version called the Courir de Mardi Gras in nearby villages.

For riders, the appeal is wide open scenery rather than twisty roads. South of town, Highway 27 crosses the Calcasieu and runs through marsh to Cameron, with views of egrets, white pelicans and herons, and the occasional alligator sunning on a bank. This is among the best birding in North America, particularly in winter and during spring migration. The Sabine National Wildlife Refuge has a boardwalk across the marsh that is worth the stop. Afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer, and mosquitoes can be fierce, so bring repellent and rain gear.

Wind is a real factor, especially near the coast where there is nothing to break it, and the roads can be slick after rain. Stations are plentiful in Lake Charles and Westlake, but fuel thins out quickly along the trail itself, so start with a full tank. For lunch, look for a roadside place with crawfish, gumbo or a plate of shrimp and rice, and plan for the heat.

Fall and spring are the best seasons, when the air is dry enough to enjoy and the birds are moving.
t.pskov@57.8,28.3:
Pskov is one of the oldest cities in Russia, first mentioned in the chronicles in 903, and it has the look of a fortress town that has seen many sieges. It stands at the meeting of two rivers, the Velikaya and the Pskova, and the stone kremlin, known as the Krom, rises on the point between them, with the white walls and tall belfry of the Trinity Cathedral inside. The city lies close to the borders of Estonia and Latvia, and for centuries it was Russia's western gate, attacked by Livonian knights, Lithuanians, Poles and Swedes.

Its history is distinctive. For much of the Middle Ages Pskov was a republic, governed by an assembly called the veche and allied to Novgorod, until Moscow annexed it in 1510. The city's architecture, with its massive walls, small, thick-walled churches and distinctive cut-stone detail, is quite unlike that of Moscow, and the icon painters of the Pskov school developed a style of their own. In 1581, a Polish army under Stefan Batory besieged the city for months and failed to take it, a defense that is remembered with pride. Much of the old town was damaged in the Second World War, and it has been carefully restored.

Beyond the city is a landscape of low hills, lakes and meadows. Lake Peipus, to the west, was the scene of the Battle on the Ice in 1242, in which Alexander Nevsky defeated the Teutonic Knights, and the Pskov-Pechory Monastery, near the Estonian border, is one of the most beautiful and best-preserved in Russia, with a cave church cut into a sandy hill. Izborsk, with its ancient fortress, lies on the way. The road to these places is a pleasure, a gentle, quiet route through farmland and birch woods, with long views and little traffic.

The practical side is easy. Pskov has about two hundred thousand people, fuel stations and plenty of cafes, and it is a good base for exploring the area. The border with Estonia and Latvia is close, and the border zone has its own rules, so check what is required if you plan to go near it.

Walk along the wall of the Krom in the evening, and the river reflects the light on the white stone. The city is quiet then.
t.jindabyne@-36.4,148.6:
Jindabyne has an odd secret: the town you drive through is not the original one. The old Jindabyne lies underwater beneath Lake Jindabyne, drowned in the 1960s when the Snowy Mountains Scheme dammed the Snowy River, and the whole community was moved uphill to its present spot. On a very dry year when the lake falls, you can sometimes see the old bridge piers. The lake itself is now the town's centrepiece, a big, blue, cold sheet of water backed by the Snowy Mountains and used for trout fishing, sailing and sitting on a bench with a pie.

With a little over six thousand people, Jindabyne is the gateway town for Kosciuszko National Park, and in winter it swells with skiers heading for Thredbo and Perisher. In summer and shoulder seasons it is quieter and much more relaxed, and bikers arrive for the mountain roads. It has the full set of fuel stations, supermarkets and cafés, and it is the last place with any real choice before the Alpine Way, so fill the tank, buy water and a sandwich, and check the weather before you go.

The Alpine Way climbs out of the Thredbo valley, crosses the Great Dividing Range and descends to the upper Murray; it is a serious road with tight bends, steep grades and surfaces that vary from good to patched. The altitudes are not extreme by European standards, but the Australian high country can be cold and wet even in summer. There can be snow and ice from autumn through spring, so check for closures and carry warm layers. A park entry fee applies for vehicles, including motorcycles, so keep some money or a card ready.

The surrounding landscape is something else. Snow gums with their twisted, mottled bark grow on the ridgelines, wildflowers cover the alpine meadows in January, and the air is thin and clean with the sharp scent of eucalypt. Kangaroos often graze near the road at dusk, as do wombats, so watch your speed after sunset. Jindabyne is a pleasant, no-nonsense start: come for the lake, stay for a good meal, and be on the road early.
t.khancoban@-36.2,148.1:
Khancoban is a town built for a purpose and still faintly wearing it. It was created in the 1950s to house the workers of the Snowy Mountains Scheme, the vast hydroelectric project that diverted rivers through the mountains and employed tens of thousands, many of them migrants from Europe. Today it is a small, tidy place on the western side of the range, close to the Murray River and the Khancoban Pondage, with a population of only a few hundred. It has what a rider needs, a pub, a shop, a place to eat and a few beds, but not much more, and the larger town of Corryong lies about twenty kilometres further west over the border in Victoria.

Most people arrive here by the Alpine Way, which is the point. The road descends from the high country in a long run of curves and tightening bends, with a lookout at Scammells Spur that gives a wide view of the Upper Murray valley. The final descent is steep, so use engine braking rather than leaning on your front brake, and watch for gravel in the corners after rain. The surface is generally good, but the road is remote, and in winter the high sections can be icy.

The landscape on this side of the divide is warmer and drier than around Jindabyne, with tall eucalypt forest, grassy flats and the occasional wedge-tailed eagle circling overhead. The Murray, which rises not far to the south, is still small and clear here, and the pondage is a pleasant place to stop and watch the light go golden. Wildlife is plentiful; kangaroos, wallabies and the odd echidna cross the road at dawn and dusk, so take it easy then.

Corryong has a particular literary pull. It is the home of the legend of the Man from Snowy River, and the grave of Jack Riley, the stockman said to have inspired Banjo Paterson's famous poem, lies in the cemetery there. Whether or not the poem was really about him is argued about, but the story gives the town a good reason to stop. If you need fuel, check your range before you leave the Alpine Way, and expect to pay a premium in a remote place.
t.port douglas@-16.5,145.5:
Port Douglas is the northern end of one of Australia's loveliest coast roads, and a town that has gone through at least three lives. It began in the 1870s as a port for the goldfields inland, was nearly abandoned when the railway went to Mossman instead, and then reinvented itself in the 1980s as a laid-back resort town. The population is a little over eight thousand, with a long main street of cafés and bars, a sheltered marina and Four Mile Beach, which is wide, pale and well patrolled by lifesavers. There is fuel, food and every kind of bed, and it is a very easy place to finish a ride.

The Captain Cook Highway that brings you here is the real attraction. It runs north from Cairns along a narrow strip between the Coral Sea and the green wall of the Great Dividing Range, with the rainforest pushing right to the edge of the road in places. The bends are gentle and the surface is good, but the scenery is the thing: little bays, headlands, the blue of the Great Barrier Reef offshore. Weekdays are quieter, and sunrise on this road is a great time to ride, when the sea is flat and the light is rose-coloured.

Just north, the Daintree rainforest begins, among the oldest rainforests on Earth, a place of strangler figs, giant ferns and cassowaries. Mossman Gorge, a short ride inland, has clear, rock-strewn water and walks through the forest. Take care near the water's edge in this region: saltwater crocodiles live in the rivers and estuaries, and the warning signs are not decorative. Swim only on beaches that are signed as safe, and only within the stinger nets in the wet season, roughly from November to May, when box jellyfish are a risk.

Mossman, ten kilometres up, is a sugar town with a working mill, and the cane fields around it are bright green and endlessly flat. Expect road trains of cane trucks in the season, and be wary of sun, heat and humidity, which can make a leather jacket feel like a mistake. The dry season, from May to October, is the comfortable time to ride. Drink water often, and enjoy a cold beer on the waterfront afterwards.
t.utena@55.5,25.6:
Utena is the main town of Aukštaitija, the Highlands of northeastern Lithuania, a region whose name simply means upper land. It is not mountainous, but the landscape rolls in low hills, glacial ridges and long blue lakes left behind by the last ice age, with pine forest, birch and farmland in between. The town has about thirty-three thousand people and sits beside a lake, Alaušas, with a pleasant park and a promenade. It is the place to buy fuel, groceries and a hot meal, with Anykščiai and Molėtai the next towns, each about thirty kilometres away.

Utena's name is known across Lithuania because of its brewery, whose beer is sold in almost every shop and bar in the country. A glass of local lager or a darker brew goes well with a plate of cepelinai, the large potato dumplings stuffed with meat and served with sour cream, or with a bowl of cold pink beetroot soup, šaltibarščiai, which is surprisingly refreshing in summer. This part of the country has a quiet, reserved, rather dry-humoured character, and people tend to be friendly once you talk to them.

The riding here is gentle rather than thrilling. The roads are mostly smooth, narrow and quiet, with long straight runs, soft curves and trees on both sides, and a lake appears every few kilometres. The pace is slow, and the reward is the scenery and the lack of traffic. Watch for tractors, cyclists and the occasional deer at dusk, and be careful on gravel side roads. Mornings can be misty, and in July the northern light stays long into the evening, so you can ride until ten without headlights.

Aukštaitija National Park, the oldest in Lithuania, lies not far to the northeast, a landscape of more than a hundred lakes and ancient forest, with villages of old wooden houses and old beehives carved into tree trunks. Molėtai, to the southwest, has an astronomical observatory that draws visitors to look at the dark sky. For a finish, Utena is calm: park by the lake, order a beer and let the long summer evening do its work. The mosquitoes around the water can be fierce at dusk, so carry repellent.
t.palmse@59.5,26.0:
Palmse is a manor, not a village, and the estate is the reason people come. The Palmse Manor was the seat of the von der Pahlen family, Baltic German nobles who held it from the late seventeenth century until the Estonian land reform of 1919, and the main house, a long, pale baroque building with a red roof, was built in the eighteenth century. The grounds include a park, a pond with a bridge, a distillery now turned into a pub, and a string of outbuildings that give the estate its sense of being a small working world. It stands in the heart of Lahemaa National Park, in northern Estonia, forty or so kilometres from the Gulf of Finland's coast.

Lahemaa, founded in 1971, was the first national park in the Soviet Union, and it protects a mixture of coastal forest, bogs, rivers and fishing villages. Pine and spruce cover most of the land, and the bogs, such as Viru, can be crossed by boardwalks that lead over a landscape of dwarf pines, cranberries and small dark pools. Big granite boulders, left by the ice, lie scattered along the coast and in the forest, among them the Majakivi, one of the largest in Estonia. Elk, brown bears and lynx live here, though you are unlikely to see them.

The roads in the park are quiet and pleasant, with a mix of paved and gravel surfaces, and the pace is gentle. The Coastal Road passes through villages such as Altja, with its fishermen's huts and wooden swings, and Käsmu, a former sea captains' village with a maritime museum. The surface is good, and the views open between the trees, with glimpses of snow-capped peaks in winter and spring. Wildlife is common, and wombats, kangaroos and wallabies graze near the road at dawn and dusk. Drive carefully, as collisions with animals are a real hazard.

Thredbo was developed after the Second World War, when Czech engineer Tony Sponar, a skiing enthusiast, found the site and persuaded the authorities to develop it. The village grew into a major resort and has a reputation for its summer mountain biking and its winter ski season. The 1997 landslide that destroyed two lodges is remembered with a memorial, and visitors may notice the quiet respect with which locals treat the subject.

The town has cafes, restaurants, bars and shops, though many close outside the ski season. Fuel is not reliably available in the village, so fill up in Jindabyne before you go. Carry water, wear sun protection and take it easy on the corners, as the surface can be slippery after rain.

t.baton rouge@30.4,-91.2:
Baton Rouge sits on the first high bluff upriver from the Gulf of Mexico, and the Mississippi bends around it, huge, brown and slow. French explorers noted a red post on the bank marking the boundary between tribal hunting grounds and called the place by that name, red stick, and the city has kept it ever since. Today it is the state capital of Louisiana, a city of over two hundred thousand, with a big university, the oil and chemical industry, and a food culture that rivals New Orleans without the tourist crowds.

The most striking building in town is the state capitol, a thirty-four-storey Art Deco tower finished in 1932 under the governor Huey Long, who wanted something taller and grander than anything in the South. Three years later he was shot in its corridors and died, and he is buried in the gardens in front. The older capitol, a Gothic Revival fantasy with turrets and stained glass, stands near the river and is worth a look in its own right.

For the ride, you are at the end of the River Road, the old route that follows the levee between New Orleans and here. It is flat, with long straight sections and gentle curves, interrupted by oaks draped with Spanish moss, sugar cane fields, and old plantation houses open to visitors. It is also an industrial corridor, with refineries and chemical plants beside the road, so the scenery is a mix of beauty and heavy industry. Traffic can be thick near the cities and trucks are common, and the heat and humidity in summer are considerable. Spring and autumn are far more comfortable.

Everything you need is available, including fuel, repair shops and cash machines, and across the river, the small town of Port Allen offers a quieter alternative. The point of Baton Rouge for a rider is lunch. Look for boudin, the spicy rice and pork sausage, or a bowl of gumbo, red beans and rice, crawfish in season, and a po'boy sandwich stuffed with fried shrimp. In Louisiana, the food is the reason to stop, and the ride is just the excuse.
t.ligatne@57.2,25.0:
Līgatne is a small town on the Gauja river in the heart of Latvia's biggest national park, and it has an unusual double character. On one side is its past as a company town, built around a paper mill that has been making paper here since the early nineteenth century and which gave the town its rows of tidy workers' houses and its handsome old buildings. On the other is its present as a gateway to nature, with forest trails and a nature park where wild animals live in large enclosures and can be seen from walkways. Bears, wolves, lynx and elk, all native to Latvia's forests, can be watched in surroundings that look more like the wild than a zoo.

There is also a surprise under the hills. Near the town stands a Soviet-era bunker, built in secret in the Cold War as a refuge for the Latvian Communist leadership in case of nuclear attack, and now open to visitors on guided tours. It is an eerie place, with long corridors, offices, a bakery and a command room, all preserved as they were when the Soviet Union collapsed. Tours should be booked in advance, and they are a good way to understand what life was like behind the Iron Curtain.

The Gauja valley is a landscape of sandstone cliffs, caves, pine forest and a winding river, and the best way to see it is slowly. A small cable ferry crosses the river here, pulled across by the current, and is a charming reminder of an older way of travel. The valley's cliffs, often covered in graffiti from centuries of visitors, are reached by short walks, and a stretch of the river is popular for canoeing in summer.

The riding is pleasant, with smooth roads through forest and farmland, gentle bends and light traffic. The roads along the valley offer views across the river and the cliffs, and cyclists are common in summer. Elk and deer can cross at dusk, so keep your speed sensible. Autumn is spectacular, when the forest turns red and gold and mist fills the valley in the mornings. Avoid gravel roads after heavy rain, since they can be soft.

For services, Līgatne has a shop, cafes and guesthouses, but the larger town of Sigulda, about fourteen kilometres away, is the main stop for fuel, restaurants and supermarkets. Sigulda also has a castle, a cable car across the valley and a bobsleigh track used in international competitions, and makes a good complement.

Plan to spend a few hours here. The nature park and the bunker are worth the time.
t.near alexandra on the way back@-37.2,145:
Alexandra is a small town on the Goulburn Valley Highway, a few kilometres from the stop, and it sits at the edge of the high country where the farmland of the Goulburn Valley meets the forested foothills of the Great Dividing Range. It was a gold and timber town in the nineteenth century, and the old buildings along the main street still show it. The Avenue of Honour, an avenue of memorial trees planted after the First World War, runs into town, and in autumn the leaves turn a spectacular red and gold, a quietly moving sight.

For a rider, this is a gateway to some good roads. To the east and north lies Lake Eildon, a huge reservoir with arms reaching into the hills, popular for boating, fishing and houseboats, while to the south the Cathedral Range State Park rises in a jagged ridge of rock, visible from the highway. Mansfield, about forty kilometres away, is the gateway to the alpine country, and the road there passes through farmland, forest and small villages.

Alexandra has about two and a half thousand people, with a fuel station, a supermarket, bakeries, pubs and cafes, which makes it a sensible start and finish. If you are staying overnight, a pub meal and a cold beer are a good way to end the day. The roads out of town are generally smooth, with long bends and rolling hills, though you should keep an eye out for kangaroos and wombats at dusk, and take care on narrow bridges.

The best time to ride here is spring or autumn, when the days are mild and the colours are strong. Summer can be hot, and bushfire danger can close roads, while winter brings cold nights and the possibility of snow on the high ground. If you are planning to continue east toward Omeo, fill the tank before leaving, since fuel is limited in the mountains. Take a moment at the river, where the water is clear and the red gums stand tall.
